name: Administrative Professionals Day
description: Administrative Professionals Day falls in late April — April 22 in 2026 and April 21 in 2027, the dates the International Association of Administrative Professionals publishes. IAAP says on its own site that the day was started by IAAP in 1952, which makes it one of the few workplace observances still run by the body that created it. Its instruction to anyone marking it is blunter than most: skip the flowers.
body:
### History

IAAP's account of the founding is short and unambiguous: "this day was started by IAAP in 1952 to provide administrative professionals a collective voice." The association began as the National Secretaries Association, whose first chapter was founded in Topeka, Kansas, and the observance began as National Secretaries Week — IAAP's history page records the "[f]irst National Secretaries Week, now known as Administrative Professionals Week."

What happened after that is documented in sequence but not in dates, and that is worth saying plainly, because this is a holiday whose history is usually told with confident years attached. IAAP's own history page carries no years at all. It records, in order: that convention delegates voted to open membership to men, with the first man joining six weeks later; that members approved a resolution supporting the Equal Rights Amendment; that the National Secretaries Association changed its name to Professional Secretaries International; that Professional Secretaries International became the International Association of Administrative Professionals; and that "Professional Secretaries Week and Day become Administrative Professionals Week and Day." Specific years are widely quoted for each of those steps. None could be confirmed against IAAP or another primary source for this page, so none is asserted here.

The same goes for the fuller founding story that circulates — that a U.S. Secretary of Commerce proclaimed the first National Secretaries Week in June 1952, sponsored by an office-equipment industry group. It is plausible and may well be right. No primary record of it could be found, so it is left out rather than repeated.

### How to observe

Take IAAP at its word and skip the flowers and the mug. The association's own framing of the day is about the profession's standing, not about treats, and a bouquet on a desk is the most easily ignored form of recognition there is.

Pay for a credential instead. IAAP runs the Certified Administrative Professional exam, which is a line on a résumé that outlasts the week; covering the fee and the study time is a concrete thing an employer can do on a specific Wednesday in April.

Or do the unglamorous version: sit down with the person and compare their actual work against their written job description. Administrative roles accumulate responsibility faster than they accumulate titles, and the gap between the two is usually invisible until someone reads both documents side by side. Bureau of Labor Statistics figures give the context — about 3.5 million people held secretarial and administrative-assistant jobs in 2025, at a median of $48,310 a year, and the category is projected to shrink by 2 percent through 2035. A day of recognition in a shrinking occupation is worth more as a pay-and-title conversation than as a gesture.
timeline:
- 1952 — IAAP starts the observance. It begins as National Secretaries Week; the association is then the National Secretaries Association, with its first chapter in Topeka, Kansas.
- Undated, in IAAP's own sequence — The National Secretaries Association becomes Professional Secretaries International; Professional Secretaries International becomes the International Association of Administrative Professionals; Professional Secretaries Week and Day become Administrative Professionals Week and Day. IAAP's history page gives this order without attaching a year to any step.
- 2025 — The Bureau of Labor Statistics counts 3,515,600 jobs in secretaries and administrative assistants, at a median of $48,310, and projects a fall of 75,300 jobs — about 2 percent — by 2035.
- April 22, 2026 — The date IAAP publishes for Administrative Professionals Day 2026, with a members' event from 11:30 a.m. to 12:45 p.m. Central.
- April 21, 2027 — The date IAAP publishes for 2027. Both dates fall on the Wednesday of the last full Sunday-to-Saturday week in April, which is the rule this site uses to project the years ahead.
faq:
When is Administrative Professionals Day?
The date moves each year. IAAP publishes April 22, 2026 and April 21, 2027; both fall on the Wednesday of the last full Sunday-to-Saturday week in April, which is the rule the dates table above uses.

Who started Administrative Professionals Day?
IAAP, the International Association of Administrative Professionals, which says on its own site that it started the day in 1952. The association was called the National Secretaries Association at the time, and the observance was called National Secretaries Week.

Is Administrative Professionals Day a federal holiday?
No. It does not appear on the Office of Personnel Management's list of federal holidays, which is set by statute at 5 U.S.C. 6103. It is an observance, not a day off.

Is it the same thing as Administrative Professionals Week?
IAAP names both. The Week is the successor to National Secretaries Week, and the dates IAAP publishes are for the Day.

What are you supposed to give?
IAAP's own answer is to give something other than a gift: "Skip the flowers and treats." Professional development, a credential fee, or a title and pay review follow from how the association describes the day.

- International Association of Administrative Professionals, About IAAP — https://www.iaap-hq.org/page/about_iaap → "this day was started by IAAP in 1952 to provide administrative professionals a collective voice"; "Skip the flowers and treats"; the published dates April 22, 2026 and April 21, 2027.
- International Association of Administrative Professionals, IAAP History — https://www.iaap-hq.org/page/iaap_history → the National Secretaries Association founded with its first chapter in Topeka, Kansas; "[f]irst National Secretaries Week, now known as Administrative Professionals Week"; membership opened to men, first man joining six weeks later; the Equal Rights Amendment resolution; NSA to Professional Secretaries International; PSI to IAAP; "Professional Secretaries Week and Day become Administrative Professionals Week and Day"; the Certified Administrative Professional exam. The page carries no years, which is why none are given above.
- International Association of Administrative Professionals, Administrative Professionals Day event, April 22, 2026 — https://www.iaap-hq.org/event/apd2026 → the 2026 date and the 11:30 a.m. to 12:45 p.m. Central event time.
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook: Secretaries and Administrative Assistants — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/office-and-administrative-support/secretaries-and-administrative-assistants.htm → 3,515,600 jobs in 2025 (SOC 43-6000); median pay $48,310 in 2025; projected decline of 2 percent, or 75,300 jobs, 2025-35.
- U.S. Office of Personnel Management, Federal Holidays — https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/pay-leave/federal-holidays/ → the statutory list of federal holidays (5 U.S.C. 6103), which does not include this day.

Not used as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate, awarenessdays, greeting-card and gift-retailer pages, and Wikipedia. IAAP's live Administrative Professionals Day page was unreachable during this run, as were archived copies of it, the Truman Library search and congress.gov; the rename years and the 1952 proclamation story are omitted for that reason rather than disputed.

name: April Fools' Day
description: April Fools' Day falls on April 1 and is kept across much of the Western world with no agreed account of where it came from. Asked the origin question directly, a Library of Congress folklorist answered: "The short answer is that nobody knows for sure." The uncertainty is not a modern failing — an almanac verse printed in 1760 already conceded that the people keeping the day could not say why.
body:
### History

The first certain reference comes from a 1561 Flemish poem by Eduard De Dene, in which a nobleman sends his servant on fruitless errands and the servant realizes he is being sent on fool's errands because it is April 1. The first English mention is John Aubrey's, in 1686, recording "Fooles Holy Day": "We observe it on the first of April... And so it is kept in Germany everywhere." The first description of an actual prank is dated April 2, 1698, when Dawk's News-Letter reported that "several persons were sent to the Tower Ditch to see the Lions washed" — the Tower of London's moat.

The familiar origin stories do not survive contact with the sources. The Library of Congress classes the 1582 Gregorian calendar story as a migratory legend, told in variants that cannot all be true at once, and points to evidence that French books were already starting the year on January 1 by 1507, before the change that supposedly caused the custom. The Roman festival Hilaria is rejected in so many words: "there's no hard evidence to connect Hilaria with April Fools' Day." And the story that the day began with the emperor Constantine and a jester named Kugel was itself an April Fools' prank, played on an Associated Press reporter by a Boston University professor in 1983 and later retracted by the wire.

### How to observe

The Library of Congress has done the useful work here. Its research guide April Fools' Day: Topics in Chronicling America picks out a dozen digitized newspaper articles running from 1871 to 1922, free to read. The best is the San Francisco Call of April 1, 1900, which opens with the Poor Robin's verse and then concedes that why people called the day so was already unclear in 1900. The guide gives its search strategy too, so you can run the same query against your own town's papers.

For the day itself, NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day has a long April 1 spoof tradition and signs each one off as a joke; the 2002 entry had Hubble resolving an expiration date for the green cheese moon.
timeline:
- 1561 — The first certain reference to April Fools' Day: a Flemish poem by Eduard De Dene, whose servant realizes he is being sent on fool's errands because it is April 1.
- 1686 — John Aubrey records the day in English for the first time, as "Fooles Holy Day," and notes it is kept in Germany everywhere.
- April 2, 1698 — Dawk's News-Letter prints the first description of an April Fool's errand: "Several persons were sent to the Tower Ditch to see the Lions washed."
- 1760 — Poor Robin's Almanac concedes the origin is already lost: "Nor I nor they themselves do know."
- April 1, 1957 — The BBC broadcasts its Swiss spaghetti harvest report, among the first television April Fools' hoaxes.
- April 1, 1996 — Taco Bell announces it has bought the Liberty Bell; public outcry follows and the company donates $50,000.
faq:
Where did April Fools' Day come from?
Nobody knows. A Library of Congress folklorist put it plainly: "The short answer is that nobody knows for sure." The earliest certain reference is the Flemish poem of 1561, which postdates every proposed origin.

Is it true that April Fools' Day comes from the switch to the Gregorian calendar?
There is no evidence for it. The Library of Congress treats the calendar story as a migratory legend told in versions that contradict one another, and cites a 1904 study showing French books were already beginning the year on January 1 as early as 1507 — before the change supposed to have caused the custom.

Does April Fools' Day appear in Chaucer?
Not reliably. The Nun's Priest's Tale, dated about 1390, contains the line "Syn March bigan, thritty dayes and two," which can be read as April 1. The Library of Congress notes that many scholars think "bigan" is a scribal error and the intended date was May 2, and says the passage "doesn't qualify as hard evidence."

What was the BBC spaghetti harvest?
On April 1, 1957, the BBC broadcast a report showing a family in Ticino, Switzerland harvesting spaghetti from trees. The narration began: "The last two weeks of March are an anxious time for the spaghetti farmer." Viewers called in to ask whether it was true and how to grow such a tree. CBC reports that the BBC considers it one of the first television April Fools' hoaxes.

Has an April Fools' hoax ever had real consequences?
Yes. In 1996 Taco Bell ran a full-page ad claiming it had bought the Liberty Bell and would rename it the Taco Liberty Bell. Angry callers flooded newspapers and the National Park Service, whose spokesperson said, "I believe I started hyperventilating." Taco Bell later donated $50,000. In 1998 two rock radio hosts were fired after telling listeners that the mayor of Boston had died in a car crash.

- Library of Congress, American Folklife Center, April Fools: The Roots of an International Tradition (Stephen Winick) — https://blogs.loc.gov/folklife/2016/03/april-fools/ → "The short answer is that nobody knows for sure"; the 1561 Eduard De Dene poem as the first certain reference and the servant's fool's errands; John Aubrey's 1686 "Fooles Holy Day" and the line that it is kept in Germany everywhere; the 1582 Gregorian calendar account as a migratory legend told in incompatible variants, and Arthur Tilley's 1904 evidence that French books were already beginning the year on January 1 by 1507; the Chaucer line, the scribal-error reading giving May 2, and that it does not qualify as hard evidence; Hilaria rejected for want of hard evidence; the 1760 Poor Robin's Almanac verse; and the Constantine and Kugel origin as a 1983 prank by Boston University professor Joseph Boskin on Associated Press reporter Fred Bayles, later retracted by the wire.
- NPR, April Fools' Day might be the world's longest-running joke. No one knows how it began — https://www.npr.org/2022/04/01/1089947257/april-fools-day-history → that nobody seems to know the day's true origins; the 1561 poem as a clear-cut reference; the Poor Robin's Almanac verse.
- Princeton University, Cotsen Children's Library blog, A Traditional April Fools Joke: Wanna Wash the Lions at the Tower of London? — https://cotsen.blogs.princeton.edu/2024/04/a-traditional-april-fools-joke-wanna-wash-the-lions-at-the-tower-of-london → Dawk's News-Letter of April 2, 1698 and the Tower Ditch lion-washing line as the first description of an April Fool's errand; the Tower Ditch as the Tower of London's moat; Aubrey as the first Englishman to mention the observance.

No source conflict needed resolving on this page. The one disagreement found was over how many newspapers carried the 1996 Taco Bell advertisement — the Philadelphia Inquirer says six, NPR says two — so the page gives no number.

Not claimed, for want of a source: the 1962 Swedish television nylon-stocking color hoax; Burger King's 1998 Left-Handed Whopper, for which no contemporaneous reporting could be found; Italy's pesce d'aprile custom; Iran's Sizdah Bedar as an ancestor of April Fools' Day, since the Associated Press report on that festival mentions neither pranking nor any April Fools connection; Holi as the origin, which the Library of Congress lists among guesses with no firm evidence; the narrator, audience size or number of calls for the 1957 spaghetti film, none of which appear in the sources reached; the volume of calls the Taco Liberty Bell drew; and any figure for the economic cost of April Fools' hoaxes or the rate of corporate participation, for which nothing reputable exists.

Rejected as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate, history.com, the Museum of Hoaxes, and content-farm or AI-generated listicles. Encyclopaedia Britannica's April Fools' Day article was reachable but its body text did not retrieve, and the BBC's own archive pages for the 1957 film could not be reached from this run, so the spaghetti harvest is cited to CBC, NPR and Radio New Zealand rather than to the broadcaster itself.

name: Ash Wednesday
description: Ash Wednesday opens Lent, the forty-day season of prayer, fasting and almsgiving that ends at sundown on Holy Thursday. It is the day Catholics and, increasingly, Protestants receive a mark of ash on the forehead — ash made by burning the palms blessed on the previous year's Palm Sunday. In the United States it is not a holy day of obligation, which makes the size of the crowds it draws one of the more interesting things about it.
body:
### History

Ashes as a sign of repentance are older than the day named for them. At Rome, Christians guilty of grave sin performed public penance through Lent: barred from Communion, dressed in sackcloth, sprinkled with ashes and kept apart until they were reconciled, a discipline Britannica traces back to Tertullian around 200. Public penance died out between roughly the eighth and tenth centuries, and as it went the ashes moved outward from the penitents to everyone. The 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia says the distribution of ashes to all the faithful arose in imitation of the penitents' rite.

The popular version of what happened next is wrong, and the correction is the most useful thing on this page. Nearly every holiday roundup credits the Synod of Benevento in 1091, often Pope Urban II personally, with extending ashes to the whole congregation. The Catholic Encyclopedia, which actually discusses that synod, says the reverse: Benevento describes the distribution of ashes as already generally observed by clerics and laity, and the homilist Ælfric assumed the practice for all classes of people nearly a hundred years earlier. Benevento records the custom; it did not create it.

The Latin name is old too: dies cinerum, "day of ashes," appears in the earliest surviving copies of the Gregorian Sacramentary and probably dates to at least the eighth century. Why the season starts on a Wednesday is less settled than most accounts admit. The Wednesday exists to yield exactly forty fast days once the six Sundays are excluded, but sources place the change anywhere from the late fifth to the seventh century. In Gregory the Great's Rome the fast ran six weeks of six days — thirty-six days, not forty.

### How to observe

For Catholics between 18 and 59 this is one of only two obligatory fast days in the year, the other being Good Friday: one full meal, plus two smaller meals that together do not add up to a full one. Abstinence from meat binds from age 14. Nobody is obliged to attend Mass.

Listen for which formula is said over you, because there are two and they are not the same prayer. "Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return" is the older one, and until 1970 it was the only one in the Roman Rite; "Repent and believe in the Gospel" was added beside it. Episcopalians use only the first.

If you cannot get to a church, look for Ashes to Go, which started on a St. Louis sidewalk in 2007 and had reached at least 49 Episcopal parishes in twelve states by 2012. And if you keep your palms from Palm Sunday, you are holding next year's ashes.
timeline:
- c. 200 — Tertullian attests penitents at Rome in sackcloth, sprinkled with ashes and excluded from Communion through Lent.
- c. 8th century — The name dies cinerum, "day of ashes," appears in the earliest surviving copies of the Gregorian Sacramentary.
- c. 990s — The homilist Ælfric already writes of ashes as applying to all classes of people, a century before the Synod of Benevento.
- 1091 — The Synod of Benevento describes the distribution of ashes to clerics and laity as already general practice, making it a witness to the custom rather than its origin.
- 1549 — The first English Prayer Book replaces the blessing of ashes with the Commination service; the American Prayer Book never adopts it, and only Psalm 51 survives.
- 1992 — The United Methodist Book of Worship adopts the first official Methodist rite using ashes, which remain optional.
faq:
Is Ash Wednesday a holy day of obligation?
No. The U.S. bishops say so in as many words — "not even a Holy Day of Obligation" — which is what makes the crowds remarkable. It still ranks in the top tier of the Roman Rite's liturgical days, just after the Easter Triduum, so nothing else can displace it.

Who has to fast, and what does fasting mean?
Latin Catholics from age 18 to 59: one full meal plus two smaller ones that together do not equal a full meal. Abstinence from meat binds from age 14. Eastern Catholics follow their own church's law.

Where do the ashes come from?
From the previous year's Palm Sunday palms, burned. Catholic, Episcopal and Lutheran practice agree on this, which ties the first day of Lent to Holy Week at the other end.

Why is the date different every year?
It is tied to Easter — 46 days before it, or forty fast days once the six Sundays come out — so it can land anywhere from February 4 to March 11.

Do Orthodox Christians observe Ash Wednesday?
No. They begin Great Lent on Clean Monday, a public holiday in Greece. Their fast historically excluded Saturdays as well as Sundays, so their Lent runs eight weeks rather than six.

name: Autumnal Equinox
description: The autumnal equinox is a moment rather than a day: the instant the center of the Sun crosses the plane of Earth's equator heading south, which begins astronomical autumn in the Northern Hemisphere and spring south of the equator. The U.S. Naval Observatory puts the 2026 equinox at September 23 at 00:05 Universal Time, which is the evening of September 22 across the United States. Its name promises equal day and night, and that is the one thing it does not quite deliver.
body:
### History

The autumnal equinox has no founder and no founding date, because it is not an invented observance. It is an astronomical event: the moment the center of the Sun crosses the plane of Earth's equator. Seasons exist because Earth is tilted 23.5 degrees on its axis, and the equinoxes are the two moments each year when that axis is tilted neither toward the Sun nor away from it. In September the Sun crosses from the northern side of the equatorial plane to the southern, and keeps traveling south until the December solstice. For an observer on the equator the Sun passes directly overhead at noon, and the North and South Poles are lit at the same time, which is true at no other point in the year.

The name is a near miss. "Equinox" comes from the Latin aequus, equal, and nox, night, and day and night are not in fact equal. The Sun is a disk rather than a point of light, and the atmosphere bends its rays so that it appears above the horizon while its true position is still below. Both effects add daylight. On and around the equinox, NOAA's National Weather Service gives the length of day as roughly 12 hours and 6.5 minutes at the equator, 12 hours and 8 minutes at 30 degrees of latitude, and 12 hours and 16 minutes at 60 degrees. NASA is blunter: the split is not precisely equal, and the date on which it comes closest depends on your latitude.

### How to observe

Because the equinox is an instant, the first thing to do is find out when it falls where you are. The Naval Observatory's Astronomical Applications Department publishes the exact Universal Time of every equinox and solstice; apply your own offset from UTC and you have the moment. For 2026 that is 00:05 UT on September 23, which is late evening on September 22 in the United States, and it is why American sources date the equinox to the 22nd while the table says the 23rd. The 2027 equinox is September 23 at 06:02 UT, landing on the 23rd in Eastern time and the 22nd in Pacific.

The better project takes a week. Look up sunrise and sunset for your own location across the days around the equinox and find the date on which they come closest to twelve hours apart. It will not be the equinox, and how far off it is depends on how far you live from the equator.
timeline:
From the Naval Observatory's seasons tables. All times are Universal Time.
- 2026 March 20, 14:46 UT — The March equinox: the Sun crosses the equatorial plane heading north.
- 2026 June 21, 08:24 UT — The June solstice, the Sun at its furthest north.
- 2026 July 6, 17:30 UT — Aphelion, Earth's greatest distance from the Sun for the year — the seasons come from the axial tilt, not from distance.
- 2026 September 23, 00:05 UT — The autumnal equinox: the Sun crosses back over the equatorial plane heading south. The evening of September 22 in U.S. time zones.
- 2026 December 21, 20:50 UT — The December solstice, where the Sun's southward travel ends.
- 2027 September 23, 06:02 UT — The next autumnal equinox, six hours later in the day than this one.
faq:
When is the autumnal equinox in 2026?
September 23 at 00:05 Universal Time, according to the U.S. Naval Observatory. In American time zones that is the evening of September 22 — 5:05 p.m. Pacific Daylight Time, by NASA's reckoning — which is why most U.S. listings give September 22.

Are day and night exactly equal on the equinox?
No. NASA states that the length of day and night on the equinox is not precisely equal. The Sun is a disk rather than a point, and atmospheric refraction lifts its image above the horizon before it has truly risen, so daylight runs a little over twelve hours: about 12 hours and 6.5 minutes at the equator and about 12 hours and 16 minutes at 60 degrees of latitude. The National Weather Service's own glossary says daylight is "everywhere 12 hours" on the equinox, which is the convenient version rather than the measured one.

What does "equinox" mean?
It is Latin: aequus, meaning equal, and nox, meaning night.

Is the autumnal equinox the first day of fall?
It is the start of astronomical autumn in the Northern Hemisphere. The same moment begins spring in the Southern Hemisphere, where the days are getting longer rather than shorter.

Is the equinox always September 22?
No. The Naval Observatory gives September 23 at 00:05 UT for 2026 and September 23 at 06:02 UT for 2027, while the National Weather Service glossary describes the date as approximately September 22. Both are true at once: the moment is fixed; the calendar date depends on your time zone.

- U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department, Earth's Seasons — Equinoxes, Solstices, Perihelion, and Aphelion (2026, Universal Time) — https://aa.usno.navy.mil/calculated/seasons?dst=false&submit=Get+Data&tz=0&tz_label=false&tz_sign=-1&year=2026 → every 2026 figure in the Timeline and the FAQ: March equinox March 20 at 14:46 UT, June solstice June 21 at 08:24 UT, aphelion July 6 at 17:30 UT, autumnal equinox September 23 at 00:05 UT, December solstice December 21 at 20:50 UT.
- U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department, Earth's Seasons (2027, Universal Time) — https://aa.usno.navy.mil/calculated/seasons?dst=false&submit=Get+Data&tz=0&tz_label=false&tz_sign=-1&year=2027 → the 2027 autumnal equinox at September 23, 06:02 UT.
- NASA Science, Embracing the Equinox — https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/skywatching/night-sky-network/embracing-the-equinox/ → the equinox as the moment the center of the Sun crosses the plane of the equator; the September crossing as southward, continuing to the December solstice; that the length of day and night on the equinox is not precisely equal and that the date of the even split depends on latitude; the Sun as a sphere rather than a point light source whose edge is refracted by the atmosphere, adding minutes of light; the Sun directly overhead at noon at the equator; both poles lit simultaneously only at the equinoxes; the Latin derivation of "equinox" as equal night; the 2026 equinox in U.S. local time as September 22 at 5:05 p.m. PDT; the hemispheres reversing at the September equinox.
- NOAA National Weather Service, Tucson, The Astronomical Seasons — https://www.weather.gov/twc/Astronomical_Seasons → Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt as the cause of the seasons; the equinoxes as the two times the axis is tilted neither toward nor away from the Sun; refraction described as bending the light so the Sun appears above the horizon when its actual position is below it; the day-length figures of about 12 hours 6.5 minutes at the equator, 12 hours 8 minutes at 30 degrees and 12 hours 16 minutes at 60 degrees; the Sun directly overhead at noon at the equator; the Latin aequus and nox.
- NOAA National Weather Service, glossary entry for equinox — https://forecast.weather.gov/glossary.php?word=equinox → the September equinox as the start of astronomical autumn in the Northern Hemisphere, with the Sun approaching the Southern Hemisphere; the date given as approximately September 22; and the statement that daylight is "everywhere 12 hours," quoted in the FAQ as the claim the other two sources correct.

Source conflict, resolved and disclosed: the National Weather Service glossary says daylight on the equinox is "everywhere 12 hours." NASA says the split is not precisely equal, and the National Weather Service's own Tucson page gives measured day lengths above twelve hours and explains the refraction that causes it. This page follows NASA and the Tucson page, because they give the physical mechanism and the figures rather than a one-line approximation, and it names the glossary's version rather than quietly dropping it.

Not claimed, for want of a source: the term "equilux"; the common claim that equal day and night falls a few days after the September equinox specifically (NASA says only that it may fall earlier or later, depending on latitude); the range of calendar dates the September equinox can occupy and why it drifts; and that the Sun rises due east and sets due west at the equinox.

Rejected as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate, and content-farm or AI-generated listicles. Encyclopaedia Britannica's article on the autumnal equinox was reachable but its body text did not retrieve, so nothing here is cited to it.

name: Black Friday
description: Black Friday is the Friday after Thanksgiving and the conventional opening of the American Christmas shopping season. The tidy explanation of its name — that it marks the day retailers' books finally turn from red ink to black — is not where the term came from, and Britannica calls that version untrue. The phrase began as a complaint about crowds, in Philadelphia, and was rebranded into a compliment by retailers roughly a quarter of a century later.
body:
### History

The name is far older than the shopping day. Researchers at the Oxford English Dictionary trace "Black Friday" to 1610, when it meant any Friday on which an examination fell. The last of the Black Fridays the OED lists is September 24, 1869, when an attempt by the Wall Street financiers Jay Gould and Jim Fisk to corner the national gold market collapsed after President Ulysses S. Grant intervened, sending the market down and thousands of Americans into bankruptcy.

The Thanksgiving link arrived much later, and not as a shopping term. The OED has found no evidence before 1951 of "Black Friday" referring to the day after Thanksgiving, and in that first instance the sense was markedly different: it described absences from factories following the holiday. The earliest citation in the modern sense — the start of the Christmas shopping season — is from 1961.

In between, the phrase belonged to Philadelphia. In the early 1960s police there used it for the congestion created by suburban shoppers and out-of-town visitors, in some years joined by the crowd for Saturday's Army-Navy football game: traffic jams, accidents, shoplifting, and longer shifts for officers. The term took hold locally, and city merchants tried to swap it for "Big Friday." That did not take.

The rehabilitation came from retailers, not police. The red-to-black account did not spread nationwide until the late 1980s, when merchants began promoting it, describing the day as the point at which stores turned a profit for the year and as the biggest shopping day in the country. Britannica notes that neither held up: most stores in fact saw their largest sales on the Saturday before Christmas.

### How to observe

Treat the advertised discount as a claim rather than a fact. The useful comparison is not the "was" price printed beside the sale price, but what the item actually sold for in the weeks before the sale — which a price-history tool, or your own screenshots from October, will tell you.

If your aim is the lowest price rather than the event itself, the Saturday before Christmas is worth knowing about. Britannica points out that this, not Black Friday, was historically the heaviest sales day for most stores.

For the history, read the Oxford University Press piece on what the OED's evidence actually shows. It is short, and it will leave you skeptical of nearly every Black Friday origin story you encounter, including the confident ones told by large retailers. And if you work in retail or law enforcement, the day is a shift rather than an event — the Philadelphia officers who coined the phrase were not shopping.
timeline:
- 1610 — The earliest evidence researchers at the Oxford English Dictionary have found for "Black Friday," used then for any Friday on which an examination fell.
- September 24, 1869 — Jay Gould and Jim Fisk's attempt to corner the US gold market collapses after President Grant intervenes. This is the last Black Friday the OED lists, and it has nothing to do with Thanksgiving.
- 1951 — The first known use of "Black Friday" for the day after Thanksgiving, describing absences from factories following the holiday rather than shopping.
- 1961 — The earliest citation of "Black Friday" in its current sense, the start of the Christmas shopping season.
- Early 1960s — Philadelphia police use the term for post-Thanksgiving crowds, traffic, accidents and shoplifting. The term takes root locally; merchants' attempt to rename it "Big Friday" fails.
- Late 1980s — Retailers spread the red-to-black profit story nationwide, recasting the day as a positive one.
faq:
Is Black Friday a federal holiday?
No. The 11 legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) include Thanksgiving Day, the fourth Thursday in November, but there is no entry for the day after it. Many employers treat it as a day off regardless, but it has no standing in the federal holiday statute.

Does "Black Friday" refer to retailers going from red ink into the black?
That is the common explanation, and it is not the origin. Britannica states plainly that it is untrue, and dates the red-to-black narrative to the late 1980s, when merchants began promoting it. The phrase was already in use for the day after Thanksgiving decades earlier, and its sense then was negative.

When is Black Friday?
It is the Friday after Thanksgiving, so it moves with Thanksgiving, which federal law sets as the fourth Thursday in November.

Why did Philadelphia police call it Black Friday?
Because of what the day did to the city. Crowds of suburban shoppers and out-of-town visitors, in some years joined by the Army-Navy game crowd, produced traffic jams, accidents, shoplifting and longer shifts for officers.

Was the 1869 gold panic the first Black Friday?
It is often described that way, but the OED's evidence for the phrase goes back further, to 1610. The 1869 crash is the last Black Friday the dictionary lists, and it is unrelated to Thanksgiving or shopping.

- Encyclopaedia Britannica, Why Is It Called Black Friday? — https://www.britannica.com/story/why-is-it-called-black-friday → the red-ink origin stated as untrue; early-1960s Philadelphia police usage; the Army-Navy game in some years; traffic, accidents, shoplifting and longer police shifts; the term taking root locally and the merchants' "Big Friday" attempt; the late-1980s nationwide spread of the red-to-black narrative; the Saturday before Christmas as most stores' largest sales day; Jay Gould, Jim Fisk and President Grant in the 1869 gold panic.
- U.S. Government Publishing Office, United States Code, 2023 Edition, 5 U.S.C. 6103 — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title5/html/USCODE-2023-title5-partIII-subpartE-chap61-subchapI-sec6103.htm → the 11 legal public holidays; Thanksgiving Day as the fourth Thursday in November; no entry for the day after Thanksgiving.

name: Chinese New Year
description: Chinese New Year, also called the Spring Festival, opens the year in the traditional Chinese lunisolar calendar and runs fifteen days, from the reunion dinner on New Year's Eve to the Lantern Festival. Its date moves: the Congressional Research Service puts the start at the second new moon after the winter solstice, which falls between January 21 and February 19. It is not a federal holiday in the United States, though five states have given it official recognition of some kind.
body:
### History

How old the festival is, the sources used for this page do not say, and this page does not guess at a date or a dynasty. What they do document is the calendar, the customs and the American half of the story.

The calendar explains the rest. Months in the traditional calendar begin at the new moon: "Months in the Agricultural Calendar start with a new moon, which occurs when the moon and the Sun move to the same longitude on the ecliptic," says the Hong Kong Observatory, which publishes the official conversion tables. Twelve such months come to about 354 days, more than ten short of the solar year, so a leap month is inserted periodically — seven every nineteen years, on the Metonic cycle. For the new year itself the Congressional Research Service gives the rule: it "starts on the second new moon after the winter solstice." The sources do not agree on this point, and the disagreement is set out below rather than smoothed over.

Years are named on a sixty-year cycle, not a twelve-year one: ten heavenly stems, each tied to one of five elements, pair with twelve earthly branches matching the zodiac animals. The current cycle began in 1984 and ends in 2043, and 2027, by the Observatory's table, is the Ding-wei year of the Goat.

Most of what the season asks of people is about clearing the ground before the year turns: cleaning the house, settling debts and disputes, gathering with family, honoring elders and ancestors, and exchanging gifts of money. The cleaning is done before the new year starts, and knives and scissors are avoided because they can cut your luck. Red envelopes of lucky money, in the Smithsonian's account, come "from a custom where people swapped coins to ward off evil spirits." Dumplings are eaten partly because the shape is said to resemble parcels of money, and a whole fish is shared as a symbol of family unity. The Nian Monster, driven off by red clothing and firecrackers, is given by the Library of Congress as a legend that customs are "believed to be based on" rather than as history.

In the United States the observance is plural and the law is patchy. The CRS states that "the Lunar New Year is not a federal holiday in the United States." California, Colorado and New Jersey have declared it an official holiday by legislation, Washington has recognized it legislatively, and New York recognizes it as a public-school holiday; some cities, San Francisco among them, close schools for the day. The Postal Service began issuing Lunar New Year stamps in 1992. The Library of Congress's photographs of the holiday in America run from Chinatown parades in Washington and San Francisco to Hmong New Year in Chico, California and Lao and Cambodian New Year in Lowell, Massachusetts.

### How to observe

Do the work before the day, not on it. The cleaning, the debts and the disputes are meant to be finished before the new year begins, which is the part most calendars leave out.

Treat the fifteen days as having a shape: a reunion dinner on New Year's Eve, and the Lantern Festival on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month to close it, with tangyuan. In the People's Republic the statutory holiday itself is a week long, and the travel around it, chunyun, is one of the world's largest annual migrations.

And check the local calendar rather than assuming a single date: whether your state recognizes the day, and whether your school district closes, varies from state to state and city to city.
timeline:
- 1984 — The current sixty-year sexagenary cycle begins; it ends in 2043.
- 1992 — The U.S. Postal Service begins issuing special stamps to commemorate the Lunar New Year.
- September 29, 2022 — California enacts AB 2596, declaring the Lunar New Year an official state holiday.
- June 2, 2023 — Colorado enacts HB23-1271; New York follows on September 9, 2023 with S7573, recognizing the day as a public-school holiday.
- January 12, 2024 — New Jersey adopts AJR201; Washington's HB 2209 follows on March 13, 2024.
- January 28, 2025 — The Lunar New Year Day Act, H.R. 794, is introduced in the 119th Congress, alongside H.Res. 75 recognizing the year's observance.
faq:
When is Chinese New Year?
It has no fixed Gregorian date. The Congressional Research Service puts the start at the second new moon after the winter solstice, which falls between January 21 and February 19. The Hong Kong Observatory notes that calculating moon phases decades ahead carries an uncertainty of a few minutes, so a new moon close to midnight can shift a published date by a day.

Is Chinese New Year a federal holiday in the United States?
No. California, Colorado and New Jersey have made it an official holiday by legislation, Washington has recognized it legislatively, New York recognizes it as a public-school holiday, and some cities including San Francisco close schools for the day.

Is it Chinese New Year or Lunar New Year?
Both, depending on who is celebrating. In the United States the season is "often known as 'Chinese New Year,'" the Library of Congress notes, but the same new moon begins the Korean Seollal and the Vietnamese Tết.

How long does it last?
Fifteen days, from the reunion dinner on New Year's Eve to the Lantern Festival on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month. In the People's Republic of China the public holiday itself is one week.

What decides the year's animal?
Ten heavenly stems pair with twelve earthly branches matching the zodiac animals, so the combination repeats every sixty years. The Observatory's table names 2027 the Ding-wei year of the Goat.

Source conflict reported rather than resolved by averaging: how the new year's start is defined. Smithsonian Magazine says the holiday marks "the first full moon of the lunar calendar"; the National Museum of Asian Art says it "begins with the first new moon of a lunar calendar"; the Congressional Research Service says it "starts on the second new moon after the winter solstice." The new-moon accounts are preferred above because they agree with the Hong Kong Observatory's own description of how the calendar is built and with the Lantern Festival falling on the fifteenth day; the full-moon wording is not adopted. The two sources also differ on the Gregorian range, the CRS giving January 21 to February 19 and Smithsonian Magazine January 21 to February 20; the CRS figure is used.

Omitted for want of an acceptable source: the age of the festival, any dynasty or era of origin, and any claim about how far back it runs — none of the sources consulted states one, so none is asserted. Also omitted: spring couplets and niangao, for which no acceptable source was reached, and the Gregorian date of the 2027 festival in prose, which the dates table below carries from the site's rule engine.

Not used as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate, and comparable aggregator and content-farm pages.

name: Christmas Day
description: Christmas Day falls on December 25 and is at once a Christian feast marking the birth of Jesus and the largest secular holiday on the American calendar. Almost nothing about how Americans keep it is as old as it feels: the date was settled by argument rather than record, the tree reached the English-speaking world from Germany by way of the British court, and the Santa Claus on the wrapping paper was assembled over fifty-eight years by a New York poet, a political cartoonist, and an advertising artist.
body:
### History

The date is not a record of anything. No one knows when Jesus was born, and some scholars think early spring more likely. There are at least three competing routes to December 25: Sextus Julius Africanus dated the conception to March 25, which puts a birth nine months later on December 25; Rome already marked the rebirth of the Unconquered Sun, Sol Invictus, on December 25, near the winter solstice and the festival of Saturnalia; and December 25 was also given as the birthday of the deity Mithra. The church in Rome began formally celebrating Christmas on December 25 in 336, under Constantine. The familiar claim that the date was picked to crowd out pagan festivals is speculation, not a documented decision.

The holiday was also, for a time, illegal in New England. In 1659 the Massachusetts Bay Colony enacted a statute its law library still publishes under the heading "Penalty for Keeping Christmas," fining anyone found observing the day five shillings for conduct it called a "great dishonor of God and offence of others."

Legal standing came much later and all at once. Congress first established public holidays in 1870, for the District of Columbia: New Year's Day, Independence Day, Christmas, and Thanksgiving.

The tree is German, and the credit is usually misassigned. Prince Albert is the name attached to it, but the Royal Collection Trust points to Queen Charlotte, George III's consort, who brought the custom to the British court in the late eighteenth century — her tree was a yew, not a fir — from a Germany where decorated evergreens had been customary since the early 1600s. What Victoria and Albert did was popularize it: an 1848 illustration of the family gathered around a decorated tree in the Illustrated London News is what carried the idea into ordinary households. In the United States, Christmas trees were still uncommon until the 1840s.

Santa was assembled in print. "A Visit from St. Nicholas" appeared anonymously in the Troy, New York Sentinel on December 23, 1823. Clement Clarke Moore claimed authorship nearly fifteen years later, saying a friend had submitted it without his knowledge; the family of Henry Livingston Jr. claimed it for him, and because Livingston died before Moore spoke up the question has never been closed — some modern scholars favor Livingston. Moore's Santa is a tiny, soot-covered elf with a pipe who looks like a peddler. The red coat, the workshop, and the North Pole come from Thomas Nast's vignettes in Harper's Weekly, where "Merry Old Santa Claus" appeared on January 1, 1881. Coca-Cola is often said to have invented the red suit; it did not. The company was using Santa in advertising as early as the 1910s, and when it hired Haddon Sundblom in the early 1930s — his first Santa ran in 1931 — red and white were already the figure's colors.

### How to observe

Read the two Santas against each other. The 1823 poem describes a pipe-smoking elf; Nast's "Merry Old Santa Claus" of January 1, 1881 is the figure on this year's wrapping paper. Fifty-eight years separate them, which is a useful thing to know about a character most people assume is ancient.

Check when your Christmas day off actually falls. Federal offices follow 5 U.S.C. 6103, and when December 25 lands on a Saturday the holiday is observed the preceding Friday. That is what happens in 2027: the federal observance is Friday, December 24.

Read the 1659 statute. The Massachusetts law library publishes it, and it is short, strange, and a better corrective to sentimentality about old-fashioned Christmases than anything written since.
timeline:
- 336 — The church in Rome begins formally celebrating Christmas on December 25, under Constantine.
- 1659 — The Massachusetts Bay Colony enacts "Penalty for Keeping Christmas," a five-shilling fine for observing the day.
- 1823 — "A Visit from St. Nicholas" is published anonymously in the Troy Sentinel on December 23.
- 1848 — An illustration of Victoria, Albert, and their children around a decorated tree appears in the Illustrated London News.
- 1870 — Congress establishes the first federal public holidays, Christmas among them, for the District of Columbia.
- 1881 — Thomas Nast's "Merry Old Santa Claus" appears in Harper's Weekly on January 1, fixing the red-coated figure in American print.
faq:
Is Christmas a federal holiday?
Yes. Federal law (5 U.S.C. 6103) lists Christmas Day as a legal public holiday. Congress first made it one in 1870, initially for the District of Columbia.

Is Christmas always on December 25?
The date is fixed; the day off is not. When December 25 falls on a Saturday, federal employees observe the holiday on the preceding Friday — December 24 in 2027. A Sunday Christmas moves the observance to the following Monday.

Was Jesus born on December 25?
No one knows. The date is not recorded, and some scholars think early spring more likely. December 25 has at least three competing explanations, none of them a documented decision.

Did Coca-Cola invent the red-suited Santa?
No. Thomas Nast was drawing a red-coated Santa for Harper's Weekly by January 1881. Coca-Cola used Santa in advertising as early as the 1910s, and Haddon Sundblom's version first ran in 1931, by which point red and white were already associated with the figure.

Did Prince Albert bring the Christmas tree to Britain?
He popularized it rather than introduced it. Queen Charlotte brought the German custom to the British court in the late eighteenth century; the 1848 Illustrated London News engraving of Victoria and Albert's tree is what spread it to ordinary households.

name: Christmas Eve
description: Christmas Eve is December 24, and in much of the English-speaking world it carries more of the holiday's weight than Christmas Day itself: the arrival, the service, the last errand, the night something is supposed to happen. It is not a federal holiday in the United States and never has been — when federal offices close on the 24th, it is because a president signed an order for that year. Most of what Americans actually do on the night can be dated, and it is newer than it feels.
body:
### History

Christmas Day has been a federal holiday since 1870, when Congress declared New Year's Day, Independence Day, Christmas and Thanksgiving holidays in the District of Columbia — the first four. Christmas Eve was not among them and has not been added since; the list of legal public holidays in 5 U.S.C. 6103 now runs to eleven and still does not include December 24. What happens instead is decided year by year. Executive Order 14129, signed December 18, 2024, closed executive departments and agencies on December 24, 2024 and excused federal employees from duty, leaving exceptions to agency heads for national security, defense or other public need. The order never calls the day a holiday, because it is not one.

The American shape of the night — a visitor arriving by chimney while the household sleeps — can be dated too. "A Visit from St. Nicholas," better known by its first line, was published anonymously in the Troy Sentinel, in Troy, New York, in 1823. Clement Clarke Moore is thought to have written it the previous year, is said to have been embarrassed by it, acknowledged authorship publicly in 1838, and published it under his own name in 1844. The attribution has been disputed ever since. Whoever wrote it, its plump, pipe-smoking, white-bearded Santa is the one that stuck.

Several of the night's fixtures are twentieth-century. The Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols, devised by Eric Milner-White, has been sung in King's College Chapel, Cambridge, on Christmas Eve since 1918, and broadcast by the BBC since 1928. In 1955 a child in Colorado Springs saw a promotion in a local newspaper and dialed the unlisted number of the Continental Air Defense Command operations center; Colonel Harry Shoup, the commander on duty, assured the caller that CONAD would see Santa safely from the North Pole. NORAD inherited the tradition when it was formed in 1958. On December 24, 1968, in lunar orbit, the crew of Apollo 8 — Bill Anders, Jim Lovell and Frank Borman — read the first ten verses of Genesis to an audience of roughly half a billion people, Borman closing with "good night, good luck, a merry Christmas, and God bless all of you."

And then the one most often told and least often believed. On the evening of December 24, 1914, British troops on the Western Front heard German soldiers singing carols and saw small fir trees and lanterns along the opposing trenches. On Christmas Day men met in No Man's Land, exchanged gifts, took photographs, buried their dead and in places kicked a football about. It was not universal — fighting and casualties continued elsewhere on the line — and the high commands moved to stop it happening again. The Imperial War Museums note that it was doubted for years afterward, until soldiers' letters printed in British newspapers from early January 1915, and the photographs that followed, settled the question.

### How to observe

Listen to one of the broadcasts the night is built on. King's College Chapel's Nine Lessons and Carols goes out on Christmas Eve afternoon, UK time, and the Apollo 8 Genesis reading is preserved in the National Archives. NORAD's Santa tracker runs on the 24th and is, by NORAD's own account, the long consequence of one wrong number in 1955.

Read the truce in the soldiers' own words. The Imperial War Museums hold the letters and the recorded recollections — including from men who were there and doubted the football match happened at all — which is more interesting than the greeting-card version.

If you work for the federal government, do not assume the 24th off. It is not a holiday; it is an executive order, issued or not, year by year.

Is Christmas Eve a federal holiday?
No. The legal public holidays in 5 U.S.C. 6103 include Christmas Day but not December 24. Federal offices sometimes close on the 24th because the president issues an executive order excusing employees from duty for that year — Executive Order 14129 did it for December 24, 2024 — but it is not a standing holiday, and one year's order says nothing about the next.

Who wrote "'Twas the Night Before Christmas"?
It was published anonymously in the Troy Sentinel in 1823. Clement Clarke Moore acknowledged authorship in 1838 and published it under his own name in 1844, and that attribution has been disputed ever since.

Did the Christmas truce of 1914 really happen?
Yes, though not everywhere. It began on the evening of December 24, 1914 and spread along parts of the Western Front, while fighting and casualties continued elsewhere. Soldiers' letters printed in British newspapers from early January 1915, and photographs, established it. Whether an organized football match took place is still unclear — some of the men who were there doubted it.

How long has NORAD tracked Santa?
Since 1955, when a child who had seen a promotion in a local newspaper dialed the unlisted number of the Continental Air Defense Command operations center in Colorado Springs. Colonel Harry Shoup, the commander on duty, promised the caller that CONAD would get Santa through. NORAD took the tradition over when it was formed in 1958.

What did the Apollo 8 astronauts read on Christmas Eve?
The first ten verses of Genesis, from lunar orbit on December 24, 1968, to an audience of roughly half a billion. Bill Anders began the reading and commander Frank Borman closed the broadcast with "good night, good luck, a merry Christmas, and God bless all of you."

name: Cinco de Mayo
description: Cinco de Mayo marks a single day's fighting: on May 5, 1862, a Mexican army stopped an elite French force at Puebla, a city about 80 miles southeast of Mexico City. It is not Mexican Independence Day, which falls on September 16, and it is observed far more widely in the United States than in Mexico. The American holiday was built in California by Mexican Americans within a year of the battle, and reinvented more than a century later by beer companies.
body:
### History

In 1861, with the country in financial ruin after two years of civil war, President Benito Juárez suspended payment of Mexico's foreign debts to the United Kingdom, Spain and France. All three sent warships to seize payment, landing at Veracruz; Britain and Spain soon settled and withdrew. France, under Napoleon III, meant to conquer the nation and install a pro-French monarchy.

On May 5, 1862, the French column advancing on Mexico City was stopped at Puebla, about 80 miles southeast of the capital. The Library of Congress credits the Texas-born general Ignacio Zaragoza, who, "working with a ragtag army," defeated a stronger force; PBS SoCal puts the French at 6,000 troops. The French fell back to await reinforcements, which took nearly a year, and that delay was the whole of the victory in military terms. Reinforced, they took Puebla on May 17, 1863, then Mexico City, and the government they installed lasted until 1867.

What makes the day American is what happened next in California, where Latinos were strong Union supporters who had helped finance Juárez's army. According to David Hayes-Bautista, director of UCLA's Center for the Study of Latino Health and Culture, the first commemorations were held in Los Angeles and San Francisco in 1863, with parades, speakers and music, and California has held them every year since. Supporters organized into Juntas Patrióticas Mejicanas, which met monthly and sent money to Juárez; there were eventually 129, mostly in California. When Puebla fell the men's juntas lost momentum, and it was Francisca Manso de Cavazos, a Mexican immigrant in Los Angeles, who called a meeting of about 100 women and founded the Junta Patriótica de Señoras Mejicanas de Los Ángeles. The men's groups started up again after the women's did.

The drinking holiday is recent and traceable. Writing for TIME and Zócalo Public Square, José M. Alamillo, professor of Chicano studies at California State University Channel Islands, dates the corporate push to the 1980s, when marketers noticed the growth of the Latino population: "Beer and alcohol companies led the charge by spending millions on marketing the holiday." Corona Extra alone spent $91 million advertising around the day in 2013, according to Kantar Media. Marketplace reported Nielsen figures showing Americans bought more than $600 million worth of beer for Cinco de Mayo in a single year, more than was sold for the Super Bowl or St. Patrick's Day.

### How to observe

Read the day as it was first reported. The Library of Congress's Chronicling America archive holds the papers that carried these celebrations while they were news, including an 1870 wire item that reads, in full: "The Mexicans are celebrating the anniversary of the defeat of the French at Puebla, by salutes, to-day."

Find a celebration with civic roots rather than a drink special. Corona, California has held one since 1923, built around the lemon harvest; a 1939 Los Angeles Times report noted that "all work in the citrus industry was suspended for the Cinco de Mayo holiday." It carries no alcohol sponsorship.

And correct the record out loud: the day commemorates a battle against a French invasion, not Mexican independence, which is September 16.
timeline:
- 1861 — Juárez suspends payment of Mexico's foreign debts; Britain, Spain and France send warships to Veracruz. Britain and Spain settle and withdraw.
- May 5, 1862 — Ignacio Zaragoza's army stops the French advance at Puebla. The French fall back to await reinforcements, which take nearly a year.
- 1863 — The first Cinco de Mayo commemorations in the United States are held in Los Angeles and San Francisco, with parades, speakers and music.
- May 17, 1863 — Reinforced French forces take Puebla; Mexico City follows.
- 1867 — The French-installed government is overthrown.
- 1980s — Corporate marketing, led by beer and alcohol companies, begins turning May 5 into a national drinking occasion.
faq:
Is Cinco de Mayo Mexican Independence Day?
No, and this is the most common error about it. The Library of Congress states it plainly: Cinco de Mayo "is not a celebration of Mexican independence, as is often assumed in the U.S." Mexican Independence Day is September 16.

Is Cinco de Mayo a federal holiday?
No. The 11 legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) do not include it, and federal offices, banks and post offices operate normally.

Where did American Cinco de Mayo celebrations begin?
In California, in 1863, organized by Mexican Americans who backed the Union. The earliest surviving description of such a celebration is a June 7, 1862 report from Columbia, California; the Library of Congress, drawing on its own newspaper holdings, dates the earliest to 1866.

Is Cinco de Mayo celebrated in Mexico?
Barely. The California Latino Legislative Caucus describes the day as "scarcely observed in Mexico" while being widely celebrated in California and across the United States.

Why is the day so tied to beer?
Because of a deliberate campaign. Alamillo dates the corporate push to the 1980s and credits beer and alcohol companies with leading it; Corona Extra's advertising around the holiday came to $91 million in 2013 alone.

name: Columbus Day
description: Columbus Day falls on the second Monday in October and is one of the eleven legal public holidays named in federal law. Its statutory history is much shorter than its popular one: Americans marked October 12 for well over a century before Congress added the day to the federal list in 1968 — in the same act that moved it off October 12 and onto a Monday. Many states and cities now observe Indigenous Peoples' Day instead.
body:
### History

The first recorded Columbus Day celebration in the United States took place on October 12, 1792, organized by the Society of St. Tammany — the Columbian Order — for the 300th anniversary of Columbus's landing. The quadricentennial a century later produced what the Library of Congress calls the first official Columbus Day holiday in the country: Benjamin Harrison's 1892 proclamation "recommending to the people the observance in all their localities of the 400th anniversary."

State recognition came next, and it was campaigned for. The Knights of Columbus, a Roman Catholic fraternal benefit society, lobbied state legislatures to make October 12 a legal holiday; Colorado was first, on April 1, 1907. New York followed in 1909, when Governor Charles Evans Hughes led an October 12 parade of Italian American societies and Knights of Columbus legions.

Federal recognition then arrived in two steps that are often collapsed into one. On April 30, 1934, Congress passed Public Resolution 21 of the 73rd Congress, which — as Franklin D. Roosevelt's Proclamation 2253 of 1937 recites it — "authorized and requested" the President to proclaim October 12 of each year as Columbus Day and to call on officials to display the flag. That created an annual presidential duty, not a day off work, and the duty persists: as modified in 1968 the resolution is codified at 36 U.S.C. 107.

The holiday itself dates from 1968. Public Law 90-363, approved June 28, added "Columbus Day, the second Monday in October" to 5 U.S.C. 6103(a), effective January 1, 1971. Its text carries no short title at all; "Uniform Monday Holiday Act" is a popular name, not a statutory one.

### How to observe

Read the two 2021 proclamations next to each other. On October 8, 2021, President Biden signed Proclamation 10281, naming October 11 Columbus Day, and Proclamation 10283, naming that same day Indigenous Peoples' Day. Neither mentions the other, though the Columbus Day one does acknowledge "the painful history of wrongs and atrocities that many European explorers inflicted" on Tribal Nations and Indigenous communities.

Find out what is actually closed where you live. Section 6103 declares these days legal public holidays without stating whom that binds, and its operative provisions concern the pay and leave of federal employees. Whether your bank, school district or employer observes the day is a local question — and in some states the second Monday in October is a different holiday entirely.

Go to the primary record. The Library of Congress holds one of four known copies of Columbus's Book of Privileges, compiled in 1502 — the documents in which he pressed the Spanish crown to honor what it had promised him.
timeline:
- October 12, 1792 — The first recorded Columbus Day celebration in the United States, organized by the Society of St. Tammany for the 300th anniversary.
- 1892 — Benjamin Harrison proclaims observance of the 400th anniversary — the first official Columbus Day holiday, by the Library of Congress's reckoning.
- April 1, 1907 — Colorado becomes the first state to make October 12 a legal holiday, after lobbying by the Knights of Columbus.
- April 30, 1934 — Public Resolution 21 of the 73rd Congress requests an annual presidential proclamation of October 12 as Columbus Day; as modified in 1968 it is codified at 36 U.S.C. 107.
- June 28, 1968 — Public Law 90-363 adds "Columbus Day, the second Monday in October" to 5 U.S.C. 6103(a), effective January 1, 1971.
- October 8, 2021 — President Biden signs separate proclamations designating October 11, 2021 as Columbus Day and as Indigenous Peoples' Day.
faq:
Is Columbus Day a federal holiday?
Yes. "Columbus Day, the second Monday in October" is one of the eleven legal public holidays listed at 5 U.S.C. 6103(a). It was added by Public Law 90-363, approved June 28, 1968, effective January 1, 1971.

Why is Columbus Day on a Monday instead of October 12?
The 1968 act that put it on the federal list set it on the second Monday rather than a fixed date, as it did for Washington's Birthday, Memorial Day and Veterans Day. Veterans Day returned to November 11 in 1975.

Did Columbus Day become a federal holiday in 1934?
Not in the sense of a day off. The 1934 measure asked the President to proclaim October 12 as Columbus Day each year and to call for the flag to be displayed on Government buildings. Some accounts describe that as making it a national holiday, but the resolution's own text, quoted in the 1937 proclamation issued under it, creates a proclamation duty and nothing more. Legal public holiday status dates from the 1968 act.

Is Columbus Day the same day as Indigenous Peoples' Day?
It is the same date, and in 2021 the President designated the single date October 11 as both. Some states and cities observe Indigenous Peoples' Day in place of Columbus Day: South Dakota's holiday statute lists Native Americans' Day on the second Monday in October and does not list Columbus Day at all.

name: Cyber Monday
description: Cyber Monday is the Monday after Thanksgiving, and unlike most days on this calendar it has a documented birth date and a traceable motive. It was invented in November 2005 by Shop.org, the online-retail arm of the National Retail Federation, to give internet stores their own answer to Black Friday. Shop.org's own executive director conceded at the time that it was not actually the biggest online shopping day of the year.
body:
### History

Cyber Monday began as a name in search of a day. Shop.org, the online-retail division of the National Retail Federation, was looking for a way to promote internet shopping, settled on the Monday after Thanksgiving, and announced it in a press release dated November 21, 2005 that described Cyber Monday as "one of the biggest online shopping days of the year."

The observation underneath the name was real enough. Shop.org's 2005 eHoliday survey, conducted with BizRate Research, found that 77 percent of online retailers said their sales had risen substantially on the Monday after Thanksgiving the previous year. The explanation offered at the time was the office connection: more than a third of the 1,890 consumers surveyed said they would use internet access at work to shop. In 2005, with home broadband far from universal, a workplace connection was often the fastest one a shopper had.

What the name was not, by the account of the people who chose it, was a description of a record. Scott Silverman, Shop.org's executive director, told BusinessWeek that the term came out of a brainstorm, and that alternatives including Black Monday, Blue Monday and Green Monday were discarded along the way. "It's not the biggest day," he said. "But it was an opportunity to create some consumer excitement." The growth around it was not invented, though: comScore Networks expected American online sales for that November and December to rise 24 percent, to more than $19 billion.

That is an unusually honest founding document for a shopping holiday, and it is worth keeping in mind every November, when the day is described as a record that was discovered rather than a label that was applied.

### How to observe

Treat the date as the arbitrary part and the prices as the thing to check. Because Cyber Monday was scheduled rather than discovered, there is no particular reason a given retailer's best online price of the year should land on it; many run the same promotion across the whole weekend, and some run it for a week.

If you want to read the day's own paperwork, both pieces are short. The Shop.org survey finding that prompted the name is quoted in CNN/Money's 2005 report, and Silverman's "It's not the biggest day" remark is in CBS News's coverage from the same week. Reading them is a good inoculation against the annual claim that the day is historically unprecedented.

It is also worth noticing what has quietly expired. The original rationale for the day was that work had faster internet than home. That stopped being true some time ago, and the day has outlived its own reasoning.
timeline:
- 2004 — Online retailers see a substantial sales increase on the Monday after Thanksgiving; 77 percent report as much in the Shop.org/BizRate Research survey conducted the following year.
- November 21, 2005 — Shop.org issues the press release that coins "Cyber Monday," describing it as one of the biggest online shopping days of the year.
- November 28, 2005 — The first Cyber Monday, the Monday after that year's Thanksgiving.
- November 2005 — Scott Silverman, Shop.org's executive director, tells BusinessWeek the name came from a brainstorm and that "It's not the biggest day."
- November-December 2005 — comScore Networks expects US online holiday sales to rise 24 percent, to more than $19 billion.
faq:
Is Cyber Monday a federal holiday?
No. The 11 legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) do not include it, and it has no official standing of any kind. It is a promotional date created by a retail trade group.

Who invented Cyber Monday?
Shop.org, the online-retail division of the National Retail Federation, in November 2005. Contemporaneous reporting credits the organization rather than one person: Shop.org's executive director described the name as the product of a group brainstorm. Accounts naming a single individual as the coiner circulate widely, but no primary source consulted for this page supports one.

When is Cyber Monday?
The Monday after Thanksgiving. Since federal law sets Thanksgiving as the fourth Thursday in November, Cyber Monday falls between November 26 and December 2.

Was Cyber Monday really the biggest online shopping day when it was named?
No, and the people who named it said so at the time. Scott Silverman of Shop.org told BusinessWeek, "It's not the biggest day. But it was an opportunity to create some consumer excitement." The press release's description of it as "one of the biggest online shopping days of the year" rested on a survey in which retailers reported a Monday sales bump the year before.

Why was it tied to Monday rather than the weekend?
The original reasoning was practical. Shoppers returning to work after Thanksgiving had access to faster internet connections there than most had at home, and more than a third of consumers in the 2005 Shop.org survey said they would shop using internet access at work.

But it was an opportunity to create some consumer excitement." CBS is relaying BusinessWeek Online's reporting, which is where the quotes originate.
- CNN/Money, After Black Friday comes Cyber Monday — https://money.cnn.com/2005/11/21/news/economy/cyber_monday/index.htm → Cyber Monday as the Monday after Thanksgiving and "quickly becoming one of the biggest online shopping days of the year"; the Shop.org/BizRate Research 2005 eHoliday survey and its 77 percent figure; more than a third of the 1,890 consumers surveyed planning to shop using internet access at work; Silverman's quote from the report; comScore Networks' expectation of 24 percent growth to more than $19 billion for November-December 2005.
- U.S. Government Publishing Office, United States Code, 2023 Edition, 5 U.S.C. 6103 — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title5/html/USCODE-2023-title5-partIII-subpartE-chap61-subchapI-sec6103.htm → the 11 legal public holidays, which do not include Cyber Monday; Thanksgiving Day as the fourth Thursday in November.

The National Retail Federation's own pages could not be retrieved for this draft, so the 2005 press release is cited as described by CBS News and CNN/Money rather than from the release itself; both date it November 21, 2005. A widely repeated alternative dates the release to November 28, 2005 and names an individual coiner. Neither detail is supported by any source reached here, so neither is asserted. The CNN/Money page displays November 28, 2005 although its address contains November 21; it is cited for the survey figures and the quote, not for the release date. No sales figure after 2005 appears on this page, because none could be traced to a primary record.
