name: Day of the Dead
description: Day of the Dead - Dia de Muertos - is the Mexican observance in which families prepare for the return of their dead: a home altar, the dead person's own favorite dishes, flower petals laid along the route from the cemetery, and time spent at the grave. It runs from the end of October into the first days of November, and in 2008 UNESCO added the indigenous form of it to the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. It is not a Mexican Halloween, and the name most Americans use for it turns out to be a translation of a translation.
body:
### History

UNESCO's own description is the most precise short account of what the day is for. "As practised by the indigenous communities of Mexico, el Dia de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) commemorates the transitory return to Earth of deceased relatives and loved ones. The festivities take place each year at the end of October to the beginning of November. This period also marks the completion of the annual cycle of cultivation of maize, the country's predominant food crop." Families "facilitate the return of the souls to Earth by laying flower petals, candles and offerings along the path leading from the cemetery to their homes," and the dead person's favorite dishes are placed "around the home shrine and the tomb alongside flowers and typical handicrafts, such as paper cut-outs."

Two things in that account tend to get lost in English. The first is that the care taken is not sentimental: UNESCO notes that "it is believed that the dead are capable of bringing prosperity (e.g. an abundant maize harvest) or misfortune (e.g. illness, accidents, financial difficulties) upon their families depending on how satisfactorily the rituals are executed." The second is that the calendar is finer than the popular two-day split suggests. "The dead are divided into several categories according to cause of death, age, sex and, in some cases, profession. A specific day of worship, determined by these categories, is designated for each deceased person."

The origins are layered rather than linear. The Smithsonian traces the observance to ancient Mesoamerica, where indigenous groups "including Aztec, Maya and Toltec, had specific times when they commemorated their loved ones who had passed away," and says that after the Spanish arrived the practice "was intertwined with two Spanish holidays: All Saints Day (Nov. 1) and All Soul's Day (Nov. 2)." The Library of Congress puts the same process in the colonial period: "In Mexico in the colonial era, a similar mingling occurred between All Souls Day and several Indigenous celebrations of the ancestors, creating Dia de Muertos, which means 'Day of the Dead' but also 'Day of the Ancestors.'" UNESCO calls the result a fusion of "pre-Hispanic religious rites and Catholic feasts," bringing together "two universes, one marked by indigenous belief systems, the other by worldviews introduced by the Europeans in the sixteenth century."

The name has its own history, and it is not the one most people assume. According to the Library of Congress, "the 'los' in 'Dia de los Muertos' seems to come from a translation of the English phrase 'Day of the Dead' back into Spanish; the 'los' was rarely used in Latin America before the 1960s - however, now both names are used." The Library hedges with "seems to," and so should anyone repeating it, but the form Americans treat as the authentic Spanish name appears to have come back from English.

The holiday's most photographed modern image has a similarly recent provenance. In 2016, Mexico City staged a large Dia de Muertos parade; PBS NewsHour reported that the previous year's James Bond film, which "opened with a 'day of the dead' parade featuring floats, puppets, and skeletons" filmed in Mexico City, "became the inspiration for yesterday's parade," and that it was "part of a campaign by the government to bring tourists." One participant, speaking about the older rituals rather than the parade, told PBS: "It is really cool, very traditional, super Mexican, but no one has heard about it."

### How to observe

Build an ofrenda, and build it to a plan. The Smithsonian's account has every ofrenda carrying the four elements: water left in a pitcher; papel picado, the cut-paper banners, for wind; earth represented by food, especially bread; and candles, often arranged in a cross for the cardinal directions so that the spirits can find their way. Sugar skulls - calaveritas de azucar - and toys are left for children who have died.

Use cempasuchil if you can get it. The Smithsonian describes it as "a type of marigold flower native to Mexico" placed on ofrendas and around graves, with the petals "used to make a path that leads the spirits from the cemetery to their families' homes" - the same practice UNESCO describes.

Cook the specific thing. UNESCO's wording is "the deceased's favourite dishes," not festival food in general, and that distinction is most of the difference between observing the day and decorating for it.

If you are in Washington in early November, the Library of Congress's Hispanic Reading Room puts up a community altar and says plainly: "Feel free to come leave an offering of your own." And if you want the primary material rather than the summaries, the Library's own guide suggests the catalog search terms it uses itself - decorated altars, calaveras, Catrina, sugar skulls, and All Souls' Day--Mexico.
timeline:
- Before the sixteenth century - Indigenous groups in Mesoamerica, among them the Aztec, Maya and Toltec, keep set times for commemorating their dead.
- Sixteenth century onward - European arrival produces what UNESCO calls a fusion of pre-Hispanic religious rites and Catholic feasts. The Library of Congress places the mingling of All Souls Day with Indigenous ancestor observances in Mexico's colonial era; the Smithsonian names the two feasts as All Saints Day on November 1 and All Souls Day on November 2.
- Before the 1960s - The form "Dia de los Muertos" is rarely used in Latin America. The Library of Congress reports that the "los" appears to have come from translating the English "Day of the Dead" back into Spanish.
- 2008 - UNESCO inscribes "Indigenous festivity dedicated to the dead" (nomination file 00054, decision 3.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity; it had originally been proclaimed in 2003.
- October 29, 2016 - Mexico City stages a Dia de Muertos parade that PBS NewsHour reports was inspired by the opening sequence of the previous year's James Bond film, shot in the city, as part of a government campaign to attract tourists. More than a thousand performers take part.
faq:
When is Day of the Dead?
UNESCO places the festivities "at the end of October to the beginning of November" without fixing a single day. The Smithsonian gives the familiar split: November 1 to remember children who have died, November 2 to honor adults. UNESCO describes a finer system still, in which the dead are sorted by cause of death, age, sex and sometimes profession, with a specific day of worship assigned for each person.

Is Day of the Dead the Mexican Halloween?
No. The Library of Congress calls it "a related but different holiday," and traces Halloween to the pre-Christian Celtic festival Samhain while tracing Dia de Muertos to the colonial-era mingling of All Souls Day with Indigenous celebrations of the ancestors. They are also on different days, and the Smithsonian notes that many communities that observe one observe the other too.

Is it "Dia de Muertos" or "Dia de los Muertos"?
Both are now used. The Library of Congress reports that the "los" seems to come from translating the English "Day of the Dead" back into Spanish, and that it was rarely used in Latin America before the 1960s.

What goes on an ofrenda?
The Smithsonian's account has four elements on every ofrenda: water in a pitcher, papel picado for wind, food - especially bread - for earth, and candles, often set in a cross for the cardinal directions. Around them go the dead person's favorite dishes, flowers, paper cut-outs, and sugar skulls and toys for children who have died.

Why marigolds?
The cempasuchil is a marigold native to Mexico. Its petals are strewn to make a path from the cemetery to the family's home so the dead can find their way, which is the same practice UNESCO describes when it speaks of laying flower petals along the path from the cemetery.

- PBS NewsHour, James Bond inspires Dia de los Muertos parade in Mexico City (October 30, 2016) - https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/james-bonds-spectre-inspires-dia-de-los-muertos-parade-mexico-city → the 2016 Mexico City parade on October 29; the previous year's Bond film opening with a day-of-the-dead parade of floats, puppets and skeletons filmed in Mexico City and becoming the parade's inspiration; "part of a campaign by the government to bring tourists"; "More than a 1,000 dancers, acrobats, and actors"; tens of thousands of spectators; the participant's remark about the older rituals; "Traditionally, Mexicans set up altars to the dead each November 1st and 2nd."

Omitted for want of an acceptable source: La Catrina and its attribution to Jose Guadalupe Posada or its naming by Diego Rivera; pan de muerto by name, as distinct from the "bread" the Smithsonian mentions; the cemetery vigils of Michoacan and Patzcuaro; the effect of the 2017 film Coco; and any count of how many people observe the day. The Smithsonian's claim that the first monarch butterflies reach Mexico on November 1 each year is stated on its page but is not repeated here, as no second source was found for it.

name: Daylight Saving Time Ends
description: Daylight Saving Time ends on the first Sunday in November, when clocks across most of the United States are set back one hour at 2:00 a.m. daylight time, which becomes 1:00 a.m. standard time. The schedule is federal law rather than custom: the dates have been fixed in the U.S. Code since 1966 and have taken their present form since 2007. Hawaii and most of Arizona never moved their clocks forward in March, so they have nothing to set back.
body:
### History

The first federal daylight saving law in the United States was the Standard Time Act, signed March 19, 1918 under the title "An Act to Save daylight and to provide standard time for the United States." It set clocks forward on the last Sunday in March and back on the last Sunday in October, both at two o'clock in the morning. The idea was contentious at the time, and Congress repealed the daylight saving half the following year, on August 20, 1919, over President Wilson's veto. The time zones the same act created stayed in law.

Daylight time returned nationally for the Second World War and was observed without a break from February 9, 1942 to September 30, 1945. For the next 21 years there was no federal law requiring it, and whether clocks moved was a local question. The Uniform Time Act of 1966 standardized the dates again, running daylight time from the last Sunday in April to the last Sunday in October, while allowing any state to exempt itself entirely.

The end of daylight time stayed on the last Sunday in October for most of a century. It moved only with the Energy Policy Act of 2005, which pushed the end to the first Sunday in November beginning in 2007.

### How to observe

The useful thing to do is deal with the clocks that will not deal with themselves. Phones, computers and most connected thermostats change on their own; ovens, microwaves, cars, wall clocks and a good number of alarm clocks do not, and a forgotten one stays wrong for the next four months.

The Consumer Product Safety Commission has tied the clock change to home safety since at least 1993, with a campaign built around the line "Change Your Clock, Change Your Battery" — the date as the annual reminder to put fresh batteries in your smoke alarms. It works precisely because it is hard to forget.

It is also worth noticing what actually happens to the hour. Clocks go back at 2:00 a.m. to 1:00 a.m., so the hour between one and two occurs twice. Any timestamp recorded in local time during that hour is ambiguous, which is why logs, schedules and billing systems are written in standard or universal time instead.
timeline:
- 1918 — The Standard Time Act, signed March 19, establishes U.S. time zones and the country's first daylight saving time, ending on the last Sunday in October.
- 1919 — Congress repeals the daylight saving provision on August 20, over President Wilson's veto. The time zones remain.
- 1942–1945 — Daylight time is observed nationally and without interruption from February 9, 1942 to September 30, 1945.
- 1966 — The Uniform Time Act sets a uniform national schedule ending on the last Sunday in October, and allows any state to exempt itself.
- 1974–1975 — Under the Emergency Daylight Saving Time Energy Conservation Act of 1973, passed amid severe energy shortages, daylight time begins on January 6, 1974 and February 23, 1975 before the regular schedule returns.
- 2005 — The Energy Policy Act moves the end of daylight time to the first Sunday in November, effective in 2007.
faq:
When does Daylight Saving Time end in 2026?
Sunday, November 1, 2026. Clocks go back one hour at 2:00 a.m. daylight time, which becomes 1:00 a.m. standard time.

Which states do not change their clocks?
Hawaii and most of Arizona stay on standard time all year, so they have no change to make. The Uniform Time Act of 1966 is what gives a state the right to exempt itself.

Is it "daylight saving" or "daylight savings"?
The law says saving, singular: the Uniform Time Act of 1966 and its codification at 15 U.S.C. 260a. "Daylight savings" is common in speech and even turns up in the official title of a 2025 House bill, but it is not the name in the statute.

Will the clock changes ever stop?
Bills to make daylight saving time permanent have been introduced repeatedly and none has become law. The Sunshine Protection Act of 2021 passed the Senate by unanimous consent on March 15, 2022, was received in the House the next day and was held at the desk without a vote. In the current Congress the House passed H.R. 139 by 308 to 117 on July 14, 2026 and the Senate referred it to the Commerce Committee the following day; its official record as of September 8, 2026 shows no Senate action since.

Why 2:00 a.m.?
That has been the changeover hour in U.S. law since the beginning: the 1918 act set it at two o'clock in the morning, and 49 CFR 71.2 still puts both transitions at 2 a.m. The Naval Observatory spells out the arithmetic — back one hour at 2:00 a.m. daylight time, which becomes 1:00 a.m. standard time.

name: Diwali
description: Diwali is the festival of lights: five days in autumn marked by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists, and named for the Sanskrit dipavali, a row of lamps. Its date is set by a lunisolar calendar rather than the Gregorian one, so it moves between mid-October and mid-November. In the United States it has recently become a legislated holiday as well as a domestic one — New York City closes its public schools for it, and Pennsylvania has designated a state Diwali Day, though without requiring anyone to close.
body:
### History

Diwali is a contraction of the Sanskrit Deepavali, which the resolution the U.S. House adopted in 2007 glossed as "a row of lamps" — the lamps being diyas, small oil lamps set along thresholds and windowsills. What they commemorate depends on who is lighting them, and saying so is more accurate than picking one story. For many Hindus they mark the return of Rama to Ayodhya; the festival is also sacred to Lakshmi, goddess of wealth and good fortune, whom a row of lamps is lit to invite. The second day commemorates Krishna's victory over the demon Narakasura. For Jains, Diwali marks the liberation of Mahavira, the most recent Tirthankara, from samsara, which Jain tradition — repeated in that 2007 resolution — places at the end of his life in 527 B.C. Sikhs keep the day as the anniversary of the release of the sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, from imprisonment by the Mughal emperor Jahangir. Britannica's biography of Hargobind records the jailing at the fortress of Gwalior and the emperor's eventual relenting but gives no year for either, and no acceptable source supplies the 1619 that circulates online, so this page does not print it. President Obama's 2009 Diwali remarks named the observing communities as "Hindus, Jains, Sikhs, and some Buddhists" — the qualifier on Buddhists is doing real work.

The date is harder to state cleanly than it looks. Britannica places the five days across the lunar months of Ashvina and Karttika and puts the main night, Lakshmi Puja, on the new moon; the Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art puts the festival in October or November, traditionally after the year's last harvest. The states that have legislated it needed a formula a school calendar could use and fixed a lunar date instead: New York's statute says "the fifteenth day of the eighth month of the Indian calendar," Pennsylvania's the fifteenth day of Kartik.

The American official record is recent. Congress began taking up Diwali resolutions in 2005, one of them asking the Postal Service for a stamp; the first to pass a chamber was H.Res. 747, agreed to in the House on October 29, 2007. In 2009 President Obama lit a diya in the East Room, the first time a president took part personally, though Diwali had been marked at the White House under earlier administrations. The stamp came in October 2016, dedicated at the Consulate General of India in New York. New York enacted its school closure in November 2023 and Pennsylvania designated Diwali Day in 2024. On scale, nobody measures it: Pew put Hindus at 0.9 percent of American adults in 2023–24 and the Census counted about 5.2 million people identifying as Indian in 2023, but no survey asks how many Americans observe Diwali, so any round number you see was invented.

### How to observe

Lamps first, because the diya is the point: a row of them along a doorway or windowsill is the observance in its simplest form. The five days each have their own character — Dhanteras opens the festival on the thirteenth lunar day of Karttika, Naraka Chaturdashi or "small Diwali" follows, Lakshmi Puja is the main night, Govardhan Puja commemorates Krishna lifting up a mountain to shelter the cowherds from the rain Indra sent, and Bhai Dooj, for the bond between brothers and sisters, closes it.

Public celebrations here are large and mostly free: Diwali at Times Square, outdoors in Duffy Square with no ticket, and the Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art in Washington, which opens after hours for rangoli-making, music, performances and curator-led tours of its South Asian collections. If you are planning around the New York City school calendar, check the year rather than assuming — the closure only produces a day off when Diwali falls on a school day. It did in 2024 and 2025; the published 2026–27 calendar carries none, because the festival lands on a Sunday in 2026. And if you would rather read the record than attend anything, New York's statute, the House resolution as adopted, the stamp release and the transcript of the 2009 diya lighting are all linked below.
timeline:
- 527 B.C. — Jain tradition places Mahavira's attainment of moksha at the end of his life in this year; the 2007 House resolution repeats the date.
- October 29, 2007 — H.Res. 747 is agreed to in the House, the first Diwali resolution to pass a chamber of Congress; the Senate adopts S.Res. 299 on November 14.
- October 14, 2009 — President Obama lights a diya in the East Room, the first time a president takes part in a White House Diwali observance.
- October 2016 — The Postal Service issues a Diwali Forever stamp, dedicated at the Consulate General of India in New York, eleven years after a 2005 House resolution asked for one.
- November 14, 2023 — Governor Hochul signs the law closing New York City public schools for Diwali; the first Diwali to fall after it took effect was Friday, November 1, 2024.
- 2024 — Pennsylvania enacts Act 112, designating the fifteenth day of Kartik as Diwali Day, while expressly not requiring schools, government offices or businesses to close.
faq:
When is Diwali?
It has no fixed Gregorian date. The Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art places the festival in October or November; Britannica puts its main night, Lakshmi Puja, on the new moon. The dates table on this page carries the computed dates for the next five years.

Is Diwali a federal holiday in the United States?
No. Federal offices, banks and post offices operate normally. Three states have acted on it: Pennsylvania designated a Diwali Day in 2024 but its law expressly does not require schools, government offices or businesses to close; California's governor signed AB 268, listed as "State holidays: Diwali," in October 2025; and New York's 2023 law applies to New York City public schools only.

Do New York City public schools close for Diwali?
Yes, under a law signed on November 14, 2023 — but only when Diwali falls on a school day. The 2024–25 calendar closed schools on Friday, November 1, 2024, and the 2025–26 calendar on Monday, October 20, 2025. The 2026–27 calendar carries no Diwali closure, because the festival falls on a Sunday in 2026.

Which religions observe Diwali?
Hindus, Jains and Sikhs, and some Buddhists. Each brings a different occasion to the same lights: Rama's return or Lakshmi's visit for many Hindus, Mahavira's liberation for Jains, Guru Hargobind's release from Gwalior for Sikhs.

What does the word Diwali mean?
It is a contraction of the Sanskrit Deepavali. Britannica and the congressional record both render it as a row of lamps or a row of lights. The Postal Service's 2016 stamp release instead called it "a necklace of lights"; that reading is an outlier.

Source conflict reported rather than averaged: which lunar month the festival falls in. Britannica's main article puts the five days across Ashvina and Karttika; its Dhanteras article puts day one on the thirteenth lunar day of Karttika; its Govardhan Puja article calls day four "the first day of Karttika"; the congressional resolutions say "the last day of the last month in the lunar calendar"; and the New York and Pennsylvania statutes fix it as the fifteenth day of the eighth month of the Indian calendar, or of Kartik. This page states the invariant they all agree on — the new-moon night of the mid-autumn lunation, in October or November — and gives the statutory formulation for the U.S. legal date, rather than presenting any one of those sentences as the rule.

Second conflict: the meaning of Deepavali. The Postal Service's 2016 release calls it "a necklace of lights"; Britannica and three congressional resolutions give a row of lamps or lights. The row reading is preferred as the better attested, and the Postal Service's is quoted as the outlier rather than averaged in.

Third conflict: who first observed Diwali at the White House. The Obama administration's blog and the President's own 2009 remarks claim a first for presidential participation, while President Biden's 2022 remarks say "there had been Diwali celebrations in previous administrations." The two are compatible, and this page says so: presidential participation began in 2009, and institutional observance predates it by an interval no acceptable source specifies.

Omitted for want of an acceptable source: any year for Guru Hargobind's release from Gwalior, including the widely repeated 1619, and the associated story of 52 princes; a start year for White House Diwali observances, including the commonly printed 2003; any claim that Newar Buddhists observe Diwali; any count of Americans who celebrate Diwali; the founding year of the Diwali at Times Square event and of the Association of Indians in America's New York festival; the exact signing date of Pennsylvania's Act 112, which is derivable only from a "yesterday" in an October 22, 2024 press release, so the year alone is used; the statutory effect of California's AB 268, whose chaptered text could not be retrieved, so only the fact of signing is stated; and Connecticut's Diwali legislation, which could be confirmed from the state's own sources only as a committee-stage proposed bill.

Less than fully confident, flagged deliberately: the characterization of November 1, 2024 as the first New York City school closure for Diwali. No government page says "for the first time." The inference is tight — the law was signed on November 14, 2023, after that year's Diwali, and the 2024–25 calendar is the first to carry the entry — and the page is worded to state the inference rather than assert the superlative.

Not used as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate, Wikipedia, and comparable aggregator and content-farm pages.

name: Earth Day
description: Earth Day falls on April 22 and began as one day of American protest in 1970, proposed by Senator Gaylord Nelson of Wisconsin and organized in about six months. The U.S. Senate's own history puts the turnout at roughly 20 million people, across some 2,000 college campuses and 10,000 schools, though no source names who counted. It has been international since 1990, and it has never been a federal holiday.
body:
### History

Nelson, a Democrat, announced the idea at a conference in Seattle on September 20, 1969, having seen the Santa Barbara oil spill earlier that year: a blowout at Union Oil's well 21 under Platform A, five and a half miles offshore, which released about 100,000 barrels before it was stopped in December. He asked his staff to work out how to sponsor nationwide campus environmental teach-ins the following spring. They picked the week of April 19 to 25 and settled on Wednesday, April 22, a weekday after winter weather and before final exams, to get the largest possible student turnout. Nelson recruited a Republican congressman, Paul "Pete" McCloskey, as co-chair so the day carried no partisan lean, and hired Denis Hayes, then a graduate student at Harvard, to organize it.

So many members of Congress were out at Earth Day events that Congress went into recess. Rallies in Chicago, New York and Philadelphia drew as many as 25,000 each, about 10,000 gathered at the Washington Monument, and Fifth Avenue was closed to traffic.

What the day caused is harder to establish than what followed it. The EPA's own archive is willing to say that the public pressure Earth Day created "provided the necessary impetus" for the 1970 Clean Air Act amendments, and that the timing was no accident. The agency itself came later that year: the Senate confirmed its first administrator on December 2, 1970, the date EPA treats as its birthday. The Clean Water Act of 1972 and the Endangered Species Act of 1973 are same-era legislation, and the government sources documenting them do not credit Earth Day.

### How to observe

Register a cleanup. EARTHDAY.ORG runs The Great Global Cleanup, accepts registrations year-round, puts each event on a public map, and publishes guides for individuals and for groups.

If you would rather contribute data than carry bags, the EPA maintains a list of participatory science projects open to the public. Among them is the Cyanobacteria Monitoring Collaborative, whose volunteers photograph and identify algal blooms through the bloomWatch app, and the Chesapeake Monitoring Cooperative's water quality work. The National Park Service runs its own citizen science and BioBlitz programs.

The archive option is better than it sounds. The Wisconsin Historical Society holds the Gaylord Nelson papers: 1,040 boxes of paper, audio recordings, film, photographs and scrapbooks, open to the public during archive hours, with a finding aid online. The Society has also published an Earth Day gallery of 130 photographs spanning 1954 to 2006.
timeline:
- January 28, 1969 — A blowout at Union Oil's well 21 off Santa Barbara, California releases about 100,000 barrels of oil before it is stopped in December.
- September 20, 1969 — Senator Gaylord Nelson announces plans for a nationwide environmental demonstration at a conference in Seattle.
- April 22, 1970 — The first Earth Day, a Wednesday, held as a nationwide environmental teach-in. Congress goes into recess.
- December 2, 1970 — The Senate confirms the Environmental Protection Agency's first administrator, the date EPA marks as its birthday.
- 1990 — Earth Day goes global, again organized by Denis Hayes.
- April 22, 2016 — The Paris Agreement opens for signature at UN headquarters in New York; 175 Parties sign, 174 countries and the European Union.
faq:
When is Earth Day?
April 22, every year. In 2027 it falls on a Thursday.

Is Earth Day a federal holiday?
No. The Congressional Research Service records resolutions in the 92nd, 93rd and 106th Congresses to designate an annual Earth Day, on none of which further action was taken.

Did 20 million Americans really take part in 1970?
The figure is everywhere and traceable to no count. EARTHDAY.ORG, the U.S. Senate's historical office, the EPA and Encyclopaedia Britannica all give about 20 million. The Wisconsin Historical Society's own archivist puts it at 10 to 20 million. The Congressional Research Service declines a number altogether and cites the New York Times of April 23, 1970, which reported "millions." The historian Adam Rome makes the more useful point: it was not one event but at least 12,000 of them.

Did Earth Day create the EPA?
Not directly, on the government's own account. EPA was established by Reorganization Plan No. 3, which President Nixon sent to Congress on July 9, 1970; the Senate confirmed the first administrator on December 2. EARTHDAY.ORG says the first Earth Day led to the agency's creation, while EPA's own history pages set out the sequence without making that claim. Where EPA does assert a causal link is the 1970 Clean Air Act amendments.

Why April 22?
For the academic calendar. Nelson's staff wanted a midweek day after winter weather had passed but before final exams, to maximize student participation, and April 22, 1970 was a Wednesday.

- UNFCCC, 175 States Sign Paris Agreement — https://unfccc.int/news/175-states-sign-paris-agreement → the signature ceremony at United Nations headquarters in New York on April 22, and that 175 Parties — 174 countries and the European Union — signed, with 15 states depositing instruments of ratification.
- University at Buffalo, Adam Rome on the 50th anniversary of Earth Day — https://www.buffalo.edu/news/tipsheets/2020/009.html → "It wasn't one event. It was at least 12,000."
- EARTHDAY.ORG, Register Your Cleanup with The Great Global Cleanup — https://www.earthday.org/actions/register-a-cleanup/ → year-round registration, the guides for individuals and groups, and the global event map.
- EPA, Examples of Participatory Science Projects Supported by EPA — https://www.epa.gov/participatory-science/examples-participatory-science-projects-supported-epa → the Cyanobacteria Monitoring Collaborative and its bloomWatch app, and the Chesapeake Monitoring Cooperative's volunteer water quality monitoring.
- National Park Service, volunteer programs — https://www.nps.gov/subjects/volunteer/programs.htm → the Park Service's citizen science programs (https://www.nps.gov/subjects/citizenscience/index.htm) and the National Parks BioBlitz (https://www.nps.gov/subjects/biodiversity/national-parks-bioblitz.htm).
- Wisconsin Historical Society, An Earth Day Gallery in Gaylord Nelson's Honor — https://www.wisconsinhistory.org/Records/Article/CS3745 → the Gaylord Nelson papers at 1,040 boxes of paper, audio recordings, films, photographs, scrapbooks and video recordings, available to the public during regular archives hours with an online finding aid; and the gallery of 130 photographs covering 1954 to 2006.

Source conflict, resolved and disclosed: the 1970 participation figure. Five sources give about 20 million, the Wisconsin Historical Society's own archivist gives a range of 10 to 20 million, and the Congressional Research Service declines a figure and falls back on the contemporaneous New York Times, which said only "millions." This page reports the spread and names who says what rather than averaging, because no source traces 20 million to a count. On causation the page follows the more primary source in each case: EPA's archive where EPA itself claims Earth Day as an impetus (the 1970 Clean Air Act amendments), and the documenting agency where it makes no such claim (the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act), rather than EARTHDAY.ORG's broader account.

Not claimed, for want of a source: that April 22 was chosen because it is Vladimir Lenin's birthday — no reputable source supports it, and the one acceptable source that touches the question renders the dates in a way that appears to be mistaken, so this page does not rely on it and gives only the documented academic-calendar reason; the enactment dates of the 1970 Clean Air Act amendments and the 1972 Clean Water Act, which EPA's own history pages do not state; any methodology or primary count behind the 20 million figure; Denis Hayes's exact age on the day itself (Harvard dates him at 25 in 1969); Pete McCloskey's district or the formal title of his role; the country counts for 1990 (EARTHDAY.ORG says 141, Britannica says more than 140) and the participation figures for 2000, 2010 and the present day, which are self-reported by the organizing body and uncorroborated; the sales figures usually given for Rachel Carson's Silent Spring; and any government assessment linking the Santa Barbara spill to the environmental movement or to legislation — NOAA confines itself to the incident and describes its environmental effects as relatively minimal.

Rejected as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate, history.com, and content-farm or AI-generated listicles. Advocacy and opinion outlets were also set aside on the Lenin question, which is why that claim is left unaddressed beyond the note above.

name: Easter Sunday
description: Easter Sunday is the central feast of the Christian year, marking the resurrection of Jesus, and it is the one major American holiday whose date is computed rather than looked up: it can land anywhere from March 22 to April 25. Much of the folklore attached to it, including the story about a pagan goddess named Eostre and her sacred hare, does not survive a look at the sources.
body:
### History

The date comes from a rule, and the rule is the interesting part. The First Council of Nicaea, convened by Constantine in 325, resolved to keep Easter on the same Sunday throughout the Christian world and had tables built to compute it; the version that became standard came from the sixth-century monk Dionysius Exiguus. Those tables are ecclesiastical, not astronomical: the vernal equinox is fixed at March 21 regardless of where the sun actually is, and the ecclesiastical full moon is the fourteenth day of a tabular lunation. Easter is the Sunday after the first ecclesiastical full moon falling on or after that fixed equinox, which is why it can come no earlier than March 22 and no later than April 25. Nicaea did its work under the Julian calendar; the reform Gregory XIII issued in 1582, in the bull Inter gravissimas, came with new Easter tables that Western churches adopted and many Eastern Orthodox churches did not. That, and not a dispute about the holiday, is why the two Easters usually fall on different days.

The holiday's American furniture arrived separately from its theology. The Easter hare is German: the first clear reference is Georg Franck von Franckenau's De ovis paschalibus in 1682, which reports that German-speaking regions called the eggs hare's eggs, from a story that the Easter Hare laid them in gardens. It reached Pennsylvania with German immigrants: the fraktur artist Johann Conrad Gilbert, who emigrated in 1757, drew hares with Easter eggs. The phrase "Easter Bunny" does not appear in American newspapers until 1883. That any of this descends from a pagan fertility goddess is not supported. Bede, in the eighth century, is the only ancient source to name Eostre at all, and he connects her to nothing but an April month name. The goddess Ostara was Jacob Grimm's conjecture in 1835, and the hare was attached to her by Adolf Holtzmann in 1874 to explain a custom that already existed.

The one Easter tradition with a documented American origin is the White House Easter Egg Roll. Children had rolled eggs on the Capitol's west grounds through the 1870s until an act to protect the turf and grass of the Capitol Grounds became law on April 29, 1876. Two years later President Rutherford B. Hayes opened the White House South Lawn to them instead, and it has been held on Easter Monday ever since, apart from the war years and the Truman renovation.

### How to observe

Look the date up rather than trusting memory: the U.S. Naval Observatory publishes computed dates for Easter and other Christian observances years ahead, alongside its explanation of the rule behind them.

If you are in Washington that week, note the day: the Egg Roll is Easter Monday, not Easter Sunday.

And if you like your traditions documented, the Library of Congress's American Folklife Center has traced the Easter Bunny through fraktur drawings, nineteenth-century Pennsylvania German accounts and digitized newspapers. It will permanently spoil the pagan-goddess story for you.
timeline:
- 325 — The First Council of Nicaea, convened by Constantine, resolves to keep Easter on one Sunday across the Christian world and has tables built to compute it.
- 1582 — Gregory XIII's reform, in the bull Inter gravissimas, produces new Easter tables; Western churches adopt them, many Eastern churches do not.
- 1682 — Franckenau's De ovis paschalibus gives the first clear reference to the German Easter Hare laying eggs in gardens.
- April 29, 1876 — An act protecting the turf and grass of the Capitol Grounds becomes law, ending egg rolling there.
- 1878 — President Rutherford B. Hayes opens the White House South Lawn to egg rollers.
faq:
Why does Easter move every year?
Because the date is computed rather than fixed. Easter is the Sunday after the first ecclesiastical full moon falling on or after March 21, which the church calendar treats as the vernal equinox whatever the sun is doing. That puts it between March 22 and April 25.

Why is Orthodox Easter on a different day?
The rule is the same; the tables are not. Western churches use the tables issued with the Gregorian reform of 1582, many Eastern Orthodox churches tables based on the older Julian calendar.

Is Easter a federal holiday?
No. Federal holidays are set by law, under 5 U.S.C. 6103, and neither Easter nor Good Friday is on it. Easter falls on a Sunday anyway, so the practical question is Good Friday and Easter Monday, which some states and employers observe and the federal government does not.

Did Easter take its name from a pagan goddess?
Very little supports the story as it is usually told. Bede is the only ancient writer to mention Eostre, and he links her only to an April month name. The fertility goddess with a sacred hare is a nineteenth-century reconstruction.

Is the White House Easter Egg Roll on Easter Sunday?
No, Easter Monday. It began in 1878, two years after Congress closed the Capitol grounds to egg rollers.

name: Father's Day
description: Father's Day falls on the third Sunday in June, and it took more than sixty years to get there. Sonora Smart Dodd proposed it in Spokane in 1909, after sitting through a Mother's Day sermon and thinking of her own father, a Civil War veteran who had raised his children alone; the first service was held the following June. Congress did not give the day a standing annual designation until 1972, which makes it one of the slowest-moving holidays on the American calendar.
body:
### History

There are two origin claims, and only one of them is firmly dated. The Library of Congress names Grace Golden Clayton, who wanted a day honoring the fathers killed in the Monongah mine disaster — an explosion in Marion County, West Virginia, on December 6, 1907, which the official list of mine disasters puts at 357 dead, and contemporary accounts at close to four hundred. The sources used for this page do not give a year for Clayton's service, so no year is assigned to it here.

The dated claim belongs to Sonora Smart Dodd. In 1909, at a Mother's Day church service in Spokane, Washington, she thought of a counterpart for fathers. Her own mother had died in childbirth when Dodd was sixteen, and her father, William Jackson Smart, a Civil War veteran, had raised the children himself. Dodd persuaded the Spokane Ministerial Alliance and the YMCA to sign a petition, and the first Father's Day was observed in Spokane on June 19, 1910, with proclamations from the city's mayor and the governor of Washington. She then spent roughly six decades pressing for national recognition.

Federal recognition came in pieces, and most of the pieces expired. Presidents Wilson and Coolidge both worked toward making the day national. In 1966 Congress enacted Public Law 89-450, which covered that year alone. Only on April 24, 1972, with Public Law 92-278, did Congress authorize the President to designate the third Sunday in June as Father's Day each year, direct that the flag be flown on federal buildings, and invite states, localities and the public to observe it with ceremonies expressing gratitude to their fathers. That is the law the holiday still runs on.

### How to observe

Be specific rather than general. The holiday was invented by a woman thinking about one man who had done something hard and unglamorous for years without being thanked for it, and a general tribute to fatherhood was not what she had in mind.

Read the law. Public Law 92-278 is about a page long and, unlike most holiday legislation, says plainly what the day is for. The 1966 version, Public Law 89-450, is worth seeing next to it: a holiday granted one year at a time.

If you are in Spokane, the Dodd House, where Sonora Smart Dodd lived, was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2010 — the holiday's centennial — under reference number 10000417. It is privately managed and not open to the public, so admire it from the sidewalk.

And if the day is a complicated one for you, the holiday's own history is not unsympathetic. On the West Virginia account, it began as a memorial for fathers who were not coming home.
timeline:
- December 6, 1907 — An explosion at Monongah, West Virginia, kills 357 miners by the official count; Grace Golden Clayton sought a day honoring the fathers lost there.
- 1909 — At a Mother's Day service in Spokane, Washington, Sonora Smart Dodd conceives a holiday honoring fathers.
- June 19, 1910 — The first Father's Day is observed in Spokane, with proclamations from the mayor and the governor of Washington.
- 1966 — Congress enacts Public Law 89-450, recognizing Father's Day for that year only.
- April 24, 1972 — Public Law 92-278 authorizes the President to designate the third Sunday in June as Father's Day each year.
- 2010 — The Dodd House in Spokane is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, on the holiday's centennial.
faq:
When is Father's Day?
The third Sunday in June, under Public Law 92-278, approved April 24, 1972.

Is Father's Day a federal holiday?
No. The 1972 law designates the day and calls for the flag to be flown on federal buildings, but the federal holidays that come with a day off are set separately, under 5 U.S.C. 6103, and Father's Day is not one of them.

Who started Father's Day?
Sonora Smart Dodd of Spokane, Washington, in most accounts: she proposed it in 1909 and held the first observance on June 19, 1910. The Library of Congress also credits Grace Golden Clayton of West Virginia, who wanted a day for the fathers killed at Monongah. Because the sources here do not date Clayton's service, the two claims cannot be cleanly ordered.

Why did it take until 1972?
Congress kept acting on the day without making it permanent. The 1966 law, Public Law 89-450, applied to 1966 only, and it was Public Law 92-278 six years later that created a standing annual designation.

Why the third Sunday in June?
The 1972 law fixed it, and the June timing traces back to the first observance in Spokane on June 19, 1910. Why that particular date was chosen is not documented in the sources used here.

name: Flag Day
description: Flag Day falls on June 14, the anniversary of the 1777 resolution in which the Continental Congress declared that the flag of the United States be thirteen stripes and thirteen stars. The observance is far younger than the flag, and its origin is contested: three men have been called the father of Flag Day by sources as official as Congress and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.
body:
### History

The resolution is one sentence, recorded in the Journals of the Continental Congress for Saturday, June 14, 1777: "Resolved, That the flag of the thirteen United States be thirteen stripes, alternate red and white: that the union be thirteen stars, white in a blue field, representing a new constellation." It appears without preamble, between Marine Committee business and John Paul Jones's appointment to command the Ranger. It said nothing about the stars' points, their arrangement, or the flag's proportions, so early flags scattered the stars, ranked them in rows, or set them in a circle. The flag drew little public notice at the time; its job was identifying ships and forts.

Betsy Ross is the name attached to it, and the record does not support the story. Congress's own flag handbook notes that although she made flags for fifty years, "there is no proof that she made the first Stars and Stripes," and that the circle-of-stars flag bearing her name did not appear until the 1790s. The claim surfaced in 1870, when her grandson William J. Canby read a paper recounting what he had heard as a boy — and Canby dated the alleged meeting to June 1776, a year before the resolution it supposedly inspired. The stars are credited instead, on stronger evidence, to Francis Hopkinson, who billed Congress for the work and was refused.

The observance accumulated claimants. A Flag Day celebration flew in Hartford in 1861, and the first national observance came on the flag's centennial in 1877. Bernard J. Cigrand had his pupils in Waubeka, Wisconsin mark June 14 as "Flag Birthday" in 1885; William T. Kerr is credited with founding the American Flag Day Association in Pittsburgh in 1888. The House recognized Cigrand's Wisconsin origin in 2004, then hedged it in 2010; Pennsylvania's marker gives the title to Kerr. No contemporaneous document settles it.

How the day reached the White House is better documented. Woodrow Wilson's Proclamation 1335 of May 30, 1916 asked that June 14 "be observed as Flag Day" — it suggested and requested, and established nothing — and the Congressional Record shows a congressman pressing for it on behalf of the Elks, whose lodges had marked the date since 1912. The statute came much later: a joint resolution approved August 3, 1949 designated June 14 as Flag Day and asked the president to proclaim it yearly.

### How to observe

Fort McHenry in Baltimore, where the flag that became the anthem flew, runs Flag Day programs around its morning and evening flag changes. If you cannot get there, the flag itself is on view at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History — a thirty-by-forty-two-foot garrison flag sewn in 1813 by Mary Pickersgill with her daughter, two nieces, and an indentured servant named Grace Wisher, whom most accounts leave out.

The useful task at home is retiring a worn flag. The Flag Code says one no longer fit for display "should be destroyed in a dignified way, preferably by burning," and American Legion and VFW posts, scout troops and many government offices collect them. Check local fire rules first; synthetic flags can be hazardous to burn and are often better recycled.
timeline:
- 1777 — On June 14 the Continental Congress adopts the flag resolution: thirteen stripes, thirteen stars, "a new constellation."
- 1861 — The Stars and Stripes flies in a Flag Day celebration in Hartford, Connecticut, the earliest such claim.
- 1885 — Bernard J. Cigrand has his pupils in Waubeka, Wisconsin observe June 14 as "Flag Birthday."
- 1916 — Wilson's Proclamation 1335 of May 30 suggests and requests nationwide observance of June 14.
- 1949 — A joint resolution approved August 3 designates June 14 as Flag Day and asks for an annual proclamation.
faq:
Is Flag Day a federal holiday?

No. The eleven legal public holidays are listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103, and Flag Day is not among them. Pennsylvania does list June 14 as a legal holiday, but that statute's effect is confined to banking and commercial paper, and the same act declares such days "secular or business days, for all other purposes." Nothing closes.

Who started Flag Day?

Nobody can say with confidence, and the official sources disagree. Congress credited Cigrand and Ozaukee County, Wisconsin in 2004 for an 1885 schoolroom observance; Pennsylvania's marker names Kerr; New York's claim dates to 1889 and Philadelphia's to 1893. Hartford's 1861 celebration predates all of them, and Congress's own handbook names no founder.

Did Betsy Ross make the first American flag?

There is no proof that she did. She was a working Philadelphia flagmaker who supplied the Pennsylvania State Navy in 1777, but the story of a commission from George Washington first appeared in 1870, told by her grandson from childhood memory, and it places the meeting a year before the resolution existed.

Is the flag flown at half-staff on Flag Day?

No. The Flag Code names Flag Day among the days the flag should especially be displayed, and Memorial Day is the only day in that list carrying a half-staff instruction.

- U.S. Congress, Joint Committee on Printing, Our Flag, H. Doc. 108-97, 2003 — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CDOC-108hdoc97/pdf/CDOC-108hdoc97.pdf → that the resolution gave no instruction on the stars' points or arrangement; "there is no proof that she made the first Stars and Stripes"; the circle-of-stars flag dating to the 1790s; William J. Canby's 1870 paper and his June 1776 dating; Francis Hopkinson and his refused request for payment; the Hartford celebration of 1861; the first national observance on June 14, 1877.
- Smithsonian National Museum of American History, Star-Spangled Banner exhibition — https://amhistory.si.edu/starspangledbanner/ and https://amhistory.si.edu/starspangledbanner/making-the-flag.aspx → the flag on display; the thirty-by-forty-two-foot garrison flag sewn in 1813 by Mary Pickersgill with her daughter, two nieces and the indentured servant Grace Wisher.

name: Friday the 13th
description: Friday the 13th is the date most Americans know to be unlucky, and nearly everything commonly said about where it came from is wrong. It is not medieval, it has no demonstrable link to the Knights Templar, and Library of Congress folklorists trace the belief no further back than 1830s France. Every year holds at least one and never more than three; 2026 has three.
body:
### History

The two halves of the superstition are old. The combination is not.

Friday has been treated as inauspicious across much of Christian Europe, which the Library of Congress links to the tradition that Jesus was crucified on a Friday and to the fasting that followed — a day fit for endings, when fishermen stayed ashore and no one began a journey. Friday is not unlucky in Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, or in most countries where the majority religion is not Christian. Thirteen carries separate baggage, most durably the belief that of thirteen people dining together one will die, which attached itself to the Last Supper; in the tarot, Death has borne the number 13 since at least 1565.

When the two were welded together is a narrower question, and the answer is recent. Library of Congress folklorist Stephen Winick's archival survey finds the earliest clear references in French works of 1834 — an article in the Revue de Paris by the Marquis de Salvo ("It is always Fridays and the number 13 that bring bad luck") and a play, Les Finesses des Gribouilles. By mid-century the belief could carry a plot: Octave Gastineau's 1870s play Lelia turns on a countess who will not dance on a Friday the 13th. Its English translations of 1878 and 1879 moved the setting to London and inserted "how unlucky" after the date, evidently doubting American audiences would catch it. In 1886 the Chicago Daily Tribune printed the superstition as a "French Joke." Only in the late 1880s and 1890s does it appear routinely in American papers, and then mostly as a joke about baseball games and marriage licenses.

An earlier post on the same Library of Congress blog found no American newspaper reference before 1900, and a folklorist quoted alongside Winick dates the belief to England, no record before 1913. Winick's is the account with the documents.

### How to observe

Do what the Thirteen Club did. In 1882 a group of New Yorkers sat down thirteen to a table on Friday, January 13, expressly to break the taboo, and kept meeting; the Library of Congress holds the address printed for its thirteenth.

Read the belief as Americans received it. Search Chronicling America, the Library of Congress's digitized newspaper archive, for "Friday the 13th" against your own town in the 1890s. What comes back is largely ridicule — the real American history here, a belief mostly held about other people.

Check which day your own calendar fears. Spain and Greece worry about Tuesday the 13th; Italy about Friday the 17th, because XVII rearranges into VIXI, "I have lived"; Japan about the number 4, which sounds like the word for death.
timeline:
- 1565 — The tarot's Death card is numbered 13 by this date, when Francesco Piscina's Discorso cites its number.
- 1834 — The earliest clear references to an unlucky Friday the 13th, both French: the Marquis de Salvo in the Revue de Paris, and the play Les Finesses des Gribouilles.
- 1882 — The Thirteen Club of Manhattan holds its first dinner, thirteen to a table, on Friday, January 13.
- 1886 — The Chicago Daily Tribune of May 28 runs the belief as a "French Joke."
- 1907 — Thomas W. Lawson's novel Friday, the Thirteenth records the belief among Wall Street traders rather than inventing it.
- 1993 — The BMJ publishes "Is Friday the 13th bad for your health?", a small single-region study.
faq:
Did the Knights Templar arrests of Friday, October 13, 1307 start this?

No. That date is right, but nobody appears to have connected it to the superstition until the twentieth century, and the link was popularized by Dan Brown's The Da Vinci Code. Without medieval evidence, the Library of Congress treats it as a modern guess.

Did a 1907 novel invent the superstition?

No, though that is often claimed. In Thomas W. Lawson's Friday, the Thirteenth the characters already call the date "the Wall Street hoodoo-day" and treat the belief as a tradition, and the plot turns on traders exploiting a fear their colleagues hold. Lawson, himself a stock manipulator, was describing the floor he worked on.

Was Loki the thirteenth guest at a dinner of the Norse gods?

There was no dinner party. Neither the Poetic nor the Prose Edda, the primary sources for Baldr's death, describes a banquet or says how many gods were present. National Geographic paraphrased the story in 2011 from an interview with Donald Dossey.

Is Friday the 13th actually more dangerous?

The best-known research is a 1993 BMJ paper covering one English health region. It found fewer vehicles on part of the M25 on Friday the 13th than on Friday the 6th, more admissions from transport accidents (65 against 45), and put the added risk at "as much as 52%." Small numbers from one place, and the closing advice — "Staying at home is recommended" — indicates the spirit of it.

How often does Friday the 13th happen?

At least once and at most three times a year, with no exceptions from 1900 to 2300. 2026 has three: February 13, March 13, and November 13. 2027 has one, August 13.

- Library of Congress, Folklife Today, Who's Afraid of Friday the Thirteenth? (Stephanie Hall, January 12, 2017) — https://blogs.loc.gov/folklife/2017/01/whos-afraid-of-friday-the-thirteenth/ → Friday as a day fit for endings, fishermen staying ashore, and journeys not begun; the Thirteen Club of Manhattan's first dinner for thirteen on Friday, January 13, 1882, and the Library's copy of the address from its thirteenth regular meeting; Tuesday the 13th in Spanish-speaking countries and Greece; Friday the 17th in Italy and the XVII-to-VIXI rearrangement; the number 4 in Japan; and this post's own finding of no American newspaper reference before 1900, which the 2024 post supersedes.
- T. J. Scanlon, R. N. Luben, F. L. Scanlon and N. Singleton, Is Friday the 13th bad for your health?, BMJ 1993;307(6919):1584-1586, doi 10.1136/bmj.307.6919.1584 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1697765/ → the South West Thames retrospective design; fewer vehicles on the southern M25 on Friday the 13th than Friday the 6th; transport-accident admissions 65 against 45 (p < 0.05); the "as much as 52%" and "Staying at home is recommended" conclusions.

name: Good Friday
description: Good Friday is the Friday before Easter, the day Christians commemorate the crucifixion and death of Jesus, and the one day in the year on which the Catholic Church celebrates no Mass. It is not a federal holiday in the United States, although the stock exchanges close for it and eleven states treat it as a holiday of some kind — which makes it one of the harder days on the American calendar to sum up in a sentence.
body:
### History

Christians kept Friday as a fast from the earliest times, and by the late fourth century Jerusalem had a Good Friday liturgy detailed enough that we can still read a description of it. Egeria, a pilgrim whose account is dated to roughly 381 to 384, records a chair set for the bishop at Golgotha behind the Cross and pilgrims filing past to touch the wood and the titulus with their foreheads and then their eyes. "The emotion shown and the mourning by all the people at every lesson and prayer is wonderful," she wrote. The veneration of the cross began there and entered the Latin liturgy in the seventh or eighth century.

The date follows Easter, and Easter follows the Council of Nicaea of 325, which acted to put the whole Church on one Sunday. The familiar formula — the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the vernal equinox — is how the Church later worked the rule out rather than a quotation from Nicaea, and its moon is a tabulated ecclesiastical one, not the astronomical moon.

The day also has a history worth stating rather than skipping. The Good Friday intercessions long carried a prayer describing the Jews as perfidis, and the kneeling that accompanied every other intercession was omitted for that one. The day was physically dangerous for Jews in medieval Europe, where Jewish houses were commonly attacked with stones. Pope John XXIII dropped perfidis from the Latin prayer in 1959, though the 1962 missal still spoke of the Jews' blindness and their conversion. In 1965 Nostra Aetate held that Christ's passion "cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction" nor against the Jews of today, and decried antisemitism "at any time and by anyone." The prayer has been reworded since; it still asks that Jewish hearts be illuminated to recognize Christ, and still troubles many.

### How to observe

The central service is the Celebration of the Lord's Passion, normally about three in the afternoon and never later than nine at night. It is not a Mass. The celebrant and deacon prostrate themselves in silence to begin; all three readings, including the Passion according to John, are required; the priest is first to venerate the cross; and Communion comes from the sacrament reserved the day before. For Catholics between 18 and 59 this is the second of the year's two obligatory fast days, with abstinence from meat from age 14.

Beyond the liturgy there is the Three Hour Service between noon and three, a Jesuit-introduced meditation on the seven last words, and the Stations of the Cross, which began with pilgrims tracing the Via Dolorosa in Jerusalem. The day also carries the collection for the Holy Land, established by Paul VI in 1974 to maintain the sacred sites and support local Christian communities.
timeline:
- 325 — The First Council of Nicaea acts to put the whole Church on a single Easter Sunday, fixing Good Friday as the Friday before it.
- c. 381–384 — Egeria, a pilgrim to Jerusalem, leaves the earliest detailed description of a Good Friday liturgy: the bishop's chair at Golgotha and the veneration of the cross.
- Good Friday 1727 — Bach's St Matthew Passion is first heard at St Thomas's Church in Leipzig, written for Good Friday vespers.
- 1959 — Pope John XXIII drops the word perfidis from the Latin Good Friday prayer for the Jewish people.
- October 28, 1965 — Paul VI promulgates Nostra Aetate, holding that the passion cannot be charged against the Jews as a people and decrying antisemitism by anyone.
faq:
Is Good Friday a federal holiday?
No. The eleven federal holidays are set by 5 U.S.C. 6103, and Good Friday is not among them. The Federal Reserve does not observe it either, so banks are generally open.

Then why is the stock market closed?
The exchanges set their own calendars, and the NYSE and Nasdaq both close. The bond market follows a SIFMA recommendation that varies year to year — a full close in 2025, an early close at noon in 2026 — and even those are advisory only.

Which states observe Good Friday?
Eleven, and not in the same way: statutory in Delaware, Indiana, Louisiana, North Carolina and North Dakota; a statutory half day in Kentucky; observed in Hawaii, New Jersey and Tennessee; designated by the governor in Connecticut; optional in Texas, where offices stay open.

Why is it called "Good" Friday?
Nobody is certain, and the reference works decline to settle it. The 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia says plainly that "the origin of the term Good is not clear," offering either a corruption of "God's Friday" or "good" in the older sense of holy. Other languages sidestep it: Holy Friday in the Romance languages, Sorrowful Friday in German.

Do Orthodox Christians keep the same day?
Usually not, because the Eastern churches reckon Pascha on the Julian calendar. In 2027 the two are five weeks apart — the maximum — with Western Good Friday on March 26 and Orthodox Pascha on May 2. In 2028 they coincide.

name: Groundhog Day
description: Groundhog Day falls on February 2, when a groundhog is lifted from a stump on a hill outside Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania and a man in a top hat announces whether winter has six more weeks to run. The custom arrived with German-speaking immigrants to Pennsylvania, who had attached the same Candlemas weather lore to a badger. It is also the rare American tradition whose central claim a federal agency has tested and rejected: NOAA's published track record finds no predictive skill in it.
body:
### History

February 2 is Candlemas, and the day carried weather lore in Europe for centuries before any groundhog was involved. John Ray's 1678 collection preserves the couplet in its most familiar form: "If Candlemas day be fair and bright / Winter will have another flight." In German-speaking Europe the day was also Dachstag, Badger Day, and the animal watched was the badger — if it saw its shadow it went back underground for four more weeks. That is the Library of Congress's account, following the folklorist Don Yoder. The Punxsutawney Groundhog Club's own history says hedgehog instead, and the two versions have never been reconciled.

Pennsylvania Dutch immigration ran from about 1727 to 1775, and the Library of Congress judges it likely that the American custom took shape in that period — likely, not documented. No source traces an unbroken line from European practice to the American one. The earliest known American reference, a Pennsylvania diary entry of 1840 found by Yoder, has the groundhog returning underground for forty days, not six weeks.

Punxsutawney enters the record in 1886, when the club says the phrase "groundhog day" first appeared in the local newspaper. February 2 of the following year, 1887, brought the first organized trek to Gobbler's Knob. Who organized it is contested: the Hagley Museum and Library credits the Punxsutawney Groundhog Club under the town's newspaper editor, Clymer H. Freas; the Library of Congress credits the local Elks Lodge. The groundhog was not called Punxsutawney Phil until the 1960s.

### How to observe

Gobbler's Knob sits almost two miles uphill from the Punxsutawney parking lots, and the club runs buses from three designated areas starting at 3 a.m. The stage entertainment starts then too, fireworks go off just after 6:30, and the prognostication happens at sunrise, around 7:20. It is standing room only in a rustic field in February: the club advises cash, no backpacks or bags, and says small children should not attend. Pennsylvania's tourism office streamed the 2026 ceremony free at visitpa.com with a second feed at pacast.com, and its Groundhog Day page is where the following year's links appear.

The better reason to mark the day is NOAA's scorecard. "Grading the groundhogs" ranks nineteen prognosticating animals with records of twenty years or more, and Punxsutawney Phil places seventeenth. Staten Island Chuck leads at 85 percent. In the 2026 edition, second place went to Lander Lil, who is a statue of a prairie dog in Wyoming. Reading that list teaches more about forecasting than any explanation of why a groundhog cannot do it.
timeline:
- 1678 — John Ray prints the Candlemas couplet in its familiar form: "If Candlemas day be fair and bright / Winter will have another flight."
- 1727–1775 — The period of Pennsylvania Dutch immigration in which the Library of Congress says the American holiday likely took shape.
- 1840 — The earliest known American reference to groundhog weather prediction, a Pennsylvania diary entry, which gives forty days rather than six weeks.
- 1886 — The phrase "groundhog day" first appears in the Punxsutawney newspaper, according to the Punxsutawney Groundhog Club.
- February 2, 1887 — The first organized trek to Gobbler's Knob. Hagley credits the Groundhog Club; the Library of Congress credits the local Elks Lodge.
- December 27, 2006 — The 1993 film Groundhog Day is added to the Library of Congress's National Film Registry.
faq:
Is Groundhog Day always February 2?
Yes. The date is fixed. In 2027 it falls on a Tuesday.

How accurate is Punxsutawney Phil?
Four federal figures exist and they do not agree. NOAA's "Grading the groundhogs" puts him at 35 percent, scored against U.S. February and March temperature averages from 2006 to 2025. NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information says 30 percent over the past ten years. The Library of Congress says about 40 percent and cites nothing for it. The most useful number is the raw one: NOAA's published track record for 1887 through 2017 counts 103 shadows, 18 no-shadows and 10 years with no record, and concludes that the table shows "no predictive skill for the groundhog during the most recent years of this analysis."

Was the original animal a badger or a hedgehog?
Contested. The Library of Congress, following Don Yoder, and Smithsonian Magazine both say badger — Candlemas was Dachstag, Badger Day, across much of German-speaking Europe. The Punxsutawney Groundhog Club says German lore used the hedgehog. Nothing resolves it.

Where does "six more weeks of winter" come from?
Not from the European lore, as far as the record goes. The German badger version gave four more weeks. The 1840 Pennsylvania diary and Hagley's account of the Candlemas belief both give forty days. No reputable source traces the six-week figure back to Europe.

Is Groundhog Day a federal holiday?
No. Federal offices, banks and post offices operate normally. Pennsylvania promotes the day through its state tourism office, which is a different thing.

Source conflicts, resolved and disclosed. First, 1886 versus 1887: the club's own pages distinguish the two, 1886 being the first newspaper mention and 1887 the first organized trek, and this page follows that split rather than picking a founding year. Second, who organized the 1887 trek: Hagley says the Punxsutawney Groundhog Club under the editor Clymer H. Freas, the Library of Congress says the local Elks Lodge, and nothing reconciles them, so both are named. Third, badger versus hedgehog: the Library of Congress citing Don Yoder, and Smithsonian, say badger; the founding organization says hedgehog; both are named. Fourth, accuracy: four federal figures disagree, so the page gives the spread and leads with NOAA's raw tally rather than averaging them.

Not claimed, for want of a source: any attendance figure (the club says over 30,000 for 2025, the Associated Press says about 10,000 in recent years, Pennsylvania's tourism office projected 40,000, and the club's own page contradicts itself at 35,000 for 1997 — there is no audited count); that Clymer Freas edited the Punxsutawney Spirit specifically, founded the holiday, or named Phil (Hagley says only that he was the town's newspaper editor and led the club); Phil's age or that he is the same groundhog seen in 1887, which is the club's own claim; any before-and-after attendance or economic figure for the 1993 film; and that the 1886 newspaper item can be read against a digitized original, which could not be confirmed.

Rejected as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate, history.com, and content-farm or AI-generated listicles. Encyclopaedia Britannica's Groundhog Day article was reachable but its body text did not retrieve, so nothing here is cited to it.

name: Halloween
description: Halloween falls on October 31 and is, by most measures, the most widely observed non-federal holiday in the United States. It is also one of the least historically tidy: what Americans do on October 31 is a composite of a Gaelic harvest festival, a Catholic feast, Scottish and Irish neighborhood customs, and a twentieth-century American candy industry that found the whole thing extremely useful.
body:
### History

The evening takes its name from the Christian calendar. In the eighth century, Pope Gregory III designated November 1 as a day to honor the saints; Christian missionaries later placed All Souls' Day on November 2. The night before November 1 became All Hallows' Eve, and then Halloween.

Older than the name is Samhain — a Gaelic festival marking the end of summer and the harvest, pronounced SAH-win. Samhain is almost always described as Halloween's ancestor, and it is a genuine precursor. But the line is not as direct as it is usually told: the specific things Americans do on October 31 arrived by way of centuries of Christian observance and then nineteenth-century Irish and Scottish immigration, not as an unbroken inheritance from pre-Christian Ireland. The jack-o'-lantern, for instance, began in Ireland as a carved turnip. Pumpkins — native to North America, larger, and far easier to hollow out — were a New World substitution.

Going door to door has two sourced precursors. Souling, a medieval practice, sent the poor and especially children from house to house on All Souls' Day offering prayers for the dead in exchange for food or money. Guising, a Scottish custom, was its secular descendant: a costume, a performance, a small payment. The phrase "trick or treat" itself is recent — first recorded in 1927 — and the practice spread through the United States during the 1920s. In the early 1930s, community groups actively promoted it as a way to redirect Halloween pranking, which had grown destructive enough to worry municipalities.

What made it universal was mass culture and sugar. A 1951 Peanuts strip had Charlie Brown saying "tricks or treats"; Disney released a Donald Duck short called Trick or Treat in 1952. The end of wartime sugar rationing did the rest, and the custom became general through the 1950s.

### How to observe

Carve a turnip instead of a pumpkin at least once. It is genuinely difficult, which is the point — it explains immediately why the pumpkin won.

Check your municipality's trick-or-treat hours before the 31st. Many American towns set official windows, and a surprising number schedule them on a different evening entirely when October 31 falls awkwardly. Local government sites post them; assuming October 31 at dusk is how families end up on empty streets.

If you want the unmediated version of Halloween's American history, the Library of Congress's Chronicling America archive holds digitized newspapers back to the 1700s. Searching "Halloween" against your own town in the 1890s through 1920s turns up the parties, the pranks, and the civic hand-wringing as they were actually reported — including the vandalism that trick-or-treating was invented to absorb.
timeline:
- 43 CE — Rome conquers the British Isles. The harvest festival of Pomona, goddess of fruit trees, is later connected to bobbing for apples.
- 8th century — Pope Gregory III designates November 1 to honor the saints. The evening before becomes All Hallows' Eve.
- Middle Ages — Souling: the poor go door to door on All Souls' Day, offering prayers for the dead in return for food or money.
- 1880s–1908 — The American Halloween candy industry takes shape. A candymaker at Philadelphia's Wunderle Candy Company is credited with candy corn in the 1880s; the Goelitz Company takes it mass-market in 1898. William W. Kolb, a Newark candymaker, is credited with the candy apple in 1908.
- 1927 — "Trick or treat" is recorded in print for the first time.
- 1951–1952 — Peanuts and Disney put the phrase in front of a national audience; trick-or-treating becomes general over the decade that follows.
faq:
Is Halloween always October 31?
Yes. Unlike Thanksgiving or Easter, the date is fixed. In 2026 it falls on a Saturday.

Is Halloween a federal holiday?
No. Federal offices, banks, and post offices operate normally, and there is no observed day off. It is among the most widely marked days in the country and has no official status at all.

Why do we say "trick or treat"?
The phrase is first recorded in 1927 and spread with the custom through the 1920s and 1930s. The "trick" was not rhetorical — Halloween pranking was serious enough in the early 1930s that community groups promoted treat-giving specifically to head it off.

Why pumpkins instead of turnips?
The jack-o'-lantern is an Irish tradition that used turnips. Pumpkins are native to North America, far bigger, and much easier to carve, so Irish immigrants switched.

When did trick-or-treating actually become common?
It spread in the 1920s, was promoted in the 1930s as an alternative to vandalism, and became general in the 1950s after sugar rationing ended.
