name: Independence Day
description: Independence Day marks July 4, 1776, the day the Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence. It does not mark the vote for independence, which came two days earlier, or the signing, which mostly happened a month later. John Adams, who was in the room, expected Americans to celebrate July 2 forever.
body:
### History

The sequence is documented in detail by the National Archives, which holds the engrossed Declaration. Richard Henry Lee of Virginia put the motion on the floor in Philadelphia on June 7, 1776, calling for the colonies to be "free and independent States." On June 11 Congress postponed consideration, seven colonies to five with New York abstaining, and recessed for three weeks — but first it appointed a Committee of Five to draft the statement of the case: John Adams, Roger Sherman, Benjamin Franklin, Robert R. Livingston, and Thomas Jefferson. Jefferson wrote the initial draft.

Congress adopted the Lee Resolution on July 2, 1776, twelve of the thirteen colonies in favor and New York not voting. That was the decision. July 4 is the day Congress finished revising Jefferson's text and adopted the Declaration itself, late that morning; John Dunlap printed the first copies that night. On July 19 Congress ordered the document engrossed on parchment and every member to sign it, and the signing began at the table on August 2, Hancock first. Eventually 56 delegates signed, not all of them present that day. The National Archives is explicit that the familiar picture of all the delegates signing on July 4 is a misconception.

Adams had no doubt which date would matter, and he was wrong. Writing to Abigail on July 3, 1776 — the letter is in the Adams Family Papers at the Massachusetts Historical Society — he said the Second Day of July "will be celebrated, by succeeding Generations, as the great anniversary Festival," a "Day of Deliverance" to be "solemnized with Pomp and Parade, with Shews, Games, Sports, Guns, Bells, Bonfires and Illuminations." He described the festivities almost exactly and missed the date by two days.

The holiday itself took decades to settle. The Library of Congress notes that observing Independence Day became commonplace only after the War of 1812. Congress made it a federal holiday on June 28, 1870, for the District of Columbia, alongside New Year's Day, Christmas, and Thanksgiving — the first four. It now sits among the eleven legal public holidays in 5 U.S.C. 6103.

The document's central contradiction was named early, by the people it excluded. On July 5, 1852, at Corinthian Hall in Rochester, New York, Frederick Douglass gave the keynote at an Independence Day celebration and told the room: "This Fourth of July is yours, not mine. You may rejoice, I must mourn."

### How to observe

Read the Declaration to the end. Nearly everyone knows the second paragraph; the bulk of it is a list of grievances against the Crown, and the closing lines carry the names of men putting their signatures to treason — which is what the August 2 signing was.

Read Douglass's 1852 address alongside it. It is one of the sharpest things ever written about the Declaration, by someone it did not cover.

Check when your day off actually falls. July 4, 2027 is a Sunday, so the federal holiday that year is Monday, July 5.
timeline:
- June 7, 1776 — Richard Henry Lee presents his resolution in Philadelphia calling for the colonies to be "free and independent States."
- June 11, 1776 — Congress postpones the resolution, seven colonies to five with New York abstaining, and appoints the Committee of Five to draft a statement of the case.
- July 2, 1776 — Congress adopts the Lee Resolution, twelve colonies in favor and New York not voting. This is the vote for independence.
- July 4, 1776 — Congress finishes its revisions and adopts the Declaration of Independence; John Dunlap prints the first broadsides that night.
- August 2, 1776 — The engrossed Declaration is signed at the table, Hancock first; 56 delegates sign in all, not all of them present that day.
- June 28, 1870 — Congress makes Independence Day a federal holiday in the District of Columbia, among the first four.
faq:
Is Independence Day a federal holiday?
Yes, and one of the original four. Congress made it a holiday in the District of Columbia on June 28, 1870, alongside New Year's Day, Christmas, and Thanksgiving. It is now among the eleven legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103.

What happens when July 4 falls on a weekend?
Federal employees observe it on the nearest weekday: the preceding Friday when July 4 is a Saturday, and the following Monday when it is a Sunday. July 4, 2027 falls on a Sunday, so the federal holiday is Monday, July 5, 2027.

Did the Founders sign the Declaration on July 4, 1776?
Mostly no. Congress adopted the text on July 4, but it did not order the document engrossed on parchment until July 19, and the signing began on August 2. Of the 56 eventual signers, not all were even present that day. The National Archives calls the July 4 signing a misconception.

Why isn't Independence Day on July 2?
Because the holiday follows the Declaration's adoption rather than the vote for independence. Congress voted to separate from Britain on July 2, 1776 and adopted the Declaration on July 4. Adams expected July 2 to be the anniversary, and wrote to Abigail on July 3 saying exactly that.

White Jr.'s quoted hope to "hail with them the approach of the glorious natal day of the Great Republic."
- Library of Congress, A Cause for Celebration: Federal Holidays and Observances, Part 1 (In Custodia Legis) — https://blogs.loc.gov/law/2024/03/a-cause-for-celebration-federal-holidays-and-observances-part-1/ → Congress first establishing public holidays in 1870 — New Year's Day, Independence Day, Christmas and Thanksgiving — in the District of Columbia, and the eleven legal public holidays now documented in 5 U.S.C. 6103.
- Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture, A Nation's Story: "What to the Slave is the Fourth of July?" — https://nmaahc.si.edu/explore/stories/nations-story-what-slave-fourth-july → the July 5, 1852 date; Corinthian Hall in Rochester, New York; Douglass delivering the keynote at an Independence Day celebration commemorating the Declaration; and the quoted lines "This Fourth of July is yours, not mine, You may rejoice, I must mourn."
- U.S. Office of Personnel Management, Federal Holidays — https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/pay-leave/federal-holidays/ → Independence Day as a legal public holiday under 5 U.S.C. 6103; the Saturday-to-preceding-Friday rule under 5 U.S.C. 6103(b) and the Sunday-to-following-Monday rule under Executive Order 11582.

Note on a source conflict: the Library of Congress describes the Declaration as "unanimously adopted" on July 4, 1776, while the National Archives records that New York abstained on June 11 and did not vote on July 2. This page follows the National Archives, as the more primary source and the custodian of the document, and gives the vote counts rather than calling July 4 unanimous.

name: Indigenous Peoples' Day
description: Indigenous Peoples' Day is observed on the second Monday in October, the same day as the federal Columbus Day holiday, and in a great many places it is marked instead of it. It began as a municipal decision: in 1992, weeks before the 500th anniversary of Columbus's arrival, Berkeley, California renamed the day — the first city in the United States to do so. It is not itself a federal holiday.
body:
### History

The immediate trigger was a celebration. In the 1980s President Ronald Reagan created the Christopher Columbus Quincentenary Jubilee Commission, whose plans included sailing replicas of Columbus's ships into San Francisco Bay. Berkeley residents and Native leaders organized to counterprotest and called themselves Resistance 500. One of them, John Curl, has described how the group persuaded the Berkeley City Council in 1992 to drop Columbus Day and observe Indigenous Peoples' Day in its place; Loni Hancock, then the city's mayor, later said the request was the first time she had understood the holiday's effect on Indigenous people. Berkeley first observed the day on October 12, 1992. The replica ships never sailed.

The city's own account is brief and unambiguous. A 2022 Berkeley council document states that "in 1992, Berkeley became the first city in the United States to rename as Indigenous Peoples' Day the federal holiday formerly recognized as Columbus Day," credits the change with prompting revisions to the school district's history curriculum, and counts nearly 130 cities and 20 states observing the day as of that year. Neither that document nor contemporary reporting gives a resolution number or a council vote date, so this page does not state one.

South Dakota had arrived somewhere similar two years earlier, under a different name. Its 1990 legislature established Native Americans' Day on the second Monday in October, a day the statute describes as "dedicated to the remembrance of the great Native American leaders who contributed so much to the history of our state." South Dakota's enumerated holidays carry that day and do not include Columbus Day.

Federal recognition has so far come by proclamation rather than statute. On October 8, 2021, President Biden signed Proclamation 10283, designating October 11, 2021 as Indigenous Peoples' Day. It names one date, sets no recurring rule, and does not mention Columbus Day — and he signed a separate Columbus Day proclamation for that same date the same day.

### How to observe

Read Proclamation 10283 and Proclamation 10281 side by side. Both were signed on October 8, 2021, both designate October 11, and neither acknowledges the other. The first recognizes Tribal Nations' "inherent sovereignty"; the second acknowledges "the painful history of wrongs and atrocities that many European explorers inflicted."

Find out what your own state or city calls the day, and whether anything closes. The designation is almost always a state statute or a municipal resolution rather than anything federal, and the name varies — in South Dakota it is Native Americans' Day.

Learn whose land you are on, by name. Berkeley's land acknowledgement work identifies the city as the ancestral and unceded home of the Ohlone people and names the Confederated Villages of Lisjan and the Sogorea Te' Land Trust. That specificity is the substance of the thing, and most places have an equivalent. Berkeley's own observance has continued since 1992 as an annual Pow Wow.
timeline:
- 1980s — President Ronald Reagan creates the Christopher Columbus Quincentenary Jubilee Commission. Its plan to sail replica ships into San Francisco Bay prompts a Bay Area counterprotest group, Resistance 500.
- 1990 — The South Dakota legislature establishes Native Americans' Day on the second Monday in October.
- 1992 — Berkeley, California becomes the first city in the United States to rename the federal Columbus Day holiday as Indigenous Peoples' Day.
- October 12, 1992 — Berkeley observes Indigenous Peoples' Day for the first time.
- October 8, 2021 — President Biden signs Proclamation 10283, designating October 11, 2021 as Indigenous Peoples' Day, and a separate proclamation naming the same date Columbus Day.
- 2022 — A City of Berkeley council document counts nearly 130 cities and 20 states observing the day.
faq:
Is Indigenous Peoples' Day a federal holiday?
No. The list of legal public holidays at 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) does not include it. The federal recognition it has had is Proclamation 10283, signed October 8, 2021, which designated one specific date, October 11, 2021.

Does Indigenous Peoples' Day replace Columbus Day?
That depends entirely on where you are. Because it is a state or local designation, some places observe it instead of Columbus Day, some alongside it, and some not at all. South Dakota's holiday statute is an example of full replacement: it lists Native Americans' Day on the second Monday in October and does not list Columbus Day.

Why does South Dakota call it Native Americans' Day?
That is the name in the 1990 statute that created it, which describes the day as "dedicated to the remembrance of the great Native American leaders who contributed so much to the history of our state." The phrase "Indigenous Peoples' Day" does not appear in South Dakota's holiday statutes.

Is Indigenous Peoples' Day always the second Monday in October?
Where it is observed as an alternative to Columbus Day, yes — that is the day the federal Columbus Day holiday falls on. The 2021 presidential proclamation, however, designated only a single date and set no recurring rule.

- City of Berkeley, Council item of October 11, 2022, Land Acknowledgement Recognizing Berkeley as the Ancestral, Unceded Home of the Ohlone People — https://berkeleyca.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2022-10-11%20Item%2019%20Land%20Acknowledgement%20Recognizing%20Berkeley.pdf → that in 1992 Berkeley became the first city in the United States to rename as Indigenous Peoples' Day the federal holiday formerly recognized as Columbus Day; that the change prompted revisions to the school district's history curriculum; the count of nearly 130 cities and 20 states as of 2022; Berkeley as the ancestral and unceded home of the Ohlone people, and the Confederated Villages of Lisjan and Sogorea Te' Land Trust.
- KQED, How Berkeley Became the First City to Ditch Columbus Day for Indigenous Peoples Day — https://www.kqed.org/news/11621763/how-berkeley-became-the-first-city-to-ditch-columbus-day-for-indigenous-peoples-day → the Reagan-era Christopher Columbus Quincentenary Jubilee Commission and the planned replica-ship voyage into San Francisco Bay; the formation of Resistance 500; John Curl as an organizer and his account of persuading the City Council in 1992; then-mayor Loni Hancock's recollection; Berkeley first observing the day on October 12, 1992; the annual Indigenous Peoples Day Pow Wow; that the replica-ship voyage never happened.
- Federal Register, Proclamation 10283, Indigenous Peoples' Day, 2021, 86 FR 57307 — https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2021/10/14/2021-22583/indigenous-peoples-day-2021 → the proclamation number and its October 8, 2021 signing by President Biden; the designation of October 11, 2021; the absence of any recurring formula; the quoted references to inherent sovereignty and to trust and treaty obligations; that it does not mention Columbus Day.
- Federal Register, Proclamation 10281, Columbus Day, 2021, 86 FR 57007 — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2021-10-14/pdf/2021-22514.pdf → the separate Columbus Day proclamation signed the same day, October 8, 2021, designating the same date, October 11, 2021; the quoted acknowledgement of wrongs and atrocities inflicted on Tribal Nations and Indigenous communities.
- South Dakota Legislature, Codified Law 1-5-1.2, Native Americans' Day established — https://sdlegislature.gov/api/Statutes/1-5-1.2.html → the statutory text establishing Native Americans' Day on the second Monday in October as a legal state holiday, and its dedication to the remembrance of Native American leaders; the source note SL 1990, ch 7, section 2, giving the 1990 enactment.
- South Dakota Legislature, Codified Law 1-5-1, Holidays enumerated — https://sdlegislature.gov/api/Statutes/1-5-1.html?all=true → that the enumerated holidays include the second Monday in October as Native Americans' Day and do not include Columbus Day.
- U.S. Government Publishing Office, 5 U.S.C. 6103, 2024 edition — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title5/pdf/USCODE-2024-title5-partIII-subpartE-chap61-subchapI-sec6103.pdf → the full list of legal public holidays, which contains Columbus Day on the second Monday in October and does not contain Indigenous Peoples' Day.

Omitted for lack of a source: the frequently repeated claim that the proposal to replace Columbus Day originated at a 1977 United Nations conference in Geneva, which none of the primary or reputable sources consulted here documents; the claim that Proclamation 10283 was the first presidential proclamation of Indigenous Peoples' Day, which the Federal Register document does not state; a Berkeley resolution number or council vote date for the 1992 action.

name: Juneteenth
description: Juneteenth marks June 19, 1865 — the day Major General Gordon Granger issued General Order No. 3 at Galveston, informing the people of Texas that all enslaved people were free. The Emancipation Proclamation had taken effect two and a half years earlier, and the distance between those two dates is the substance of the holiday: a freedom declared and a freedom enforced are not the same thing. Texas made the day a legal state holiday in 1980; Congress added it to the federal holiday list in 2021.
body:
### History

President Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation declared enslaved people free as of January 1, 1863, but it did not end slavery in the nation. Enforcement followed the Union Army, and the Army had not reached Texas. The Library of Congress records that Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox Court House on April 9, 1865 "had not impacted Texas," and that many plantation owners refused to acknowledge the war was over or to release the people they held — a refusal that continued even after General Order No. 3 was issued.

Two Union arrivals changed that. On June 5, 1865, a brigade of the 25th Army Corps, more than 1,000 soldiers of African descent, captured Galveston and spread word of freedom; Civil War historians estimate that thousands of enslaved people reached freedom because of them. On June 19, Granger, commanding the Headquarters District of Texas, issued General Order No. 3 and read it to the people of Galveston.

The order is short and worth reading whole. It announces that "in accordance with a proclamation from the Executive of the United States, all slaves are free," involving "an absolute equality of personal rights and rights of property between former masters and slaves." It then advises the freed people "to remain quietly at their present homes and work for wages" and warns that they "will not be supported in idleness." The National Archives, which holds the original handwritten record, notes that the racist language of those closing sentences foreshadowed how long the fight for equal rights would run. The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified later that year, made slavery unconstitutional nationwide.

### How to observe

Read General Order No. 3 in full. It takes a minute, and the National Archives prints the complete text. The closing lines, telling newly freed people not to collect at military posts and not to expect support "in idleness," are the part commemorations leave out, and they change the document's character.

Visit an emancipation ground. In many parts of Texas, freedmen and women bought land specifically for Juneteenth gatherings: Emancipation Park in Houston, purchased in 1872, is the best documented, and what is now Booker T. Washington Park in Mexia and Emancipation Park in Austin were acquired the same way.

Put red soda water on the table. The Texas State Library and Archives records it alongside prayer services, readings of the Emancipation Proclamation, accounts from formerly enslaved people, rodeos and dances in the early celebrations, which African American Texans treated like the Fourth of July. For the documentary version, the Library of Congress's Chronicling America archive holds the Dallas Herald of July 1, 1865, which printed the order two weeks after Galveston heard it.
timeline:
- January 1, 1863 — The Emancipation Proclamation takes effect, declaring enslaved people in the rebelling states free. It does not end slavery nationwide.
- June 19, 1865 — Major General Gordon Granger issues General Order No. 3 at Galveston, announcing that all enslaved people in Texas are free.
- 1866 — Large June 19 celebrations begin in Texas and continue regularly into the early twentieth century.
- 1872 — Freedmen and women in Houston purchase the land that becomes Emancipation Park, one of several Texas "emancipation grounds."
- January 1, 1980 — Texas House Bill 1016, passed by the 66th Legislature, takes effect, making June 19 a legal state holiday as Emancipation Day in Texas.
- June 17, 2021 — President Biden signs the Juneteenth National Independence Day Act, Public Law 117-17, adding Juneteenth to the federal holiday list.
faq:
Is Juneteenth a federal holiday?
Yes. The Juneteenth National Independence Day Act, Public Law 117-17, was approved June 17, 2021, inserting "Juneteenth National Independence Day, June 19" into the legal public holidays at 5 U.S.C. 6103(a), directly after Memorial Day. It is the eleventh holiday on that list and the first added since the Martin Luther King, Jr. holiday in 1983.

Why is Juneteenth on June 19 and not January 1?
January 1, 1863 is when the Emancipation Proclamation took effect; June 19, 1865 is when enforcement reached Texas. Juneteenth commemorates the second date, which is rather the point: the proclamation freed people on paper in places the Union Army did not yet control.

Did General Order No. 3 end slavery in the United States?
No. It applied to Texas. People remained enslaved in the border states that had stayed loyal to the Union, and the Thirteenth Amendment, ratified later in 1865, made slavery unconstitutional throughout the country.

When did Juneteenth become a Texas state holiday?
House Bill 1016, passed in the regular session of the 66th Texas Legislature, made June 19 a legal state holiday as "Emancipation Day in Texas," effective at the start of 1980.

name: Kwanzaa
description: Kwanzaa runs for seven days, from December 26 through January 1, and is an African American and Pan-African holiday organized around seven principles rather than a single event. Maulana Karenga created it in 1966, which makes it unusual among holidays: its founder is living, has published a book on it, and maintains an authoritative account of what it is. One thing it is not, on his own insistence, is a substitute for Christmas.
body:
### History

Karenga created Kwanzaa in 1966 out of Kawaida, a cultural nationalist philosophy holding that the central challenge in Black life is the challenge of culture — that what is needed is to bring forth the best of that culture, ancient and current, and build from it. By his own account the holiday was made "in the midst of our struggles for liberation" and formed part of the work of his organization, Us, "to create, recreate and circulate African culture as an aid to building community, enriching Black consciousness, and reaffirming the value of cultural grounding for life and struggle." The Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture describes the same founding more plainly, as a response to cultural disconnection among African Americans.

The name comes from the Swahili phrase matunda ya kwanza, "first fruits," and the holiday is modeled on African first-fruits harvest celebrations — Karenga names the seven-day Umkhosi of Zululand in particular as a reason for its length. The larger reason is the Nguzo Saba, the seven principles, one per day: Umoja (unity), Kujichagulia (self-determination), Ujima (collective work and responsibility), Ujamaa (cooperative economics), Nia (purpose), Kuumba (creativity), and Imani (faith). Swahili is used because it is a Pan-African language rather than the language of one nation or group. Even the spelling carries its own history: kwanza has six letters, and in the early days of Us there were seven children who each wanted one, so an extra "a" was added.

Karenga is direct about two misreadings. Kwanzaa is a cultural choice, not a religious one, and so not an alternative to anyone's faith. And he draws a sharp line between Ujamaa, the cooperative economics of artists and vendors supplying Kwanzaa materials, and corporate attempts to "penetrate and dominate the community Kwanzaa market" by borrowing the holiday's language to sell things.

### How to observe

Kwanzaa has a set form, and the founder's site is blunt that without definite guidelines and core values there is no holiday. A Kwanzaa Set is arranged in a central place at home: African cloth, then the mkeka (mat), then the kinara (candle holder) holding the mishumaa saba, the seven candles — one black, three red, three green, for the people, their struggle, and the hope that comes from the struggle. The black candle, Umoja, stands at the center and is lit first; the rest follow left to right over the week, so that the people come first, then the struggle, then the hope.

The greeting is "Habari gani?" and the answer is the day's principle: Umoja on the 26th, Kujichagulia on the 27th, and so on through Imani.

Gifts go mainly to children and should always include a book and a heritage symbol — the book for the African value of learning, the symbol to reaffirm tradition. On December 31, the sixth day, comes Karamu, a large feast. Karenga asks that Kwanzaa's symbols not be mixed with those of another culture, which he frames as a matter of Kujichagulia.
timeline:
- 1966 — Maulana Karenga creates Kwanzaa, out of the Kawaida philosophy and the work of his organization Us.
- 1997 — The U.S. Postal Service issues the first Kwanzaa commemorative stamp on October 22, from a painting by Synthia Saint James commissioned the year before.
- 2004, 2009, 2011, 2013 — The Postal Service issues four further Kwanzaa stamp designs.
- 2008 — Karenga publishes Kwanzaa: A Celebration of Family, Community and Culture (University of Sankore Press), the book his official site summarizes.
- 2016 — A Kwanzaa Forever stamp is dedicated at Charleston's MOJA Arts Festival; December 26 of that year marks the holiday's fiftieth anniversary.
faq:
What are the seven dates of Kwanzaa?

December 26 through January 1, every year. The dates are fixed, so unlike Easter or Thanksgiving there is nothing to look up.

Is Kwanzaa a religious holiday?

No. Karenga is explicit that it is a cultural choice rather than a religious one, and that nobody has to give up a religion to practice a culture. The Postal Service and the Smithsonian both describe it as non-religious.

Is Kwanzaa meant to replace Christmas?

No, and the founder says so directly: Kwanzaa "is not a reaction or substitute for anything." Some celebrants treat it as an alternative to the commercial side of other holidays, but Karenga's position is that this is not its function. Many families keep both.

Why is there an extra "a" in Kwanzaa?

The Swahili word kwanza has six letters. In the early days of the Us organization seven children each wanted to represent a letter, so a seventh was added.

Can people who are not of African descent take part?

Karenga's answer is yes, with a distinction: Kwanzaa is an African holiday created for African peoples, and while public celebrations — at a school or college, say — can include others, the ritual itself should be conducted by the community whose holiday it is. As he puts it, audience attendance is one thing and conducting a ritual another.

name: Labor Day
description: Labor Day falls on the first Monday in September and honors the American labor movement and the people whose work built the country. It began as a union parade in New York City on a Tuesday in September 1882, spread one state legislature at a time through the 1880s, and became a federal holiday in June 1894 — in the middle of a national railroad strike that federal troops had been sent to break. The timing is part of the story, not a coincidence.
body:
### History

Who first proposed Labor Day is genuinely unsettled, and the U.S. Department of Labor says so on its own history page. One candidate is Peter J. McGuire, general secretary of the Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners and a co-founder of the American Federation of Labor, reported to have called in 1882 for a general holiday for the laboring classes. The other is Matthew Maguire, a machinist who later served as secretary of Local 344 in Paterson, New Jersey, and whom many credit with proposing the holiday that same year while secretary of the Central Labor Union in New York. A Paterson newspaper called Maguire "the undisputed author of Labor Day as a holiday." The near-identical surnames have not helped, and the Labor Department declines to pick.

What is documented is the event. The Central Labor Union held the first Labor Day in New York City on Tuesday, September 5, 1882, and a second a year later on the same date. The plan was a street parade showing the strength and esprit de corps of a community's trade and labor organizations, followed by a festival for workers and their families. Speeches came later.

The states moved first. Oregon passed the first Labor Day law on February 21, 1887; Colorado, Massachusetts, New Jersey and New York followed within the year, and Connecticut, Nebraska and Pennsylvania by the decade's end. By 1894 another 23 states had adopted it.

Congress acted mid-strike. The Pullman strike ran from May 11 to July 20, 1894; President Grover Cleveland declared it a federal crime and sent troops, and two men were killed. On June 28, 1894, Congress made the first Monday in September a legal holiday and Cleveland signed it. The Library of Congress connects that speed to the need to calm tensions after the deaths.

### How to observe

Read the Department of Labor's own history of the holiday. It is short, and it refuses to settle who founded Labor Day — which makes it a better document than most of what is written about the day.

Visit Pullman National Historical Park if you are near Chicago. The planned industrial town at the center of the 1894 strike still stands as a neighborhood, and the Park Service runs a visitor center at 610 E. 111th Street. The holiday and the strike are the same year; standing in one explains the other.

Look up what your own town did. The Library of Congress's Chronicling America holds digitized American newspapers published through 1963 from nearly every state and territory. Searching your city against the 1880s and 1890s turns up the parades, picnics and arguments as they were reported — the only way to see a holiday that arrived one state at a time.
timeline:
- September 5, 1882 — The Central Labor Union holds the first Labor Day in New York City, on a Tuesday: a street parade followed by a festival for workers and their families.
- September 5, 1883 — The Central Labor Union holds its second Labor Day on the same date.
- February 21, 1887 — Oregon passes the first state Labor Day law. Colorado, Massachusetts, New Jersey and New York follow the same year.
- May 11, 1894 — The Pullman strike begins, running until July 20. Cleveland declares it a federal crime and sends troops; two men are killed.
- June 28, 1894 — Congress makes the first Monday in September a legal holiday and President Grover Cleveland signs it. By then 23 more states had adopted the holiday.
- June 28, 1968 — The Uniform Monday Holiday Act (Pub. L. 90-363) reworks the federal calendar, adding Columbus Day and moving Washington's Birthday, Memorial Day and Veterans Day. Labor Day is not among the holidays it changes.
faq:
Is Labor Day a federal holiday?
Yes. It is one of the eleven legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103, observed on the first Monday in September. Federal offices, banks and post offices close.

Who invented Labor Day?
Nobody knows for certain, and the Department of Labor says so. The two candidates are Peter J. McGuire, general secretary of the Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners, and Matthew Maguire, a machinist from Paterson, New Jersey. Both are tied to proposals in 1882, and the nearly identical surnames have kept the question open ever since.

When was the first Labor Day?
Tuesday, September 5, 1882, in New York City, organized by the Central Labor Union. It was a parade and a festival, not a day off.

Why is Labor Day in September rather than May 1?
There is no primary source for that decision in the record this page relies on, so it will not guess at one. What is documented is that the September date came from the Central Labor Union's 1882 celebration and was already law in more than twenty states before Congress adopted it in 1894.

When did Labor Day become a federal holiday?
June 28, 1894. Congress made the first Monday in September a legal holiday and President Cleveland signed it, during the Pullman strike that his own administration had sent troops to break.

name: Mardi Gras
description: Mardi Gras is Shrove Tuesday, the day immediately before Ash Wednesday, and the last day of the Carnival season. In Louisiana it is not a figure of speech but a statutory one: state law lists "the day of Mardi Gras" among the state's days of public rest and legal holidays. Almost everything Americans picture when they hear the word — krewes, floats, purple and green and gold — was worked out in New Orleans between the 1850s and the 1880s.
body:
### History

The name is French for Fat Tuesday, which Britannica traces to "the custom of using all the fats in the home before Lent." Shrove Tuesday is "the day immediately preceding Ash Wednesday (the beginning of Lent in Western Christian churches)." Pinned to Ash Wednesday rather than to a calendar date, the day moves every year; the New Orleans Public Library's City Archives publish the dates from 1947 through 2050.

Louisiana dates its own connection to 1699. "Since 1699, when Pierre Le Moyne, Sieur d'Iberville celebrated his arrival at the mouth of the Mississippi on Shrove Tuesday, Mardi Gras has been integrally linked to Louisiana's cultural heritage," the Louisiana State Museum writes. Evidence for the century that follows is thin — the museum notes "scant evidence of Carnival during the early 1700s" — but by 1781 the season was established enough that Spanish colonial authorities forbade free people of color and enslaved people to mask or mimic whites during it. The first parades were improvised, "impromptu processions formed by maskers already in the streets," with young Creole men organizing informal processions by the 1830s.

The modern machinery arrives in the 1850s. The City Archives date the Mistick Krewe of Comus to 1856 and record that "the first Mardi Gras parade was held in 1857, featuring the Mistick Krewe of Comus"; the state museum instead describes the krewe as emerging in 1857, and both years are reported below rather than reconciled. Comus staged a nighttime procession followed by a private ball, and set the pattern for everything after it, secrecy included: "the aura of mystery and surprise associated with krewes to this day was conceived by Comus."

Others followed quickly: the Twelfth Night Revelers in 1870, the Knights of Momus and Rex in 1872, the Krewe of Proteus in 1882. Rex supplied the parts that now read as official, billing its monarchs as the king and queen of Carnival and introducing a daytime parade. Purple, green and gold, the City Archives state, "are the official colors of carnival and represent justice, faith, and power."

The sharpest modern break came in 1992, when the city tied parade permits to Councilmember Dorothy Mae Taylor's ordinance barring discrimination in krewe membership. Comus, Momus and Proteus all stopped parading that year; Proteus resumed in 2000, and the Comus and Momus parades never returned.

### How to observe

Find out whether you actually have the day off, because the answer is unusually technical. Louisiana lists "the day of Mardi Gras" among its statewide legal holidays and names it for state employees, but local closure is a separate question: the statute names twenty-nine parishes, plus all municipalities, where "Mardi Gras shall be a holiday when the governing authorities so declare by ordinance."

Leave the French Quarter. Rex, the King of Carnival, parades Mardi Gras morning, and the mayor of New Orleans traditionally toasts the kings and queens of Rex and Zulu on the steps of Gallier Hall.

For the older tradition rather than the spectacle, go to a rural courir, or run — "a seemingly chaotic quest to obtain ingredients for a communal gumbo" that in fact "involves a complex system of rules." Because courirs were held in isolated areas where illiteracy was prevalent, the state museum notes, "the historical record is sketchy."
timeline:
- 1699 — Pierre Le Moyne, Sieur d'Iberville celebrates his arrival at the mouth of the Mississippi on Shrove Tuesday.
- 1781 — Spanish colonial authorities forbid free people of color and enslaved people to mask or mimic whites during the Carnival season.
- 1857 — The first Mardi Gras parade, staged by the Mistick Krewe of Comus, which the City Archives date to 1856.
- 1872 — Rex and the Knights of Momus are founded; Rex introduces a daytime parade and the king and queen of Carnival.
- 1896 — Les Mysterieuses becomes the first large-scale women's krewe.
- 1992 — A city ordinance ties parade permits to non-discrimination in krewe membership; Comus, Momus and Proteus stop parading. Proteus returns in 2000.
faq:
When is Mardi Gras?
It has no fixed date. Mardi Gras is Shrove Tuesday, the day immediately before Ash Wednesday, so it moves each year with the start of Lent. The New Orleans Public Library's City Archives publish the dates from 1947 through 2050.

Is Mardi Gras a public holiday?
In Louisiana, yes: the statute listing the state's days of public rest and legal holidays includes "the day of Mardi Gras," and state departments are told that no employee shall work on it insofar as practicable. Local closures depend on local action, since the same statute lets twenty-nine named parishes and all municipalities declare it a holiday by ordinance. It is not among the 11 federal holidays in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a).

What do purple, green and gold mean?
They are the official colors of Carnival, and the City Archives give their meanings as justice, faith and power.

What is a krewe?
A private Carnival organization that stages a parade, a ball, or both. The oldest — Comus, the Twelfth Night Revelers, Momus, Rex and Proteus — are known as the old line krewes, and three of them stopped parading in 1992.

name: Martin Luther King, Jr. Day
description: The federal holiday on the third Monday in January is, in the statute, the Birthday of Martin Luther King, Jr. — though almost everyone says Martin Luther King, Jr. Day. It took fifteen years to create: a bill was introduced four days after King was killed in 1968 and died without a vote, and the law establishing the holiday was not signed until November 2, 1983. Since 1994 federal law has also pointed the day toward community service, which makes it one of the few American holidays with an instruction attached.
body:
### History

Representative John Conyers of Michigan introduced the first bill to make King's birthday a national holiday four days after the assassination, in April 1968. Congress took no action. The campaign that eventually won ran another fifteen years and was fought in public more than in committee: Stevie Wonder's 1980 song "Happy Birthday" became its anthem, Coretta Scott King testified repeatedly, millions signed petitions, and marches in Washington in 1982 and 1983 kept the pressure on.

The bill passed both houses in 1983. President Ronald Reagan signed Public Law 98-144 on November 2, 1983, amending section 6103(a) of title 5 of the United States Code to insert a new line immediately below New Year's Day: the Birthday of Martin Luther King, Jr., the third Monday in January. The law deliberately delayed itself — the amendment took effect on January 1, 1986, more than two years after enactment. In August 1984 Reagan established a commission to prepare the first observance, and he proclaimed Monday, January 20, 1986 as the first Martin Luther King, Jr. Day.

The states moved at their own pace. South Carolina did not make the third Monday in January a regular state holiday — rather than an optional one state employees could take in place of a Confederate holiday — until an act ratified on April 26, 2000.

The service dimension came later still. On August 23, 1994, President Bill Clinton signed the King Holiday and Service Act, authorizing the Corporation for National and Community Service, in consultation with the Martin Luther King, Jr. Federal Holiday Commission, to fund service projects on the holiday reflecting King's legacy — among them "cooperation and understanding among racial and ethnic groups, nonviolent conflict resolution, equal economic and educational opportunities, and social justice."

### How to observe

Read King himself rather than quotations of him. The long pieces — the letter from the Birmingham jail, the later speeches on poverty and war — are the ones holiday programming skips in favor of four lines from 1963.

Serve, if there is something near you worth doing. The 1994 act built grant-funded projects into the day, but almost all of it is organized locally — a city volunteer office, a school district, a congregation, a food bank. Listings go up in the first week of January and the useful ones fill fast.

Visit Martin Luther King, Jr. National Historical Park in Atlanta. It holds King's birth home, the historic Ebenezer Baptist Church where he and his father preached, and the tomb of Dr. and Mrs. King on a brick island in a reflecting pool. Ranger-led programs are free. Birth home tours take fifteen people at a time, hourly from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and you register in person at Historic Fire Station No. 6 — so arrive early.
timeline:
- April 1968 — Four days after King's assassination, Rep. John Conyers of Michigan introduces the first bill to make his birthday a national holiday. Congress takes no action.
- 1980 — Stevie Wonder releases "Happy Birthday," which becomes the campaign's rallying song; marches in Washington in 1982 and 1983 build on it.
- November 2, 1983 — President Ronald Reagan signs Public Law 98-144, adding the Birthday of Martin Luther King, Jr. to 5 U.S.C. 6103 as the third Monday in January, effective January 1, 1986.
- August 27, 1984 — Reagan establishes a commission to prepare the first observance of the new holiday.
- January 20, 1986 — The first Martin Luther King, Jr. Day is observed, two days after Reagan's proclamation naming the date.
- August 23, 1994 — President Bill Clinton signs the King Holiday and Service Act, authorizing federal grants for service projects on the holiday.
faq:
What is the official name of the holiday?
The Birthday of Martin Luther King, Jr. That is how 5 U.S.C. 6103 lists it. "Martin Luther King, Jr. Day" is the common name and the one Reagan used in the 1986 proclamation.

Is the holiday on King's actual birthday?
No. King was born on January 15, 1929. The holiday is the third Monday in January, which can only fall between January 15 and January 21, so it lands on his birthday only in years when January 15 happens to be a Monday.

Why did it take fifteen years?
Conyers' 1968 bill died without action and no measure cleared both houses until 1983. The White House's own account credits public pressure rather than legislative maneuvering: Stevie Wonder's "Happy Birthday," Coretta Scott King's repeated testimony, millions of petition signatures, and the 1982 and 1983 marches in Washington.

Is it a day off or a day of service?
Both, legally. It is a federal legal public holiday, so federal offices close. The King Holiday and Service Act of 1994 separately authorized federal grants for service projects on the day, which is why much of what happens is volunteer work rather than ceremony.

Do all states observe it?
It is a federal holiday, so federal offices close everywhere. State practice took much longer to converge: South Carolina made the third Monday in January a regular rather than optional state holiday only in 2000, by an act ratified that April.

The Obama White House archive page is internally inconsistent on the signing date (a caption says November 2, 1983 and the text says November 20); this page follows the Statutes at Large, which is the primary record and gives November 2, 1983. The claim that South Carolina was the last state to adopt the holiday is widely repeated but is not asserted here, because the South Carolina act does not say so and no primary source for the ranking was found.

name: Memorial Day
description: Memorial Day falls on the last Monday in May and honors Americans who died in military service — which is the distinction that matters, because Veterans Day honors everyone who served. It began as Decoration Day, a Civil War observance of strewing flowers on graves, and carried both names for most of a century. Where it started first is genuinely disputed, and the federal government's own answer is not the only credible one.
body:
### History

The holiday's official origin is a general order. On May 5, 1868, John A. Logan, commander-in-chief of the Grand Army of the Republic — the Union veterans' organization — issued General Orders No. 11, setting aside May 30 for "strewing with flowers or otherwise decorating the graves of comrades" and asking that the country guard those graves "with sacred vigilance." Late May was chosen for the flowers: the order wanted "the choicest flowers of springtime." Logan's adjutant general, Norton P. Chipman, drafted it; Logan added several paragraphs of his own.

The first national observance followed on May 30, 1868, at Arlington National Cemetery, on grounds that then held roughly 11,250 Union dead, Black and white, and about 350 Confederate dead, more than half of them unknown. General and Mrs. Ulysses S. Grant were among those presiding, James A. Garfield — then both a general and a congressman — spoke, and the Department of Veterans Affairs puts the crowd at about 5,000.

The practice was older than the order, and the claims are crowded. Southern women were decorating soldiers' graves before the war ended, with precedents recorded in Mississippi, Virginia and South Carolina by 1865. On April 25, 1866, a women's memorial association in Columbus, Mississippi, decorated Confederate graves and the neglected Union graves beside them. Waterloo, New York, holds the federal title — Congress and President Lyndon Johnson named it the birthplace of Memorial Day in 1966, for observances beginning May 5, 1866 — while Boalsburg, Carbondale, Macon, Columbus and Richmond all have claims of their own. Earlier still, on May 1, 1865, freed Black residents of Charleston, South Carolina, together with soldiers of the 35th and 104th United States Colored Troops and the 54th Massachusetts Infantry, gathered at the city's old racetrack to honor and decorate the graves of 257 Union prisoners of war whom the retreating Confederate army had buried there in haste. The National Park Service calls it one of the earliest recorded observances and says the question of which came first is still debated.

Decoration Day gave way to Memorial Day around the turn of the twentieth century, without a decisive moment. The Uniform Monday Holiday Act of 1968 took effect in 1971, moving the holiday to the last Monday in May and extending it to Americans who died in all the nation's wars; a few states still mark May 30. In December 2000 the National Moment of Remembrance Act created the commission behind a minute of silence at 3 p.m. local time.

### How to observe

Take the 3 p.m. minute. It is the one part of this holiday with a fixed national time, and, unlike a parade, it asks nothing but that you stop.

Visit a national cemetery instead of a sale. The Department of Veterans Affairs' National Cemetery Administration keeps cemeteries in most states and publishes their locations; many hold a ceremony and a flag placement over the holiday weekend.

Read Logan's order. It is short, it is the document the holiday rests on, and its instruction — that the graves be guarded "with sacred vigilance" and kept tended for the generations that follow — is a plainer statement of the point than most of what gets said on the day.
timeline:
- May 1, 1865 — Freed Black residents of Charleston, South Carolina, with Black and white Union troops, honor and decorate the graves of 257 Union prisoners of war at the city's old racetrack — among the earliest recorded observances.
- May 5, 1866 — Waterloo, New York, begins the annual observance that Congress and President Johnson would cite in 1966 in naming it the birthplace of Memorial Day.
- May 5, 1868 — John A. Logan, commander-in-chief of the Grand Army of the Republic, issues General Orders No. 11, setting May 30 aside for decorating the graves of the war dead.
- May 30, 1868 — The first national Decoration Day is held at Arlington National Cemetery, with the Grants among those presiding and James A. Garfield speaking.
- 1971 — The Uniform Monday Holiday Act takes effect, moving the holiday to the last Monday in May and extending it to the dead of all American wars.
- December 2000 — The National Moment of Remembrance Act (Public Law 106-579) establishes the commission behind the 3 p.m. minute of silence.
faq:
Is Memorial Day a federal holiday?
Yes. It is one of the eleven legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103 and falls on the last Monday in May, so its date moves between May 25 and May 31.

What is the difference between Memorial Day and Veterans Day?
Memorial Day honors military personnel who died in service, particularly those killed in battle or from wounds sustained in battle. Veterans Day, on November 11, honors everyone who served honorably, and is largely a day for thanking living veterans.

Where did Memorial Day start?
There is no settled answer. The federal government named Waterloo, New York the birthplace in 1966; the National Park Service records a May 1, 1865 observance in Charleston, South Carolina as one of the earliest; and Boalsburg, Carbondale, Columbus, Macon and Richmond all have claims. What is documented is the start of the national observance: Logan's order of May 5, 1868 and the ceremony at Arlington that May 30.

When did Memorial Day stop being May 30?
The Uniform Monday Holiday Act of 1968 took effect in 1971, moving the observance to the last Monday in May and extending it to Americans who died in all the nation's wars. A few states still mark May 30.

What is the National Moment of Remembrance?
A minute of silence at 3 p.m. local time on Memorial Day. The National Moment of Remembrance Act of December 2000 created the White House commission that endorsed it.

name: Mother's Day
description: Mother's Day falls on the second Sunday in May, a date Congress fixed in 1914, and it was the work of one woman who spent much of the rest of her life objecting to what it became. Anna Jarvis built it as a memorial to her own mother and insisted on the singular possessive: one mother, your mother, not a general tribute to motherhood. The apostrophe held. Almost nothing else she wanted did.
body:
### History

Unusually for an American holiday, this one has a documented founder and a documented first day. Anna Maria Jarvis was born in Webster, West Virginia, on May 1, 1864. Her mother, Ann Reeves Jarvis, had organized Mothers' Day Work Clubs that cared for sick and wounded soldiers from both sides during the Civil War, and afterward arranged a Mother's Friendship Day meant to bring together the mothers of Union and Confederate veterans. When Ann died in 1905, her daughter began campaigning for a national day in her memory.

The first formal Mother's Day service was held on May 10, 1908, at Andrews Methodist Episcopal Church in Grafton, West Virginia. Jarvis herself was not there — she was at a Mother's Day event at Wanamaker's in Philadelphia — but she sent 500 white carnations for the congregation. Philadelphia newspaper publishers promoted the second Sunday in May, West Virginia passed a law recognizing the day in 1910, and other states followed.

Congress acted on May 8, 1914, with a joint resolution, H.J. Res. 263, entered in the statutes as Public Resolution No. 25 and titled "Designating the second Sunday in May as Mother's Day, and for other purposes." Woodrow Wilson issued the proclamation the next day, asking Americans to display the flag in honor of mothers whose sons had died in war.

What followed is the part Jarvis is least remembered for. She spent her later years opposing the holiday's commercial turn, objecting to florists who raised carnation prices for the occasion and to standardized greeting cards, which she regarded as a way of not writing to your mother. She died on November 24, 1948, in West Chester, Pennsylvania, at 84, having outlived her own holiday's original form by decades.

### How to observe

Write something. Jarvis's specific complaint about printed cards was that buying one is a way of avoiding the harder thing, and she is the person who built the holiday, so the objection carries some weight.

Find out about the woman the day is actually for. The original Mother's Day was a memorial service for one person, held by a daughter who had lost her, and the questions you can only ask while someone is alive are the ones the holiday was invented around.

The Grafton church where that first service was held still stands as the International Mother's Day Shrine; the National Park Service documents its place in the holiday's history and the Library of Congress holds photographs of it.

And if you want the holiday's arrival as it was actually reported, the Library of Congress's Chronicling America guide to Mother's Day collects newspaper coverage from 1908 onward. The years between 1908 and 1914 show a holiday being argued into existence rather than handed down.
timeline:
- 1905 — Ann Reeves Jarvis dies; her daughter Anna begins campaigning for a national day in her memory.
- May 10, 1908 — The first formal Mother's Day service is held at Andrews Methodist Episcopal Church in Grafton, West Virginia; Jarvis sends 500 white carnations.
- 1910 — West Virginia passes a law designating the holiday, and other states follow.
- May 8, 1914 — Congress passes H.J. Res. 263, Public Resolution No. 25, designating the second Sunday in May as Mother's Day.
- May 9, 1914 — Woodrow Wilson proclaims the first national Mother's Day, asking Americans to display the flag.
- November 24, 1948 — Anna Jarvis dies in West Chester, Pennsylvania, after years of opposing the holiday's commercialization.
faq:
Why is it "Mother's Day" and not "Mothers' Day"?
Because the singular possessive was the point. Jarvis meant a day for each person's own mother rather than a tribute to mothers in general, and the 1914 joint resolution uses that spelling in its title.

Is Mother's Day a federal holiday?
No. Federal holidays are set by law, under 5 U.S.C. 6103, and Mother's Day is not among them. The 1914 resolution designated the day and asked for the flag to be displayed; it did not create a day off.

Who founded Mother's Day?
Anna Maria Jarvis, born in Webster, West Virginia, on May 1, 1864. She began campaigning after her mother's death in 1905, the first service was held in 1908, and Congress designated the day in 1914.

Did the founder really turn against the holiday?
Yes. The National Park Service records her objecting to florists raising carnation prices for the occasion and to standardized greeting cards.

Is Mother's Day the same date everywhere?
No. Many countries observe it on the American date, the second Sunday in May, while others mark a day for mothers at a different time of year entirely, with separate origins.

name: National Boss' Day
description: National Boss's Day falls on October 16 and has an unusually specific origin story: a secretary in suburban Illinois created it in 1958 and chose the date because it was her father's birthday. It is also a holiday whose documented record is far thinner than its reach, which is worth knowing before anyone organizes a group card.
body:
### History

The account traces to one place, and it is specific. ABC7 Chicago reports that the day "was created in 1958 when Patricia Bays Haroski, a secretary at State Farm in Deerfield, Illinois," registered it with the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. On the date: "Haroski chose October 16th as the date, because it was her father's birthday. She was working for him at the time." Four years later, by the same account, "In 1962, Illinois Governor Otto Kerner made the date official by proclamation."

Two things are worth being precise about. First, a governor's proclamation makes a date official in that governor's state and nowhere else, so Kerner's 1962 action is an Illinois matter rather than a national designation. There is no federal status behind National Boss's Day, then or now.

Second, the record itself is thin. The story above rests on local Chicago news coverage of its own hometown holiday. No corresponding record could be found at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, at State Farm, or in Illinois state records available online, so the registration and the proclamation are reported here as that coverage reports them, and not as independently confirmed. Other details that circulate — an exact registration date, a national proclamation — have no source that could be found, and are left out.

### How to observe

The structural problem with Boss's Day is that the gift flows upward, which makes any gift slightly compromised. The honest version is to write something specific instead of buying something generic: one decision your manager made this year that was difficult and correct, named plainly. It costs nothing, it cannot be read as currying favor the way a purchase can, and it is the only form of this that a good manager actually keeps.

If you are the boss, the useful move is to decline in advance. Say that nothing is expected, and if the office wants a day for recognition, point at Administrative Professionals Day in April, when the gesture runs the other way.

A manager who wants to mark it from their own side can use the date as a standing prompt: one unhurried conversation with each person about what they want to be doing in a year, kept separate from any review cycle. The date is arbitrary; a reliable annual prompt is not.

And nothing obliges anyone to take part. Organized pressure to contribute to a group gift for a supervisor is a misuse of a day that a secretary invented, in part, to honor her own father.
timeline:
- 1958 — Patricia Bays Haroski, a secretary at State Farm in Deerfield, Illinois, creates National Boss's Day and registers it with the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.
- October 16 — The date she chooses: her father's birthday. She was working for him at the time.
- 1962 — Illinois Governor Otto Kerner makes the date official by proclamation. The proclamation is a state act and confers no national status.
- Since 1962 — No further milestone in the day's history could be documented from a primary or news source. It has never been a federal holiday and does not appear on the Office of Personnel Management's statutory list.
faq:
When is National Boss's Day?
October 16, every year.

Who invented National Boss's Day?
Patricia Bays Haroski, a secretary at State Farm in Deerfield, Illinois, who created it in 1958 and registered it with the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

Why is it on October 16?
It was her father's birthday, and she was working for him at the time.

Is National Boss's Day a federal holiday?
No. It does not appear on the Office of Personnel Management's list of federal holidays, which is set by statute at 5 U.S.C. 6103. The only official recognition on record for it is a 1962 proclamation by the governor of Illinois, which applies to Illinois.

Am I expected to give my boss a gift?
No. No convention requires it, and the direction of the gesture makes a purchased gift awkward by design. A specific written note is the version that holds up.

name: National Cat Day
description: National Cat Day falls on October 29 and was founded in 2005 by Colleen Paige, the pet lifestyle expert who created National Dog Day the year before. Unlike the dog day, this one comes with no explanation for its date: the founding site says what the day is for but never says why October 29. What it is for is adoption, and specifically the number of cats sitting in American shelters.
body:
### History

National Cat Day has a documented founder and an undocumented date. Its official site states that it was founded in 2005 by Colleen Paige, a pet and family lifestyle expert and animal welfare advocate, to help galvanize the public to recognize the number of cats needing rescue each year and to encourage owners to celebrate the cats in their lives. Paige also founded National Dog Day, National Puppy Day, National Pet Day and National Wildlife Day.

Why October 29 is explained nowhere: not on the site, not on the founder's own page, not in any acceptable source. National Dog Day's date has a reason on the record, the day Paige's family adopted her first dog. This one does not. Any confident explanation you find for October 29 is unsourced.

The founding site's headline statistic is the one place this page departs from it. The site says approximately 4 million cats enter shelters every year with 1 to 2 million euthanized, and cites nothing for either figure. The ASPCA's numbers, compiled by Shelter Animals Count from full-year national data, are better documented and considerably lower: 3 million cats entered U.S. shelters and rescues in 2025, about 2.2 million were adopted and 277,000 were euthanized. The gap between "1 to 2 million euthanized" and 277,000 is wide enough to matter, so this page uses the sourced figures and says why.

October 29 is also not the only cat day on the American calendar, which causes genuine confusion. Global Cat Day, still also called National Feral Cat Day, falls on October 16 and belongs to Alley Cat Allies, which launched National Feral Cat Day in 2001 and uses both names together. That day is about community cats and trap-neuter-return rather than pet cats. National Cat Day, two weeks later, is the one aimed at shelter adoption.

### How to observe

Paige's suggestions are modest and mostly domestic: a new toy, better food than usual, considerably more cuddling, a donation to a local shelter in your cat's honor. The site is blunt about the one that matters, telling readers to adopt rather than shop, and closes by asking people to spay and neuter.

If you want the version of this day with the most leverage, the useful target is the cats nobody is going to adopt. Alley Cat Allies, which formed in 1990 to bring trap-neuter-return from the United Kingdom to the United States, describes the process in three steps: community cats are humanely trapped, taken to a clinic to be spayed or neutered, vaccinated and eartipped, then returned to the outdoor homes they are bonded to. The eartip is the universal mark of a cat already through a program. Local groups are chronically short of trappers and transport, and both are things one person with a car and a free morning can supply.

The other practical move, if you are adopting: ask which cats have been at the shelter longest rather than looking at the kittens. Kittens leave on their own.
timeline:
- 1990 — Alley Cat Allies forms to bring trap-neuter-return, already working in the United Kingdom, to the United States.
- 2001 — Alley Cat Allies launches National Feral Cat Day on October 16, the day now also called Global Cat Day.
- 2004 — Colleen Paige founds National Dog Day, the first of her animal observances.
- 2005 — Paige founds National Cat Day. The founding site gives no reason for the October 29 date, then or since.
- 2019 — The shelter euthanasia rate for dogs and cats stands at 10 percent, per ASPCA figures compiled by Shelter Animals Count.
- 2025 — 3 million cats enter U.S. shelters and rescues. About 2.2 million are adopted and 277,000 euthanized, with cat euthanasia down about 2 percent against 2024.
faq:
Who started National Cat Day, and when?
Colleen Paige, a pet and family lifestyle expert and animal welfare advocate, in 2005. She founded National Dog Day the year before, along with National Puppy Day, National Pet Day and National Wildlife Day.

Why is National Cat Day on October 29?
No source explains it. The founding site states the year and the purpose but never the reason for the date, and neither does the founder's own page. National Dog Day's August 26 has a documented explanation; this one does not.

Is National Cat Day the same as Global Cat Day?
No. Global Cat Day, also still called National Feral Cat Day, falls on October 16 and belongs to Alley Cat Allies, which launched it in 2001; it is about community cats and trap-neuter-return. National Cat Day is October 29 and is aimed at shelter adoption.

How many cats are in U.S. shelters?
Per ASPCA figures compiled by Shelter Animals Count, 3 million cats entered U.S. shelters and rescues in 2025. About 2.2 million were adopted, 362,000 returned to their owner or the field, and 277,000 euthanized.

Why does the official site's statistic differ from the ASPCA's?
Because the official site cites no source for its figure. nationalcatday.com states roughly 4 million cats entering shelters annually and 1 to 2 million euthanized; the ASPCA's figures come from full-year national data and are considerably lower. This page uses the sourced numbers.

- Alley Cat Allies, Trap-Neuter-Return — https://www.alleycat.org/our-work/trap-neuter-return/ → Alley Cat Allies formed in 1990 to bring trap-neuter-return from the United Kingdom to the United States; the trap, spay or neuter, vaccinate, eartip and return process; the eartip as the universal sign of a cat already through a program; microchipping as best practice registered to the caregiver or the group.

Omitted for lack of a source: the reason for the October 29 date. Nothing on the founding site, the founder's page or any acceptable source explains it, so the page says so rather than guessing.

Source conflict, resolved toward the better documented figure rather than averaged: the founding site's unsourced estimate of about 4 million cats entering shelters annually and 1 to 2 million euthanized, against the ASPCA's 2025 figures of 3 million entering and 277,000 euthanized. The page uses the ASPCA numbers and discloses the discrepancy in both the body and the FAQ rather than splitting the difference. The founding site gives no year and no methodology for its figure at all, which is itself the reason to prefer the ASPCA.

Dropped for lack of a source: a reference to International Cat Day on August 8, which would have been useful for disambiguation. International Cat Care's own home and history pages do not mention the day, a founder or a year, so the claim is not on the page.

Rejected as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate and content-farm pages, including every page that supplies a reason for the October 29 date.

name: National Cheeseburger Day
description: National Cheeseburger Day falls on September 18, and its own origin is not well documented — no founding organization, proclamation, or first observance can be traced to the date. The sandwich it honors has a better-attested history, though a contested one: several American restaurants have claimed the invention, and the oldest hard evidence for it is not a claim at all but a Los Angeles menu from 1928.
body:
### History

The origin of this observance is not well documented. The September 18 date circulates widely and is marked every year by restaurant promotions, but no founding body, proclamation, or first observance for it could be traced to a primary or news source, and this page will not supply one.

The cheeseburger's own history is better attested, and still unsettled. Lionel C. Sternberger is the name most often attached to it. Reviewing the accounts in 2004, the Metropolitan News-Enterprise found that he was "believed to have invented the 'cheese hamburger' in the 1920s in the Northeast portion of Los Angeles County," but added that "[t]ales differ, however, as to precisely when this occurred, and where." Some accounts put it in 1924, others in 1926. Pasadena is the usual location, though readers of a 1994 Los Angeles Times column placed the moment in Highland Park at Sternberger's Rite Spot, and another remembered a smaller Sternberger hamburger stand on Colorado Boulevard in Pasadena earlier still. The paper also noted an arithmetic problem with the earliest date: Sternberger was born on February 21, 1907, so in 1924 he was seventeen, and more plausibly working in his father's kitchen than running a kitchen of his own.

What is firm is a piece of paper. A 1928 menu from O'Dell's at 4922 S. Figueroa in Los Angeles lists "CHEESEBURGER, smothered with chili" at 25 cents; the same sandwich on a bun cost five cents more. Merriam-Webster independently dates the first known use of the word cheeseburger to 1928. Between them, the menu and the dictionary put both the sandwich and its name in Los Angeles by the late 1920s, which leaves the later claims stranded. The Metropolitan News-Enterprise concluded that the 1928 menu "debunks the notion that Carl Kaelin ... invented it in 1934," and treated the other 1930s claims as "doubtful 'firsts.'"

### How to observe

Order one with American cheese at least once. The slab of processed American cheese is what the Sternberger story turns on, and it melts into the patty in a way an aged cheese will not — which is why the original choice stuck.

Or order the oldest documented version instead: a cheeseburger smothered with chili, which is how O'Dell's was selling it in 1928, and which is still on menus across Southern California.

If the history is the interesting part, go and look at menus yourself. The Los Angeles Public Library's TESSA archive includes a Menu Collection, and an old restaurant menu is one of the few food-history sources that cannot be embellished after the fact: a price and a line of type, printed before anyone was arguing about who was first.

Worth knowing while you eat. In 2021, 56.2 pounds of beef per person were available for consumption in the United States, against 68.1 pounds of chicken, according to USDA Economic Research Service data; chicken has been ahead of beef since 2010.
timeline:
- February 21, 1907 — Lionel C. Sternberger, the man most often credited with the cheeseburger, is born.
- 1920s — Sternberger is "believed to have invented the 'cheese hamburger'" somewhere in the northeast of Los Angeles County. Accounts split between 1924 and 1926, and between Pasadena and Highland Park.
- 1928 — O'Dell's, at 4922 S. Figueroa in Los Angeles, lists a cheeseburger smothered with chili at 25 cents. Merriam-Webster dates the word's first known use to the same year.
- 1934 — The year of a rival claim to the invention, which the 1928 menu contradicts.
- January 30, 1964 — Sternberger dies in Los Angeles. Accounts at his death identify him as the cheeseburger's inventor.
- 2010 — Chicken passes beef in per-person availability in the United States and stays ahead; by 2021 the figures are 68.1 pounds against 56.2.
faq:
When is National Cheeseburger Day?
September 18, every year. The date is fixed and does not shift for weekends.

Who started National Cheeseburger Day?
The origin of this observance is not well documented. No founding organization, proclamation, or first observance could be traced to the date from a primary or news source, and the pages that name a founder do not cite one.

Is National Cheeseburger Day a federal holiday?
No. It does not appear on the Office of Personnel Management's list of federal holidays, which is set by statute at 5 U.S.C. 6103. Offices, banks, and post offices operate normally.

Who invented the cheeseburger?
Nobody can prove it. Lionel C. Sternberger is the usual answer, and the accounts place him in Los Angeles County in the 1920s, but they disagree on the year — 1924 or 1926 — and on the place, and he was seventeen in 1924. A 1928 Los Angeles menu is the earliest documented cheeseburger, and it does not say who thought of it.

Why do both 1924 and 1926 get quoted?
Because the story was reconstructed decades later from memory and newspaper columns rather than from records. Neither year has a document behind it, so the two have circulated side by side ever since.
