name: National Coffee Day
description: National Coffee Day falls on September 29 in the United States, and what it mostly consists of is free coffee: chains and roasters use the date for giveaways and discounts. Nobody has documented who created it or why the date is September 29. The adjacent International Coffee Day, on October 1, does have a paper trail, and the contrast between the two is the most interesting thing about either.
body:
### History

The origin of this observance is not well documented. No founding organization, proclamation or recorded first observance meets this site's sourcing standard, and the National Coffee Association, the U.S. coffee trade association and the body most likely to have created it, makes no such claim anywhere on its site. The NCA marks the day publicly and repeatedly without ever saying where it came from: a September 2024 release described its polling as "published ahead of National Coffee Day on September 29," and on September 30, 2025 it reported briefing members of Congress on coffee's economic contribution as part of that year's observance. That is an organization marking a date it inherited, not one claiming to have set it.

The international day is the instructive contrast. The International Coffee Organization's own page states that "in March 2014, the Member States of the ICO agreed to organize International Coffee Day on 1 October to create a single day of celebration for coffee lovers around the world," noting that many countries already kept their own coffee days. The widely repeated claim that the day was launched in Milan in 2015 appears nowhere on the ICO's pages, which date the decision to 2014 and name no launch location.

What September 29 is actually for, on the evidence, is promotions. An ABC News owned-station report from September 29, 2021 listed free brewed coffee at Starbucks for customers who brought a clean reusable cup, a free medium coffee at Dunkin' for rewards members, and free coffee at Panera for parents and caregivers, with Dunkin' calling the date "the biggest coffee holiday of the year." Those offers expired in 2021; the shape of the day has not.

The drink is better recorded than the holiday, though its beginning is not. Britannica traces wild coffee plants "probably from Kefa (Kaffa), Ethiopia," taken to southern Arabia and cultivated in the fifteenth century, and files the Kaldi story, the goatherd who around 850 CE "supposedly" tried the berries after watching his flock, as one of many legends. The drink went on to produce a social institution that had not existed before: the coffeehouse.

Americans have not let up. The NCA's 2026 National Coffee Data Trends Fall Report, conducted in June 2026 among 1,882 adults, found past-day coffee consumption steady at 66 percent of American adults, more than any other beverage including tap or bottled water. Specialty coffee reached a record 48 percent, now ahead of traditional, and 83 percent of past-day drinkers have it at home.

### How to observe

Check the offers the day before rather than the morning of. Nearly all now require an app order, a loyalty account or a code, and the reusable-cup conditions are specific; the people who miss out arrive at the counter expecting a free cup.

If you want the day to be about coffee rather than discounts, buy a single-origin bag from a roaster who names the farm or cooperative and the harvest year. That information is the entire argument of the ICO's October 1 day, which points at the people who grow the crop rather than the ones who drink it.
timeline:
- About 850 CE — The traditional date of the Kaldi story, in which a goatherd notices his flock's behavior after it eats coffee berries. Britannica calls this one of many legends.
- 15th century — Wild coffee plants, probably from Kefa (Kaffa) in Ethiopia, are taken to southern Arabia and placed under cultivation.
- Through the 17th century — Nearly the entire world supply comes from Yemen, and by the century's close coffeehouses are flourishing across Britain, its American colonies and continental Europe.
- March 2014 — The member states of the International Coffee Organization agree to organize International Coffee Day on October 1.
- September 30, 2025 — The National Coffee Association marks National Coffee Day with a briefing for members of Congress on coffee's economic contribution.
- September 15, 2026 — The NCA's Fall 2026 report puts past-day coffee consumption at 66 percent of American adults.
faq:
Who started National Coffee Day?
Nobody credible has documented it. There is no founding organization, proclamation or recorded first observance this site can cite, and the National Coffee Association marks the day every year without ever claiming to have created it.

Is National Coffee Day the same as International Coffee Day?
No. National Coffee Day is September 29 in the United States. International Coffee Day is October 1, and it has a documented origin: the member states of the International Coffee Organization agreed to it in March 2014.

Was International Coffee Day launched in Milan in 2015?
That claim circulates widely but appears nowhere on the International Coffee Organization's own pages, which date the agreement to March 2014 and give no launch location. This site follows the ICO.

How many Americans drink coffee every day?
Sixty-six percent of American adults had coffee in the past day, per the National Coffee Association's Fall 2026 report, conducted in June 2026 among 1,882 adults, more than any other beverage including tap or bottled water. Its Spring 2025 report put the average at three cups a day.

Is the free coffee real?
Yes, but conditional. Most offers require a loyalty account, an app order or a specific action; Starbucks' 2021 giveaway required bringing a clean reusable cup. The deals change every year, so last year's list is not a guide.
sources:
- International Coffee Organization, International Coffee Day — https://ico.org/international-coffee-day/ → the October 1 date; "In March 2014, the Member States of the ICO agreed to organize International Coffee Day on 1 October to create a single day of celebration for coffee lovers around the world"; the note that many countries already celebrated their own national coffee days at various dates.
- International Coffee Organization, home page — https://www.ico.org/ → October 1 as International Coffee Day and its framing around support for the farmers whose livelihoods depend on the crop.
- National Coffee Association USA, Coffee tops beverage charts again, specialty coffee hits new high, September 15, 2026 — https://www.ncausa.org/newsroom/NCA-Coffee-tops-beverage-charts-again-specialty-coffee-hits-new-high → the 2026 National Coffee Data Trends Fall Report, conducted by Dig Insights in June 2026 among 1,882 U.S. adults; past-day coffee consumption at 66 percent; specialty coffee at a record 48 percent past-day and now ahead of traditional coffee; 47 percent having an espresso-based beverage in the past week, up 17.5 percent since 2022; 83 percent of past-day drinkers having coffee at home; coffee consumed by more adults each day than any other beverage including tap or bottled water.
- National Coffee Association USA, More Americans Drink Coffee Each Day Than Any Other Beverage, April 15, 2025 — https://www.ncausa.org/Newsroom/More-Americans-Drink-Coffee-Each-Day-Than-Any-Other-Beverage-Bottled-Water-Back-in-Second-Place → the average of three cups per day per coffee drinker, from the Spring 2025 NCDT report conducted in January 2025.
- National Coffee Association USA, Newsroom — https://www.ncausa.org/Newsroom → polling "published ahead of National Coffee Day on September 29" (September 19, 2024), which is the September 29 date stated by the trade association itself; and National Coffee Day gives Grounds for Celebration on Capitol Hill (September 30, 2025), the congressional briefing. The NCA makes no claim anywhere on its site to having founded the day.
- Encyclopædia Britannica, Coffee — https://www.britannica.com/topic/coffee → wild coffee plants "probably from Kefa (Kaffa), Ethiopia" taken to southern Arabia and cultivated in the 15th century; the Kaldi story of about 850 CE labeled one of many legends, with "supposedly"; the line that whatever the actual origin of coffee, its stimulating effect undoubtedly made it popular; Yemen as nearly the entire world supply until the close of the 17th century; the Islamic prohibition and coffee's adoption as a substitute for alcohol; the coffeehouse as a new social and cultural entity; coffeehouses flourishing across Britain, the British colonies in America and continental Europe by the end of the 17th century.
- ABC News owned station (ABC7, via GMA), Starbucks, Dunkin', more offer National Coffee Day freebies, deals, September 29, 2021 — https://abc7news.com/post/free-coffee-day-national-2021-starbucks-dunkin/11060228/ → September 29 for National Coffee Day and October 1 for International Coffee Day; the promotional character of the day; the Starbucks reusable-cup condition, the Dunkin' rewards-member offer, Panera's offer for parents and caregivers and Tim Hortons' donut offer; Dunkin' calling it "the biggest coffee holiday of the year." This source says nothing about the day's origin.

Omitted for lack of a source: any founder, founding year or first observance for the September 29 American date, and any reason for the choice of September 29. The NCA's silence on its own site is the strongest evidence available, and it is silence rather than a competing account.

Source conflict, resolved toward the more primary source rather than averaged: the widely repeated claim that International Coffee Day was launched in Milan in 2015, against the ICO's own statement that its member states agreed the October 1 date in March 2014. The ICO is the body that created the day, so its account governs, and the page notes the discrepancy rather than hiding it. The two are not strictly incompatible, since an agreement in 2014 and a first celebration in 2015 could both be true, but this page will not assert a 2015 Milan launch that the founding organization's own pages do not mention.

Figure dated rather than presented as current: the three-cups-a-day average, which comes from the NCA's Spring 2025 report that the NCA itself now flags as out of date. The 2026 report does not restate a cups-per-day number, so the page gives the figure with its date attached.

Not checked, and therefore not claimed: whether any U.S. presidential proclamation or congressional resolution has ever recognized a National Coffee Day. No such record surfaced in the sources consulted and none of the coffee-industry sources references one, but congress.gov and the Federal Register were not searched. The page says the origin is undocumented rather than that no government record exists.

Rejected as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate and content-farm pages, including every page that names a founder or founding year for the September 29 date.

name: National Dog Day
description: National Dog Day falls on August 26 and is one of the few "national days" with both a documented founder and a documented reason for its date. Colleen Paige, a pet lifestyle expert and animal welfare advocate, founded it in 2004 and chose August 26 because it was the day her family adopted her first dog from a shelter, when she was ten. The day's stated purpose is narrower than general dog appreciation: it is an adoption campaign.
body:
### History

Most "national days" cannot tell you who started them. This one can. National Dog Day was founded in 2004 by Colleen Paige, a pet and family lifestyle expert and animal rescue advocate who also founded National Puppy Day, National Mutt Day and National Cat Day. Her stated mission is to help galvanize the public to recognize the number of dogs needing rescue each year, and to acknowledge family dogs alongside dogs that work to save lives and bring comfort.

The date is not arbitrary, which is rarer still. Paige's site explains it: August 26 is the day her family adopted her first dog, a Sheltie, from the local animal shelter, when she was ten. UPI and NBC New York report the same explanation, but both are repeating the founder's account rather than confirming it, and no source gives the year.

The day's official standing is softer than usually stated. UPI reported in 2022 that it "was officially recognized by the New York State Senate in a 2013 resolution," and Paige's site says the same. This site could not retrieve the resolution from the New York State Senate's own database to confirm it, and the UPI article contradicts itself: its photo caption gives 2004 for the recognition and the wrong date, August 24, for the holiday. Treat it as reported rather than verified. One position on the founder's site is worth noting, because observances of this kind rarely take one: National Dog Day is against any kind of breed ban.

The problem the day points at is documented better elsewhere. Per ASPCA figures compiled by Shelter Animals Count, 2.8 million dogs entered U.S. shelters and rescues in 2025; about 2 million were adopted and 320,000 were euthanized. Dog euthanasia fell nearly 7 percent against 2024, and the overall rate has dropped from 10 percent in 2019 to 8 percent in 2025. One trend runs the other way: the ASPCA notes that the time dogs, especially large dogs, spend in shelters before adoption has increased over the past five years.

### How to observe

The founder's suggestions are specific, and most cost nothing. Consider adoption first. If you want a particular breed, look for a breed-specific rescue rather than a breeder; they exist for most breeds and they are full. If you do go to a breeder, check licensing, reviews and local references, including from a veterinarian. Paige's site warns against pet stores supplied by puppy mills, backyard breeders, internet listings and newspaper ads. Her lowest-effort suggestion is a five-dollar donation to a local shelter on August 26, for people who do not have a dog and are not getting one.

If you want to move a number rather than a sentiment, ask your shelter about its longest-staying dog instead of its newest arrival. Length of stay for large dogs is the part of the problem the ASPCA's own data says is getting worse, and those are the dogs that adoption-day traffic walks past.
timeline:
- 2004 — Colleen Paige founds National Dog Day, choosing August 26 because it is the date her family adopted her first dog, a Sheltie, from a local shelter when she was ten.
- 2005 — Paige founds National Cat Day, one of several animal observances she creates alongside National Puppy Day and National Mutt Day.
- 2013 — Per the founder's site and a later UPI report, New York State recognizes the day. This site could not retrieve the resolution from the state Senate's legislative database to verify it.
- 2019 — The shelter euthanasia rate for dogs and cats stands at 10 percent, per ASPCA figures compiled by Shelter Animals Count.
- 2022 — UPI reports on the day's founding, repeating Paige's account of why the date is August 26.
- 2025 — 2.8 million dogs enter U.S. shelters and rescues. About 2 million are adopted and 320,000 euthanized, with dog euthanasia down nearly 7 percent against 2024 and the overall rate down to 8 percent.
faq:
Is National Dog Day a federal holiday?
No. It has no federal status, no day off and no federal proclamation. The founder's site reports recognition by New York State in 2013, which this site could not verify directly.

Who started National Dog Day?
Colleen Paige, a pet lifestyle expert and animal welfare advocate, in 2004. She also founded National Cat Day, National Puppy Day and National Mutt Day. This is unusual: most observances of this kind have no documented founder at all.

Why is it on August 26?
Because that is the date Paige's family adopted her first dog, a Sheltie, from a local animal shelter when she was ten. The explanation comes from Paige's own site, and the news coverage repeating it is repeating her.

Does National Dog Day take a position on anything?
Yes, one. The founder's site states that National Dog Day is against any kind of breed ban, a more specific stance than most days of this kind take.

How many dogs are actually in U.S. shelters?
Per ASPCA figures compiled by Shelter Animals Count, 2.8 million dogs entered U.S. shelters and rescues in 2025. About 2 million were adopted, 542,000 returned to their owners and 320,000 euthanized.

- UPI, National Dog Day has encouraged adoption since 2004 — https://www.upi.com/Odd_News/2022/08/26/National-Dog-Day-founded-2004/9571661525115/ → the 2004 founding and Colleen Paige; the August 26 date and its reason; "officially recognized by the New York State Senate in a 2013 resolution."
- NBC New York, Happy National Dog Day: what to know about the day dedicated to our canine companions — https://www.nbcnewyork.com/clear-the-shelters/happy-national-dog-day-august-26-what-to-know/5731865/ → observed since 2004, founded by Colleen Paige; the August 26 explanation, attributed by NBC to the National Dog Day site.
- ASPCA, U.S. Animal Shelter Statistics, 2025 data compiled by Shelter Animals Count — https://www.aspca.org/helping-shelters-people-pets/us-animal-shelter-statistics → 2.8 million dogs entering shelters and rescues in 2025; about 2 million dogs adopted, 542,000 returned to owner, 320,000 euthanized; dog euthanasia down nearly 7 percent against 2024; the euthanasia rate falling from 10 percent in 2019 to 8 percent in 2025; increasing length of stay for dogs, especially large dogs.

Unverified claim, flagged rather than dropped: the 2013 New York State recognition. The founder's site and UPI both report it and UPI is an acceptable source, so it is on the page, but attributed rather than asserted. The New York State Senate's legislation database refused automated retrieval, so the resolution number, sponsor and adoption date are unconfirmed. UPI's own photo caption contradicts its body text, giving 2004 for the recognition and August 24 for the holiday; the body text is the more considered of the two and is what this page follows.

Source dependency, disclosed: UPI and NBC New York both attribute the August 26 explanation to the founder's own site. They are independent outlets but not independent evidence on this point, so the reason for the date rests on Paige's account alone.

name: National Doughnut Day
description: National Doughnut Day falls on the first Friday in June, and it is one of the few food holidays with a documented founder, a documented year, and a reason for existing that has nothing to do with selling doughnuts. The Salvation Army created it in Chicago in 1938 as a Great Depression fundraiser, in tribute to the volunteers who had fried doughnuts for American soldiers in France two decades earlier. The free-doughnut promotions came much later, and from somewhere else.
body:
### History

In 1917, after the United States entered the First World War, the Salvation Army sent about 250 officers and volunteers to France to support American troops. Evangeline Booth led the group. Among them was Helen Purviance of Huntington, Indiana, who with Margaret Sheldon began frying doughnuts for soldiers near the front at Montiers-sur-Saulx. The women became known as the Donut Lassies, and the Salvation Army credits returning troops with carrying a taste for the pastry home.

Accounts of that first batch disagree. The Salvation Army says the two hand-patted and fried 150 doughnuts on the first day, using soldiers' steel helmets for want of pans. The Indiana War Memorials Foundation says nearly 200 were made, eight at a time, on a small low stove, and does not mention helmets at all. Both put peak production near 9,000 doughnuts a day. The helmet detail, the most repeated part of the story, comes from the organization that founded the holiday — the best-placed source and an interested one.

The holiday itself dates to 1938, when the Salvation Army in Chicago held the first National Donut Day: a tribute to the Lassies twenty years on, and a fundraiser for families hit by the Depression.

### How to observe

Give to the organization that started it. The point of the first National Donut Day was fundraising, and the Salvation Army still runs Donut Day events through its local divisions. The free doughnut offered elsewhere on the first Friday in June is a promotion that borrowed the date.

If you want to fry them the hard way, the Salvation Army's Great Lakes division publishes the Donut Lassies' recipe, scaled to about sixty doughnuts. It is a useful corrective to the image of two women turning out thousands a day on a camp stove.

Look up the Lassies as individuals rather than as a story. Helen Purviance had a documented life well beyond the trenches: a Salvation Army captain who later taught and became a college dean, who by 1936 said she was sick of doughnuts and tried to distance herself from the treat, and who died in February 1984 at ninety-five.
timeline:
- 1917 — The Salvation Army sends about 250 officers and volunteers to France to support American troops; Evangeline Booth leads the group.
- 1917 — Helen Purviance and Margaret Sheldon fry the first doughnuts for soldiers near the front at Montiers-sur-Saulx. Accounts of the first day's count differ: 150 by the Salvation Army's telling, nearly 200 by the Indiana War Memorials Foundation's.
- November 1918 — Purviance serves through the end of the war.
- 1936 — Purviance says publicly that she is sick of doughnuts, and tries to distance herself from the treat.
- 1938 — The Salvation Army in Chicago holds the first National Donut Day, a Depression-era fundraiser and a tribute to the Donut Lassies.
- February 1984 — Purviance dies at ninety-five.
faq:
When is National Doughnut Day?
The first Friday in June. The Salvation Army, which created the day, states that rule on its own pages.

Who started National Doughnut Day?
The Salvation Army, in Chicago, in 1938. Every one of the organization's own accounts agrees on the year, the city, and the organization. It was created as a Depression-era fundraiser and as a tribute to the First World War Donut Lassies.

Is it donut or doughnut?
Both are in use for this holiday. The Salvation Army mostly writes National Donut Day, and uses Doughnut Lassies and Donut Lassies interchangeably across its own pages. This site lists the day as National Doughnut Day.

Did the Donut Lassies really fry doughnuts in soldiers' helmets?
The Salvation Army says so, consistently, across several of its own accounts. The Indiana War Memorials Foundation's profile of Helen Purviance describes the same scene in more mechanical detail — eight at a time on a small low round stove — and does not mention helmets anywhere. The helmet version comes from the founding organization, which makes it the best-sourced version available and also the one with an interest in the telling.

Is National Doughnut Day a federal holiday?
No. It has no official status, and nothing closes.

- The Salvation Army, The Sweet History Behind National Donut Day — https://www.salvationarmyusa.org/stories/the-sweet-history-behind-national-donut-day/ → the 1938 founding in Chicago by the Salvation Army during the Great Depression; the 1917 mission to France; about 250 volunteers and the huts near the battlefields; Ensign Margaret Sheldon and Adjutant Helen Purviance; 150 doughnuts on the first day and about 9,000 a day at peak; frying in soldiers' steel helmets for want of pans; the Donut Lassies nickname; returning troops popularizing the doughnut; the first Friday in June.
- The Salvation Army (Great Lakes), National Donut Day: A Historical Look at The Salvation Army's Iconic Treat — https://www.salvationarmyusa.org/usa-central-territory/great-lakes/stories/national-donut-day-the-sweet-history-behind-the-salvation-army-s-most-famous-treat/ → 1938 as the founding year and Chicago as both fundraiser and tribute; up to 9,000 doughnuts served daily; the first Friday in June; the published Donut Lassies recipe yielding about sixty doughnuts. This page alone attributes the 1917 deployment to a request from General John J. Pershing; that claim is not used in the text above, because the organization's other accounts tie the mission to American entry into the war instead.
- The Salvation Army, National Donut Day: A Sweet Celebration with a Noble Cause (Commissioner Kenneth Hodder) — https://www.salvationarmyusa.org/stories/national-donut-day-a-sweet-celebration-with-a-noble-cause/ → the Salvation Army of Chicago and 1938; the day's dual purpose of honoring the Donut Lassies and raising funds for the organization's social service programs during the Depression; the first Friday in June.
- The Salvation Army (Northern Division), Donut Day — https://centralusa.salvationarmy.org/northern/donut-day/ → the 1938 Chicago origin as a tribute to the Doughnut Lassies; the 1917 mission in France; Sheldon and Purviance frying in soldiers' helmets; the first Friday in June; continued service in the Second World War; local Donut Day events.
- Indiana War Memorials Foundation, Helen Purviance: Salvationist, Doughnut Girl, Teacher and Groundbreaker for Women — https://www.indianawarmemorials.org/2021/03/08/helen-purviance-salvationist-doughnut-girl-teacher-and-groundbreaker-for-women/ → Purviance's birth in Huntington, Indiana; her rank of captain and her departure for France in August 1917; Evangeline Booth leading 250 Salvationists to France in the fall of 1917; Montiers-sur-Saulx; Margaret Sheldon as co-originator; nearly 200 doughnuts on the first day, eight at a time on a small low round stove, with no mention of helmets; 2,000 to 9,000 a day as the equipment improved; service through the end of the war in November 1918; her 1936 remark that she was sick of doughnuts; her later teaching and college deanship; her death in February 1984 at ninety-five.

name: National Hugging Day
description: National Hugging Day falls on January 21 and is one of the rare modern observances whose founder is both known and still running it. Kevin Zaborney created it in 1986 in Caro, Michigan, and placed it deliberately in late January, when the holidays are over and winter is not. Four decades on, its organizers spend as much effort on consent, and on alternatives for people who do not want to be touched, as on hugging itself.
body:
### History

National Hugging Day was founded in 1986 by Kevin Zaborney in Caro, Michigan, and the name is trademarked; National Hugging Day LLC runs it now. Zaborney's account is that the day spread after it was published in Chase's Calendar of Annual Events, the long-running reference of American observances — which is how one person's idea became a dated entry other people could find and mark. The organization states that the name was established in 1986 and formally registered with the U.S. Copyright Office in 1989, under the title "National Hugging Day Collection."

The date was a choice rather than an accident. The organizers put it in late January specifically because of what that stretch of the calendar does to people: the holidays are finished, social contact drops off, and post-holiday flatness arrives in the coldest and quietest weeks of the year. The day is meant to sit in that gap.

Two caveats belong here. The founding rests on a single source, the founder's own site, because no independent reputable account of the 1986 origin could be found. And the organization's reach claims — millions of participants across more than 100 countries — are its own figures rather than independently measured ones.

What has changed most over forty years is the framing. The organizers now state the day plainly as consensual: ask first, and if the answer is no or you cannot predict it, do something else. They publish non-touch alternatives — heart-hand gestures, a note, a gentle high-five — aimed particularly at autistic and sensory-sensitive people, so that a day built on physical contact is not a day that quietly excludes them.

The health claim usually attached to hugging has better evidence behind it than most holiday-page assertions, and less than the headlines suggest. In a study led by Sheldon Cohen at Carnegie Mellon and published in Psychological Science, 404 healthy adults were interviewed by telephone on 14 consecutive evenings about interpersonal conflicts and hugs received, then deliberately exposed to a common cold virus and monitored in quarantine. Perceived social support reduced the risk of infection associated with conflict, and hugs accounted for about one-third of that protective effect; among those who did get infected, more frequent hugs went with less severe symptoms. Cohen's own reading was careful — the effect may come from the physical contact itself, or from hugging simply being a reliable sign of a close and supportive relationship.

### How to observe

Ask before hugging anyone whose reaction you cannot predict. The organizers say so themselves, and it is the whole difference between a day that works and a day people brace for.

If touch is not for you, or not for the person you want to reach, use one of the substitutes the organizers publish: a heart-hand gesture, a card, a short message saying you were thinking of them. The point of the day is the signal, and the signal travels without contact.

Pick someone outside your own household. Late January is when people living alone go longest without a real conversation, which is the gap the date was chosen to address. A phone call to someone you would otherwise only text does more work than a hug given to a person you already hug daily.
timeline:
- 1986 — Kevin Zaborney founds National Hugging Day in Caro, Michigan, for January 21.
- 1986 — The day spreads after being published in Chase's Calendar of Annual Events, by the founder's account.
- 1989 — The name is formally registered with the U.S. Copyright Office under the title "National Hugging Day Collection."
- December 2014 — Carnegie Mellon researchers led by Sheldon Cohen publish a study in Psychological Science finding that frequent hugs account for about one-third of social support's protective effect against stress-related infection.
- 2026 — The organizers mark the day's 40th anniversary, with a global Hug Challenge and autism-friendly participation as its stated centerpiece.
faq:
When is National Hugging Day?
January 21, every year. The date is fixed and does not move.

Who started National Hugging Day?
Kevin Zaborney, in 1986, in Caro, Michigan. He still runs it through National Hugging Day LLC. This page's source for the founding is Zaborney's own site, as no independent reputable account of the 1986 origin was available.

Why is it in January?
By design. The organizers chose late January because it falls after the holidays, when social contact drops and spirits are low, in the coldest and quietest part of the year.

What if I do not want to be hugged?
Then you should not be. The organizers ask people to seek consent first, and publish non-touch alternatives — heart-hand gestures, kindness notes, gentle high-fives — for autistic and sensory-sensitive people and anyone else who prefers them.

Is there real evidence that hugs help?
Some. The Carnegie Mellon study described above found that people reporting more frequent hugs were somewhat more protected against stress-related infection and had milder symptoms if infected. The researchers noted the effect might be the contact itself, or simply that hugging indicates a close, supportive relationship.

A Study of Susceptibility to Upper Respiratory Infection and Illness, Psychological Science, 2015 — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25526910/ → the peer-reviewed publication behind the Carnegie Mellon release above.

Sourcing note: the founding — 1986, Kevin Zaborney, Caro, Michigan — rests on the founder's own site alone. That is an acceptable source under this site's rule, being the organization that founded the observance, but no independent reputable account was reachable, so the claim carries no corroboration. The organization's participation figures (millions of participants, more than 100 countries) are stated on the page as the organization's claims rather than as verified counts.

Rejected as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate, nationaldayarchives, Grokipedia, and other aggregator, content-farm and AI-generated pages. Several were returned by searches for this day's origin and none was read or cited.

name: National Ice Cream Day
description: National Ice Cream Day falls on the third Sunday in July, and it is one of the few food holidays with a presidential signature behind it. Ronald Reagan signed Proclamation 5219 on July 9, 1984, naming July 1984 National Ice Cream Month and July 15 of that year National Ice Cream Day. The recurring third-Sunday rule, which is how the day is actually kept, is not in the proclamation.
body:
### History

Congress acted first. Proclamation 5219 states that "The Congress, by Senate Joint Resolution 298, has designated July 1984 as 'National Ice Cream Month,' and July 15, 1984, as 'National Ice Cream Day,'" and authorized and requested that the President issue a proclamation. Reagan signed it on July 9, 1984, calling on Americans "to observe these events with appropriate ceremonies and activities." The document makes its own case with numbers: ice cream "enjoyed by over ninety percent of the people in the United States," more than 887 million gallons consumed in 1983, roughly $3.5 billion in annual sales, and nearly ten percent of all milk produced by American dairy farmers going into ice cream.

Here is the part usually left out. The proclamation names one date, July 15, 1984, and nothing more. It contains no recurring rule — no "third Sunday," no "annually." July 15, 1984 happened to be the third Sunday of that month, and the third-Sunday pattern is how the observance has been kept since, by the dairy industry rather than by law. Both the Government Publishing Office's feature page and the International Dairy Foods Association describe the 1984 proclamation as having designated the third Sunday. The signed text does not.

### How to observe

Read Proclamation 5219. It runs to a few paragraphs, it is free at the Reagan Library and at the American Presidency Project, and it is a tidy specimen of the genre: a federal document arguing by statistic that a dessert deserves a month of national attention.

Note which figures are current and which are from 1983. The proclamation's numbers are four decades old. The International Dairy Foods Association's own current accounting puts 2025 US production at 1.23 billion gallons and per-capita consumption at roughly 18 pounds a year, against the more than 23 pounds the same association reported with its 2017 figures, on a basis it does not reconcile. Any "Americans eat X pounds of ice cream" claim you meet in July is worth tracing to its year.

And if you only want the ice cream: the third Sunday in July is when the deals land, not July 15.
timeline:
- 1744 — The first account of ice cream in the New World appears in a letter written by a guest of Maryland's Governor William Bladen.
- May 12, 1777 — The first American advertisement for ice cream runs in the New York Gazette, placed by the confectioner Philip Lenzi.
- 1851 — Jacob Fussell, a Baltimore milk dealer, pioneers ice cream manufacturing as an American industry.
- 1904 — At the St. Louis World's Fair, Ernest A. Hamwi rolls a waffle-like zalabis pastry into a cone for an ice cream vendor who has run out of dishes.
- July 9, 1984 — Reagan signs Proclamation 5219, designating July 1984 as National Ice Cream Month and July 15, 1984 as National Ice Cream Day, at the request of Congress under Senate Joint Resolution 298.
- 2025 — American manufacturers produce 1.23 billion gallons of ice cream.
faq:
When is National Ice Cream Day?
The third Sunday in July. That rule is not in the 1984 proclamation, which named only July 15, 1984. It is the convention that has been kept since, and the U.S. Government Publishing Office describes the day the same way.

Did Ronald Reagan create National Ice Cream Day?
He signed it, but Congress asked for it. Proclamation 5219 states that it was issued at the request of Congress under Senate Joint Resolution 298, which had itself designated both the month and the day.

Is National Ice Cream Month the same thing?
They came out of the same document. Proclamation 5219 designated July 1984 as National Ice Cream Month and July 15, 1984 as National Ice Cream Day. As with the day, the month's annual recurrence is convention rather than text.

How much ice cream do Americans actually eat?
The International Dairy Foods Association currently puts it at roughly 18 pounds, or about 4 gallons, per person per year, with 2025 production at 1.23 billion gallons. The same association reported more than 23 pounds alongside its 2017 figures. Neither per-capita number carries a stated year, and the association does not reconcile them, so treat any single figure with care.

Is National Ice Cream Day a federal holiday?
No. A presidential proclamation of this kind is ceremonial. Nothing closes, and no one gets the day off.

name: National Margarita Day
description: National Margarita Day falls on February 22 and lives almost entirely in bars and restaurants, in specials priced to the date and frozen-machine promotions. Britannica dates the observance itself to 2008 but names no founder. The drink behind it has an origin even less settled: at least seven people have been credited with inventing the margarita, and the evidence decisively favors none of them.
body:
### History

The observance is recent and thinly documented. Britannica states that margarita fans began celebrating National Margarita Day in 2008, observed annually on February 22. It names no founder, and no organization publishes a sourceable account of having started it. Several aggregator sites name a specific person and year; none cites anything, so this page does not repeat them. What is well recorded is what the day actually looks like — restaurant and tequila-brand specials, frequently priced at $2.22.

The drink's own history is a genuine muddle, and the honest summary is that nobody knows who invented it. Britannica puts the likely origin in the 1930s or 1940s and describes the invention claims as disputed. The claimants include David Daniel "Danny" Negrete, said to have made it in 1936 at the Hotel Garci Crespo in Tehuacán for a girlfriend named Margarita; Carlos "Danny" Herrera of Rancho La Gloria near Tijuana, who said he made it in the late 1940s for the actress Marjorie King and adapted her name; Don Carlos Orozco, who claimed 1941 at Hussong's Cantina in Ensenada; Francisco "Pancho" Morales, said to have produced it by accident in Ciudad Juárez in 1942 while attempting a magnolia; the Texas socialite Margaret Sames, credited with a 1948 party in Acapulco; Johnny Durlesser in Los Angeles, around 1936–37; and Doña Bertha of Taxco, in 1930. It may not have been invented at a single moment at all: the margarita closely resembles the daisy, a sour-family cocktail that eventually took tequila, and the picador — tequila, Cointreau and citrus — published in 1937 in William J. Tarling's Café Royal Cocktail Book.

The rise is traceable even where the invention is not. The Smithsonian places the drink's first mixing in bars along the California–Mexico border in the 1940s, and it was popularized in southern California before spreading. Young's Market Company put it into José Cuervo advertising in 1945, and Esquire named it Drink of the Month in December 1953. By the 1970s it had passed the martini as the most popular American cocktail.

The frozen version has the clearest paper trail here, because the machine ended up in a museum. On May 11, 1971, the Dallas restaurateur Mariano Martinez — whose bartenders could not keep up with demand and whose blenders produced a different drink every time — adapted a soft-serve ice cream machine, with help from a chemist friend named John Hogan and using his father's recipe. He had taken the idea from a 7-Eleven Slurpee machine. The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History acquired that original machine in 2005.

### How to observe

Order one made with fresh lime juice, and ask what is in it. The drink is three ingredients, and the distance between a good one and a bad one is almost entirely the lime and the proportions — not the price of the tequila.

For the frozen one with its history attached, the National Museum of American History's online exhibition carries the Martinez machine's object record and the Tex-Mex story it belongs to.

The bar specials are real and cluster on the date itself, often priced at $2.22. A virgin margarita is a documented variation rather than an improvisation, so it is a reasonable thing to order by name.
timeline:
- 1930–1948 — The window in which the margarita is variously claimed to have been invented, by at least seven different people in Mexico and the United States. Britannica describes the claims as disputed and the origin as uncertain.
- 1937 — The picador — tequila, Cointreau and citrus, closely related to the margarita — is published in William J. Tarling's Café Royal Cocktail Book.
- 1945 — Young's Market Company advertises José Cuervo using the margarita, with the line "Margarita: it's more than a girl's name."
- December 1953 — Esquire names the margarita its Drink of the Month, giving a recipe of tequila, Triple Sec and lime or lemon juice, salt on the rim.
- May 11, 1971 — Mariano Martinez puts the first frozen margarita machine into service in Dallas, adapted from a soft-serve ice cream machine.
- 2008 — National Margarita Day begins to be observed, on February 22. The Smithsonian had acquired the Martinez machine three years earlier, in 2005.
faq:
When is National Margarita Day?
February 22, every year. The date does not move.

Who invented the margarita?
No one knows. Britannica dates the drink to the 1930s or 1940s, calls the origin uncertain, and lists at least seven disputed claimants across Mexico and the United States, named in the history section above. It may also have evolved out of the daisy or the picador rather than being invented at a single moment.

Who started National Margarita Day?
Britannica says margarita fans began celebrating it in 2008 and gives no founder. Named founders circulate online without sources, so this page does not repeat them.

Where is the first frozen margarita machine?
In the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, which acquired it in 2005. Mariano Martinez built it in Dallas in 1971 out of a soft-serve ice cream machine, after seeing a 7-Eleven Slurpee machine.

Is there a version without alcohol?
Yes, and it has a name. Britannica describes the virgin margarita, which replaces the tequila and orange liqueur with club soda and lemons or limes.

- Smithsonian National Museum of American History, press release: National Museum of American History Acquires Frozen Margarita Machine (September 27, 2005) — https://americanhistory.si.edu/press/releases/national-museum-american-history-acquires-frozen-margarita-machine → the machine invented May 11, 1971 by Dallas restaurateur Mariano Martinez; the 2005 acquisition and the Tupperware and Krispy Kreme comparison; blenders' inconsistency under high demand.
- Smithsonian National Museum of American History, Frozen Margaritas! (Resetting the Table / Mexican Food Revolution online exhibition) — https://americanhistory.si.edu/explore/exhibitions/food/online/resetting-table/mexican-food-revolution/frozen-margaritas → the drink first mixed in bars along the California–Mexico border in the 1940s; frozen versions popular in the 1950s; the margarita surpassing the martini by the 1970s; the 7-Eleven Slurpee machine, in use since 1965, as the specific inspiration; chemist John Hogan's help and Martinez's father's recipe.
- TODAY (NBC News), National Margarita Day deals — https://www.today.com/food/drinks/national-margarita-day-deals-2025-rcna192074 → the February 22 date and the day's character as restaurant and tequila-brand specials, including $2.22 pricing.

Source conflict, disclosed rather than averaged: the museum's press release says only that Martinez was inspired by "a frozen drink machine he saw at a local convenience store," while the museum's own exhibition page identifies it as a 7-Eleven Slurpee machine and adds John Hogan and the father's recipe. The page follows the exhibition page — the more specific statement, from the same institution — rather than splitting the difference. The press release also notes that frozen margaritas existed from the invention of the blender in the 1930s; the exhibition dates their popularity to the 1950s. Those are not in conflict, and the page states existence and popularity separately.

Not claimed for want of a source: any named founder for this observance. nationalmargaritaday.com was examined and is a tequila-brand promotional page with no founding account, so it is not cited.

Rejected as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate, and content-farm and AI-generated pages.

name: National Pizza Day
description: National Pizza Day falls on February 9, and what it mostly consists of is discounts: chains, pizzerias and frozen-pizza brands use the date to run free-slice and two-for-one offers. Nobody has documented who started it or when. The food itself is better recorded — though less settled than it looks, because the standard story of how pizza reached America has been seriously challenged in the last decade.
body:
### History

The origin of this observance is not well documented. No founding organization, proclamation or recorded first observance meets this site's sourcing standard. The earliest solid trace is news coverage of the promotions, which reports February 9 as settled fact without saying where the date came from. Any confidently named founder for this day is unsourced.

The food has a longer and more contested history than it usually gets credit for. Pizza took its recognizable shape in Naples as cheap food for the working class — the National Park Service dates that to 17th-century Naples, Smithsonian to the 1700s. The Margherita, dough with tomato, mozzarella and basil, is popularly said to be named for Queen Margherita, wife of Umberto I, who supposedly remarked that its colors matched the Italian flag. Britannica files that as legend rather than history. Naples' claim on the craft is official in one sense: in 2017 UNESCO inscribed the art of the Neapolitan Pizzaiuolo on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, counting roughly 3,000 working pizzaiuoli in the city.

The American story is where the ground has moved. The standard account credits Gennaro Lombardi with the first licensed American pizzeria, on Spring Street in Manhattan in 1905, and Britannica still prints it. Independent researcher Peter Regas, working through New York's Italian-language newspapers, reported finding the Spring Street shop already in business years earlier — likely opened in 1898 by a largely forgotten immigrant named Filippo Milone, who had a habit of opening pizzerias and selling them on, and who passed it to Giovanni Santillo, advertising pizza there by 1901. Regas could not locate the 1905 license at all, and found that Lombardi arrived in New York in 1904 at seventeen, classified on his papers as a laborer. Britannica's own general pizza article says only that the first pizzeria appeared "about the turn of the 20th century." The honest summary is that the date is open.

What made pizza general was not a pizzeria but a war. Few Americans outside Italian neighborhoods knew what pizza was before 1945. Servicemen stationed in Italy came home wanting it, one of them an oven repairman named Ira Nevin, who designed a gas-fired pizza oven that freed restaurateurs from temperamental coal and wood. The chains followed in the 1950s.

### How to observe

Order from the oldest pizzeria within reach and ask who owned it before the current owners. The Regas research turned on exactly that kind of record — ownership changes nobody bothered to document because nobody thought pizza mattered.

For the real numbers behind the day, the USDA's Food Surveys Research Group publishes a short, free data brief on pizza consumption: who eats it, what share of a day's calories and sodium it accounts for, and where it is bought.

The promotions are real, and worth checking the day before rather than the day of: most require an app order or a coupon code, and the frozen-pizza deals usually run a few days either side of the 9th.
timeline:
- 17th–18th century — Pizza takes shape in Naples as cheap food for the working class. The National Park Service dates the dish to 17th-century Naples; Smithsonian puts it in the 1700s.
- 1898–1901 — By Peter Regas's research, the Spring Street pizzeria in Manhattan is already in business: opened by Filippo Milone, then sold to Giovanni Santillo, advertising pizza there in 1901.
- 1905 — The traditional date for the first licensed American pizzeria, G. Lombardi's on Spring Street. Britannica still gives it; Regas could not find the license.
- After 1945 — Servicemen returning from Italy create the first broad American demand. Ira Nevin designs a gas-fired pizza oven; the chains arrive in the 1950s.
- 2017 — UNESCO inscribes the art of the Neapolitan Pizzaiuolo on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
- November 2024 — The USDA publishes its most recent pizza data brief: on any given day, about 11 percent of the U.S. population eats pizza.
faq:
Is National Pizza Day the same as Pi Day?
No. National Pizza Day is February 9; Pi Day is March 14 and is about the number, not the food. February 9 is also shared with a separate observance called Pizza Pie Day.

Who started National Pizza Day?
Nobody credible has documented it. There is no founding organization, proclamation or recorded first observance this site can cite, and the founders named on aggregator sites carry no sources.

Was Lombardi's really the first pizzeria in America?
The question is open. Britannica still credits Gennaro Lombardi with the first licensed American pizzeria in 1905, but research by Peter Regas, reported by Smithsonian, indicates the same Spring Street location was selling pizza years earlier and that the 1905 license cannot be found.

Is the Queen Margherita story true?
It is a legend. Britannica describes the naming of the Margherita for Umberto I's queen, and her remark about the flag's colors, as popular legend rather than established fact.

How much pizza do Americans actually eat?
Per the USDA's most recent data brief, about 11 percent of the population eats pizza on any given day, and on the day they do it supplies roughly 27 percent of their calories. Men average four slices at a sitting, women three.

Lombardi's in 1905 as the first licensed pizzeria; postwar spread.

- Smithsonian Magazine, The Father of American Pizza Is Not Who We Thought He Was — https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/father-american-pizza-not-who-we-thought-it-was-180971454/ → Peter Regas's research; Filippo Milone and the 1898 Spring Street opening; Giovanni Santillo advertising pizza there in 1901; the missing 1905 license; Lombardi's 1904 arrival at seventeen as a laborer; Naples in the 1700s; postwar demand and Ira Nevin's gas-fired oven; the 1950s chains.
- UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Art of Neapolitan 'Pizzaiuolo' — https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/art-of-neapolitan-pizzaiuolo-00722 → inscription in 2017 on the Representative List; about 3,000 pizzaiuoli living and working in Naples.
- U.S. National Park Service, A Slice of History: Pizza in America — https://www.nps.gov/articles/pizza-in-usa.htm → pizza traced to 17th-century Naples and brought to America by Italian immigrants in the late 19th century.
- USDA Agricultural Research Service, Food Surveys Research Group, Dietary Data Brief No. 62, Pizza Consumption in the U.S. (What We Eat in America, NHANES 2017–March 2020 Prepandemic), November 2024 — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK610659/ → 11 percent of the population on any given day; 27 percent of energy intake on the day consumed; about one-third of total fat, saturated fat and sodium; over half from restaurants and about a quarter from grocery stores; four slices for males and three for females.
- TODAY (NBC News), It's National Pizza Day! Here's where to get freebies and meal deals — https://www.today.com/food/when-national-pizza-day-where-go-free-pizza-t173243 → the February 9 date; the day's character as chain and grocery promotions; the distinction from Pi Day.

Source conflict, disclosed rather than averaged: the National Park Service dates the recognizable dish to 17th-century Naples, while Smithsonian puts its coming-of-age in the 1700s. Both are acceptable sources and neither is more primary on an 18th-century question, so the page gives the range both support rather than picking one.

On the 1905 question the page does not split the difference either: it states the traditional Britannica account, then the Regas findings reported by Smithsonian, and says the date is unsettled.

Rejected as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate and content-farm pages, including every page that names a founder for this observance.

name: National Taco Day
description: National Taco Day is listed on October 4 on most American calendars, but since 2024 the observance has officially sat on the first Tuesday in October — a change Taco Bell campaigned for and announced jointly with the calendar registry that lists it. The day has no verifiable founder and no founding year that survives checking, which is an odd position for a holiday attached to one of the most thoroughly researched foods in North America. The taco's history is the solid part; the holiday's is not.
body:
### History

The taco's history is well documented. The holiday's is not. No founder, organization, or founding year for National Taco Day can be confirmed from a primary source. The fullest account available is Taco Bell's own, published while the company was campaigning to move the date: it says several unnamed businesses settled on October 4 in 2009, and that the date was established on the National Day Calendar by 2013. The same page credits an earlier, locally observed San Antonio version in the 1960s to Roberto L. Gomez, attributing that history to the journalist Gustavo Arellano. All of it is one interested party's telling.

The food is firmer ground. The historian Jeffrey M. Pilcher traced "taco" through eighteenth-century Spanish dictionaries, where it meant a ramrod, a billiard cue, or a carpenter's hammer; the Spanish Royal Academy extended it to a snack of food only in the mid-nineteenth century. Manuel Payno's 1891 novel Los bandidos de Río Frío carries what Pilcher calls perhaps the first unequivocal reference to the Mexican taco. The pre-fried hard shell, by contrast, is an American industrial object with a paper trail: Juvencio Maldonado, a New York restaurateur, filed for a frying form in 1947 and received US patent 2,506,305 in 1950.

### How to observe

Check which date your local restaurants are actually honoring. Since 2024 the observance has officially fallen on the first Tuesday in October, but October 4 is still printed on most calendars and still drives the promotions, so the two run in parallel and a deal advertised for National Taco Day may be either.

Read the Maldonado patent. It is short, public, and free, and it is the clearest single artifact of how the hard-shell taco became a mass-produced American thing: a hinged metal form that folds and locks several tortillas at once so they can be dropped into hot fat together. The drawings explain the shape of nearly every supermarket taco shell sold since.

If you want the argument rather than the object, Pilcher's 2008 article in Gastronomica asks whether the taco was invented in Southern California, and answers carefully enough to be worth the hour.
timeline:
- 1891 — Manuel Payno's novel Los bandidos de Río Frío carries what Pilcher calls perhaps the first unequivocal reference to the Mexican taco.
- 1914 — Bertha Haffner-Ginger, a Los Angeles Times columnist, publishes a recipe for tacos dorados.
- July 21, 1947 — Juvencio Maldonado files a patent application for a form that folds and fries tortillas into taco shells.
- May 2, 1950 — That patent, US 2,506,305, is granted.
- 1962 — The first Taco Bell opens in Downey, California.
- September 17, 2024 — Taco Bell and National Day Calendar announce that National Taco Day moves to the first Tuesday in October, shifting it that year from Friday, October 4 to Tuesday, October 1.
faq:
Is National Taco Day on October 4 or the first Tuesday in October?
Both dates are in use. October 4 was the long-standing date; on September 17, 2024, Taco Bell and National Day Calendar announced the move to the first Tuesday in October, which that year meant October 1. Most calendars, including this one, still list October 4.

Who created National Taco Day?
Not documented. No founder or founding year can be confirmed from a primary source. Taco Bell's own account names several unnamed businesses adopting October 4 in 2009, and an earlier 1960s San Antonio observance credited to Roberto L. Gomez, which it attributes to the journalist Gustavo Arellano.

Why did Taco Bell want the date changed?
The company's stated reason, from its chief marketing officer Taylor Montgomery, is that "it felt unnatural for it to not fall on a Tuesday." Taco Bell says the day had landed on a Tuesday only four times since 2000.

Who invented the hard-shell taco?
The pre-fried U-shaped shell has a patent record. Juvencio Maldonado, a New York restaurateur, filed in July 1947 and received US patent 2,506,305 in May 1950. Glen Bell, Taco Bell's founder, claimed to have invented the fast-food taco and built a taco fryer in 1951; Pilcher reports that Bell was apparently unaware Maldonado had reached the patent office first.

Is National Taco Day a federal holiday?
No. It has no official status. Nothing closes, and no one gets the day off.

name: National Teacher Appreciation Day
description: National Teacher Appreciation Day falls on the Tuesday of the first full week of May, in the middle of National Teacher Appreciation Week. It reached that spot in the calendar only in 1985, after four decades of false starts, two single-year acts of Congress, and a stretch in March that almost nobody remembers. The National Education Association, which sets the date, opens its own account of the day by conceding that the origins are murky.
body:
### History

The trail starts with a teacher. Around 1944, Mattye Whyte Woodridge, an Arkansas teacher, began corresponding with political and education leaders about the need for a national day to honor teachers. One of the people she wrote to was Eleanor Roosevelt, and in 1953 Roosevelt persuaded the 81st Congress to proclaim a National Teacher Day.

That proclamation did not create a recurring holiday. Nearly three decades later the National Education Association, together with its Kansas and Indiana state affiliates and the Dodge City, Kansas, local, lobbied Congress again. Congress declared March 7, 1980, National Teacher Day — for that year only.

So the NEA went on marking the day in March on its own authority. That lasted until 1985, when the NEA Representative Assembly voted to move the observance to the Tuesday of the first full week of May, where it has stayed. Teacher Appreciation Week was established around it the same year.

The NEA's own history of the day begins by saying its origins are "murky" — an unusually candid line from the organization that runs it, and a fair description of a date that took three separate attempts and forty years to settle.

### How to observe

Check the date before you plan anything. "First full week of May" means the first week whose Monday through Friday all fall inside May, so the date moves: in 2026 the week ran May 4–8 with the Day on Tuesday, May 5, and in 2027 it is the week of May 3 with the Day on Tuesday, May 4.

Write to a specific teacher about a specific thing. A note naming the class, the year, and the one thing that stuck is worth more than a generic thank-you, and it is the form of recognition that survives in a desk drawer.

If you want the recognition to reach past the classroom, the NEA points out that the day is also an opening for school boards, administrators, and community members to say something on the record. A board meeting in the first week of May is a place where that lands.

The same week carries other observances: the NEA lists National Black Teachers Day inside Teacher Appreciation Week as well. Worth knowing before you compress everything into one Tuesday.
timeline:
- c. 1944 — Mattye Whyte Woodridge, an Arkansas teacher, begins corresponding with political and education leaders about a national day honoring teachers.
- 1953 — Woodridge's correspondent Eleanor Roosevelt persuades the 81st Congress to proclaim a National Teacher Day.
- 1980 — After lobbying by the NEA, its Kansas and Indiana affiliates and the Dodge City, Kansas, local, Congress declares March 7 National Teacher Day — for that year only.
- 1980–1985 — The NEA and its affiliates keep observing the day in March, with no Congressional designation behind it.
- 1985 — The NEA Representative Assembly votes to move the observance to the Tuesday of the first full week of May, and Teacher Appreciation Week is established.
- 2026 — Teacher Appreciation Week runs May 4–8, with National Teacher Day on Tuesday, May 5.
faq:
When is National Teacher Appreciation Day?
It is the Tuesday of the first full week of May, so the date moves each year. In 2026 it fell on Tuesday, May 5, inside Teacher Appreciation Week of May 4–8. In 2027 it falls on Tuesday, May 4.

Is National Teacher Appreciation Day a federal holiday?
No. It is not among the federal holidays, and there is no day off. Both Congressional actions on record covered a single day each — the 1953 proclamation and the March 7, 1980 declaration — and the date in use today was set by the NEA, not by statute.

Why is the day in May when Congress picked March?
Because the NEA moved it. The 1980 Congressional declaration applied to March 7 of that year only, and the NEA kept observing in March until its Representative Assembly voted in 1985 to shift the day to the first full week of May.

What is the difference between National Teacher Appreciation Day and Teacher Appreciation Week?
The Week is the Monday-to-Friday span of the first full week of May. The Day is the Tuesday inside it, and the NEA treats that Tuesday as the focal point of the week.

Who started National Teacher Appreciation Day?
There is no single founder. The earliest named figure is Mattye Whyte Woodridge, whose letters around 1944 reached Eleanor Roosevelt, but the NEA's own history describes the origins as murky and names no founder.

name: National Teacher Appreciation Week
description: National Teacher Appreciation Week runs Monday through Friday of the first full week of May, with National Teacher Appreciation Day on the Tuesday. The National Education Association established the week in 1985, in the same decision that moved the single day out of March. The date on this page is the Monday the week opens.
body:
### History

The week is younger than the day it contains. A National Teacher Day existed, intermittently, from 1953, when Eleanor Roosevelt persuaded the 81st Congress to proclaim one after years of letters from an Arkansas teacher named Mattye Whyte Woodridge. Congress returned to the subject once more, declaring March 7, 1980 National Teacher Day — and only that one date, in that one year.

What the National Education Association did in 1985 was turn an on-and-off single day into a fixed annual week. The NEA Representative Assembly voted that year to move the observance to the Tuesday of the first full week of May, and Teacher Appreciation Week was established around that Tuesday. The NEA describes the week as officially established by the NEA in 1985, and it has run on the same rule since.

That rule is worth stating plainly, because it is the part people get wrong: the week is not the first week of May, it is the first full week — the first Monday-to-Friday span that falls entirely inside the month.

### How to observe

Start by working out the dates, since they shift by up to six days year to year. In 2026 the week ran May 4–8; in 2027 it runs May 3–7.

Spread the recognition across the five days rather than stacking it on Tuesday. The NEA itself distinguishes observances inside the week, listing National Black Teachers Day separately from National Teacher Appreciation Day, which is a reminder that the week has room for more than one gesture.

If you are organizing on behalf of an institution rather than a family, the NEA frames the week as an opportunity for school boards, administrators, community members, and students to put appreciation on the record. A proclamation read into the minutes of a May board meeting outlasts a catered lunch.

And check whether your district already has something scheduled before you plan a parallel event. Districts and states frequently run their own versions, and two uncoordinated celebrations in one week ask more of teachers than they give.
timeline:
- c. 1944 — Arkansas teacher Mattye Whyte Woodridge begins writing to political and education leaders about a national day honoring teachers.
- 1953 — Eleanor Roosevelt, one of her correspondents, persuades the 81st Congress to proclaim a National Teacher Day.
- 1980 — Congress declares March 7 National Teacher Day, for that year only, after lobbying by the NEA and its Kansas and Indiana affiliates.
- 1985 — The NEA Representative Assembly moves the observance to the Tuesday of the first full week of May; Teacher Appreciation Week is established around it.
- 2026 — The week runs May 4–8, with National Teacher Appreciation Day on Tuesday, May 5.
faq:
When is National Teacher Appreciation Week?
It is the first full week of May — the first Monday-to-Friday span that falls entirely within the month. In 2026 that was May 4–8; in 2027 it is May 3–7.

Is it the first week of May or the first full week?
The first full week, which is not always the same thing. If May opens mid-week, the first full week begins on the following Monday, which is why the dates can move by nearly a week from one year to the next.

How is the Week different from National Teacher Appreciation Day?
The Day is the Tuesday inside the Week. The NEA treats that Tuesday as the focal point, with the surrounding Monday-to-Friday span as the broader observance.

Who established National Teacher Appreciation Week?
The National Education Association, in 1985, in the same decision by its Representative Assembly that moved National Teacher Day from March to the first full week of May.

Is it a federal holiday?
No. Neither the week nor the day inside it has federal status, and no school or workplace closes for it. The dates are set by the NEA rather than by statute.

name: New Year's Day
description: New Year's Day falls on January 1, which is an administrative decision rather than a fact of nature. The date has been moved, abandoned, and restored more than once in Western Europe — Britain and its American colonies did not adopt it until 1752 — and most of what Americans actually do on the day, from the parade in Pasadena to the ball in Times Square, was invented between 1788 and 1907.
body:
### History

January 1 has no astronomical claim on the new year. Tradition credits Numa Pompilius, around 715 to 673 BCE, with reordering the Roman calendar so that January replaced March as the first month, though that attribution is traditional rather than documented; there is evidence that January 1 was not made the official start of the Roman year until 153 BCE. Julius Caesar's reform of 46 BCE produced the Julian calendar, which kept January 1 as the year's opening date.

Then it moved. After the fifth century much of Christian Europe shifted the new year off January 1, and March 25 and December 25 both became common starting dates. Pope Gregory XIII's calendar of 1582 restored January 1; Italy, France, and Spain adopted it immediately, while Protestant and Orthodox countries took far longer. Britain and its American colonies did not switch until 1752, having kept New Year's Day on March 25 until then — which makes the January 1 holiday younger, in English-speaking America, than most of the colonies observing it.

Legal standing is younger still. Congress first established public holidays in 1870, for the District of Columbia: New Year's Day, Independence Day, Christmas, and Thanksgiving.

The two American set pieces are both promotional in origin and both well documented. Times Square got its crowd in 1904, when Adolph Ochs staged an all-day street festival with fireworks to mark the opening of The New York Times' new headquarters — he had already persuaded the city to rename Longacre Square after the paper — and more than 200,000 people came. The city banned the fireworks two years later, and in 1907 a lighted ball descended the flagpole atop One Times Square instead: iron and wood, five feet across, 700 pounds, one hundred 25-watt bulbs, built by a young immigrant metalworker named Jacob Starr. It has gone down every year since except 1942 and 1943, when New York's wartime dimout darkened the square. The ball unveiled in November 2025 is 12.5 feet across and weighs 12,350 pounds.

Pasadena's parade is older and was frank about its purpose. Members of the Valley Hunt Club, led by Charles Frederick Holder, staged the first Tournament of Roses on New Year's Day in 1890. Holder's pitch to the club was advertising copy: "In New York, people are buried in snow. Let's hold a festival to tell the world about our paradise."

### How to observe

Find out when your New Year's Day off actually falls. Federal employees follow 5 U.S.C. 6103, and when January 1 lands on a Saturday the holiday is observed the preceding Friday. The federal New Year's Day for 2028 is therefore Friday, December 31, 2027.

Sing the song wrong knowingly. Robert Burns did not so much write "Auld Lang Syne" as compile it, in 1788, from older material reaching back as far as the sixteenth century. The tune was his publisher's choice and derives from a traditional Scottish folk-dance tune, possibly Sir Alexander Don's strathspey, though the Library of Congress notes the exact source is difficult to establish.

Watch the Rose Parade knowing what it was for. The Tournament of Roses began in 1890 as a winter-climate advertisement for Southern California, and the man who proposed it said so out loud at the meeting that launched it.
timeline:
- 153 BCE — Evidence indicates January 1 becomes the official start of the Roman year.
- 46 BCE — Julius Caesar's reform produces the Julian calendar, which keeps January 1 as the year's opening date.
- 1582 — Pope Gregory XIII's calendar restores January 1; Italy, France, and Spain adopt it immediately.
- 1752 — Britain and its American colonies adopt the Gregorian calendar, having observed New Year's Day on March 25 until then.
- 1870 — Congress establishes the first federal public holidays for the District of Columbia, New Year's Day among them.
- 1907 — A lighted ball descends One Times Square for the first time, after the city banned the fireworks of the 1904 celebration.
faq:
Is New Year's Day a federal holiday?
Yes, and one of the original four. Congress first established public holidays in 1870 — New Year's Day, Independence Day, Christmas, and Thanksgiving — for the District of Columbia. It is now listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103.

What happens when January 1 falls on a weekend?
Federal employees observe the holiday on the nearest weekday: the preceding Friday when January 1 is a Saturday, the following Monday when it is a Sunday. January 1, 2028 is a Saturday, so the federal observance is Friday, December 31, 2027.

Why does the year start on January 1?
Because it was legislated that way, repeatedly. Rome appears to have fixed January 1 as the official new year by 153 BCE, and the Julian calendar of 46 BCE kept it. Medieval Christian Europe largely moved the date to March 25 or December 25. The Gregorian calendar of 1582 restored January 1, and Britain and its colonies followed only in 1752.

Has the Times Square ball ever not dropped?
Twice. It was not lowered in 1942 or 1943, when New York's wartime dimout darkened the square. Crowds gathered anyway and marked midnight with a minute of silence and chimes rung from sound trucks at the base of the tower.

Where do New Year's resolutions come from?
The custom is usually traced to Babylonian or Roman vow-making, but that lineage is asserted far more often than it is documented, and this page has no primary source for it. Resolving at the turn of the year is an old habit; its specific ancestry is not established.

name: New Year's Eve
description: New Year's Eve is December 31, and in the United States it holds two very different midnights. One is a commercial spectacle a newspaper owner invented in 1904 to publicize his new building. The other is a vigil that Black congregations have kept since the night of December 31, 1862, when people waited in the dark for the Emancipation Proclamation to take effect.
body:
### History

The Times Square version began as advertising, and the Times Square Alliance, which runs the celebration today, says so plainly. Adolph Ochs, the German Jewish immigrant who owned The New York Times, had persuaded the city to rename Longacre Square after his paper in 1904. That December he marked the opening of the Times Tower with an all-day street festival ending in fireworks shot from the base of the building, and more than 200,000 people came.

The city banned the fireworks two years later. Ochs's replacement was a lighted ball lowered down the tower's flagpole at midnight to begin 1908, built by a young immigrant metalworker named Jacob Starr: iron and wood, five feet across, 700 pounds, lit by one hundred 25-watt bulbs. Starr's company, Artkraft Strauss, lowered it for most of the century that followed. The ball changed with its materials — wrought iron in 1920, aluminum in 1955, crystal in 2000, LEDs in 2007 — and the one unveiled in November 2025 is 12.5 feet across and weighs 12,350 pounds. It has descended every year since 1907 except 1942 and 1943, when New York's wartime dimout darkened the square; crowds gathered anyway and marked midnight with a minute of silence and chimes rung from sound trucks at the tower's base.

The other American tradition is quieter and was built on far higher stakes. Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation on September 22, 1862, declaring enslaved people in the rebelling states free — but it would not take effect until the new year. So on the night of December 31, 1862, as the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture records, enslaved and free African Americans gathered, many of them in secret, to wait. The proclamation took effect at midnight, at the start of January 1, 1863, and the night became known as Watch Night, or Freedom's Eve.

Gathering at all carried risk: Georgia's slave code of 1848 barred people of color from preaching or joining a religious meeting where more than seven were present. People worshipped anyway, in plantation praise houses and in "hush harbors" out in the woods, and the museum records the account of Charlotte Martin, a formerly enslaved woman in Florida whose brother was beaten to death for taking part. Watch Night services are still kept, generally beginning around 7 p.m. and running through midnight.

### How to observe

Look for a Watch Night service. They are widely held and generally open, and the history above is why the room goes quiet in the minutes before midnight rather than loud.

Do not plan the night around a federal day off: December 31 is not a federal holiday, and reaches that calendar only when January 1 falls on a Saturday. The next of those is 2028.

Arrange the ride before you drink. NHTSA counted 11,904 deaths in drunk-driving crashes in 2024, about 32 a day. It publishes no New Year's Eve-specific figure, so treat the familiar "deadliest night of the year" line with suspicion.
timeline:
- September 22, 1862 — Lincoln issues the Emancipation Proclamation, declaring enslaved people in the rebelling states free, to take effect with the new year.
- December 31, 1862 — African Americans gather, many in secret, to await its effect; the night becomes known as Watch Night, or Freedom's Eve. The proclamation takes effect at midnight on January 1, 1863.
- 1904 — Adolph Ochs marks the opening of the Times Tower with an all-day festival ending in fireworks; more than 200,000 people attend.
- 1907 — With the fireworks banned, a lighted ball descends the Times Tower flagpole to begin 1908: iron and wood, five feet across, 700 pounds, built by Jacob Starr.
- 1942–1943 — The ball is not lowered, because of New York's wartime dimout; crowds mark midnight with a minute of silence and chimes.
- November 2025 — The newest ball is unveiled: 12.5 feet across, 12,350 pounds.
faq:
Is New Year's Eve a federal holiday?
No. The Office of Personnel Management lists eleven legal public holidays under 5 U.S.C. 6103 and December 31 is not among them. It reaches the federal calendar only as the in-lieu-of date for New Year's Day when January 1 falls on a Saturday, as it does in 2028.

What is Watch Night?
A New Year's Eve service rooted in the night of December 31, 1862, when enslaved and free African Americans gathered, often in secret, to wait for the Emancipation Proclamation to take effect at midnight on January 1, 1863. Services are still held, generally beginning around 7 p.m. and running through midnight.

Has the Times Square ball ever failed to drop?
Twice, in 1942 and 1943, when New York's wartime dimout darkened the square. Crowds gathered anyway and marked midnight with a minute of silence and chimes rung from sound trucks at the base of the tower.

Why did the ball drop start in the first place?
Because the city banned the fireworks. Adolph Ochs's 1904 celebration for the opening of the Times Tower ended in a fireworks display, which was prohibited two years later, so to begin 1908 he had a lighted ball lowered down the tower's flagpole instead.

NHTSA publishes no New Year's Eve-specific breakdown on this page, which is why no such figure is given above.

Note on a source inconsistency: the Times Square Alliance page states that seven Ball versions have been designed while also calling the Constellation Ball the ninth Ball, and does not reconcile the two. This page therefore gives no count of how many balls there have been, and cites only the individual balls and dates the page states directly.

Rejected as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate, and content-farm or AI-generated listicles.
