description: Oktoberfest begins in September, which is the first thing worth knowing about it. The festival opens on the Theresienwiese in Munich on the first Saturday after September 15 and runs to the first Sunday in October — a window the city moved earlier in 1872 to catch better weather. The name stayed where the calendar used to be.
body:
### History

Oktoberfest started as a wedding party. On October 17, 1810, a large horse race was held on a meadow at the edge of Munich to celebrate the marriage of the Bavarian crown prince Ludwig — later King Ludwig I — to Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen. The city puts the crowd at around 50,000, watching from the slope above the meadow. With royal permission the ground was named in the bride's honor: Theresienwiese, Therese's meadow. A follow-up race the next year turned a one-off wedding entertainment into a tradition.

Munich residents found the full name unwieldy and shortened it, and the festival took the name of its ground. Locals still call it the "Wiesn," the Bavarian form of Wiese, meadow — a name about the field, not the beer.

The horse race that started everything remained part of Oktoberfest until the 1960s. The move into September came in 1872, to take advantage of the milder, sunnier late-summer weather, and the start and end rule has been fixed to that window since.

Two things in the festival's modern record are worth stating rather than skipping. On September 26, 1980, a bomb at the main entrance killed 12 visitors and the bomber and injured more than 200 people. And in 2020 Oktoberfest was canceled for the first time in decades because of the coronavirus pandemic — the city counted it as the 25th cancellation in 210 years — with 2021 canceled as well.

### How to observe

If you are going, the dates are not a guess: Oktoberfest 2027 runs September 18 to October 3 on the Theresienwiese.

Know why the length changes. The festival normally runs 16 days, but October 3, German Unity Day, always falls inside the Oktoberfest period. If it lands on a Monday the festival is extended a day, to 17. If it lands on a Tuesday, the city council can decide to run through it, making 18. That is the whole mechanism, and it is why published end dates differ year to year.

Plan for the scale. The Theresienwiese covers about 42 hectares — roughly 60 soccer fields — and holds 17 large festival tents, 21 small ones, and over 120 fairground attractions. Construction starts in mid-July, so the site is a building project for two months before anyone drinks anything.

The part most visitors miss is the Oide Wiesn, the historic section, which drew 447,000 paying visitors in 2026. It steps aside every fourth year for the Central Agricultural Festival, so whether it is there at all depends on the year you go.
timeline:
- October 17, 1810 — A horse race on a meadow outside Munich celebrates the wedding of Bavarian crown prince Ludwig and Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen; around 50,000 spectators watch from the slope above. The ground is named Theresienwiese in the bride's honor.
- 1811 — A follow-up race is held on the same meadow, and the festival becomes a tradition.
- 1872 — The festival is moved into September to take advantage of milder, sunnier late-summer weather.
- September 26, 1980 — A bomb at the festival's main entrance kills 12 visitors and the bomber and injures more than 200 people.
- 2020–2021 — Oktoberfest is canceled two years running because of the coronavirus pandemic; the city counts 2020 as the 25th cancellation in 210 years.
- 2026 — Around 7.4 million people attend, a record, and beer consumption is estimated at about 6.7 million liters.
faq:
Why does Oktoberfest start in September?
Because Munich moved it. The city says the festival was shifted into September in 1872 to take advantage of the milder, sunnier late-summer weather. Since then it has traditionally started on the first Saturday after September 15 and ended on the first Sunday in October, which leaves most of it in September.

When is Oktoberfest 2027?
September 18 to October 3, 2027, on the Theresienwiese in Munich.

Why does Oktoberfest last 16 days some years and 17 or 18 in others?
October 3, German Unity Day, always falls within the Oktoberfest period. If it falls on a Monday the festival is extended by one day, to 17. If it falls on a Tuesday, the city council can decide to end the festival on that day instead, making 18 days in all.

How did Oktoberfest begin?
As a wedding celebration. A horse race was held on October 17, 1810 to mark the marriage of the Bavarian crown prince Ludwig and Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen, the meadow was named Theresienwiese after the bride, and a repeat race the following year made it annual.

Why do people call it the "Wiesn"?
Theresienwiese was too long for everyday use, so the festival took the name of its ground. "Wiesn" is the Bavarian form of Wiese, meadow.

How big is Oktoberfest?
Around 7.4 million people attended in 2026, a record, up from about 6.5 million the year before. The grounds run to roughly 42 hectares and hold 17 large tents, 21 small ones and over 120 fairground attractions.

- Oktoberfest.de, Worth knowing about Oktoberfest — https://www.oktoberfest.de/en/magazine/worth-knowing-about-oktoberfest → the 16 / 17 / 18-day rule, agreeing with the city's statement; the Oide Wiesn standing aside every fourth year for the Central Agricultural Festival.

Source conflict resolved, not averaged: the city's history page calls Ludwig "Bavarian King Ludwig I" at the time of the 1810 wedding, while the city's own Theresienwiese page and Oktoberfest.de both call him Crown Prince — the Theresienwiese page explicitly as "Crown Prince Ludwig, later King Ludwig I." This page follows the Crown Prince reading: two of the three pages agree on it and it is the more precise statement, since Ludwig did not become king until 1825.

Omitted for lack of a source: the commonly repeated list of earlier Oktoberfest cancellations attributed to wars, cholera epidemics and the 1923–24 inflation. The city states only the 2020 and 2021 cancellations and a running total of 25 in 210 years, and does not enumerate the others, so neither does this page. Also omitted: a competing account on the city's FAQ page of how the nickname "Wiesn" arose, which appears garbled on that page and conflicts with the Theresienwiese page's straightforward explanation.

name: Passover
description: Passover begins on 15 Nisan and retells the Exodus from Egypt at a ritual meal, the seder, held in the home rather than the synagogue. Because a day in the Hebrew calendar begins at sundown, the first seder falls on the evening before the Gregorian date of the first day — a distinction worth holding on to when reading any calendar, including this one. It runs seven days in Israel and for most Reform Jews and eight in traditional Diaspora practice, and it is the most widely kept Jewish observance in the United States: six in ten American Jews told Pew they had held or attended a seder in the previous year.
body:
### History

The instructions are in Exodus 12, and they are specific. A lamb for each household, taken on the tenth day of the month; its blood "on the two side-posts and on the lintel"; the flesh eaten that night "roast with fire, and unleavened bread; with bitter herbs," in haste, "with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand." The name is explained inside the text: "when I see the blood" — "I will pass over you, and there shall no plague be upon you." Passover renders the Hebrew pesach, from the verb for passing over. The same chapter sets the seven days of unleavened bread and the evening-to-evening boundary that still governs the holiday, "the fourteenth day of the month at even" until "the one and twentieth day of the month at even." Quotations here follow the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation.

While the Temple stood, Passover was one of three festivals that required a pilgrimage to Jerusalem; Exodus 23 commands that "three times in the year all thy males shall appear before the Lord GOD." The destruction of the Second Temple ended the sacrifice, and what replaced it was the seder. Robert Harris of the Jewish Theological Seminary calls the change a "seismic shift": in place of the now impossible Temple ritual the rabbis adopted the form of the Roman symposium, a meal built around questions and discourse — and he adds that they could have told Jews to perform the sacrifice at home, and chose not to.

The seder's furniture is older than most people assume. Mishnah Pesachim 10, compiled around 200 CE, already has the four cups of wine, the reclining that "even the poorest of Jews" should not eat without, the child's question — "Why is this night different from all other nights?" — the bitter herbs, and the line that carries the whole evening: "In each and every generation a person must view himself as though he personally left Egypt." The same passage notes that eating charoset "is not a mitzva but merely a custom." The Haggadah, which scripts the evening, is attested in a tenth-century prayer book compiled by Rabbi Saadia Gaon; the Library of Congress calls it the most widely read classic text in the Jewish tradition after the Bible, and holds more than three thousand printed editions.

### How to observe

Chametz — leaven — is what the holiday turns on practically. The prohibited grains are wheat, rye, barley, oats and spelt, and the prohibition runs the whole festival, while eating matzah is an obligation only at the seder. Commercial matzah production runs on an eighteen-minute limit for how long dough may sit before baking, after which the lines are stopped and cleaned. Ashkenazi practice additionally avoids kitniyot, foods resembling the forbidden grains, including rice; Mediterranean and Middle Eastern traditions generally do not.

The seder plate is where meaning gets attached to food: parsley dipped in salt water for the tears of slavery, an egg for the rebirth of spring, bitter herbs for bitterness, charoset as custom rather than commandment, and the broken matzah whose larger piece is hidden and eaten later as the afikoman. Many American plates now also carry an orange, added as a symbol of feminism. The meal ends with "Next year in Jerusalem."

The most distinctly American thing about Passover is what Americans have used it to say. On April 4, 1969, the first anniversary of Dr. King's assassination, Arthur Waskow wrote a new Haggadah and about 800 people — Black and white, Jewish and Christian — gathered in the basement of Lincoln Temple, a Black church in Washington, for what became the Freedom Seder, weaving the liberation of the ancient Hebrews together with the liberation struggles of Black America.

For primary sources this is one of the better-served holidays online. The Library of Congress has digitized the Washington Haggadah, written in 1478 by the itinerant scribe Joel ben Simeon, and holds Abraham Berman's collection of 600 more. The National Library of Israel's 8,500 is the largest such collection in the world. All of it is free to read.
timeline:
- c. 200 CE — The Mishnah, at Pesachim 10, records the four cups of wine, the reclining, the child's question and the bitter herbs, and notes that charoset is a custom rather than a commandment.
- 10th century — The oldest complete version of the Haggadah appears in a prayer book compiled by Rabbi Saadia Gaon.
- 1478 — Joel ben Simeon, an itinerant scribe from Germany, writes what is now the Library of Congress's Washington Haggadah; the Library published a facsimile of it in 1993.
- 1846 — The Breslau rabbinical conference judges the second days of festivals to "have no longer any significance for our time," the step behind the Reform movement's seven-day Passover.
- April 4, 1969 — The first Freedom Seder is held in the basement of Lincoln Temple in Washington, DC, on the first anniversary of Dr. King's assassination; about 800 people attend.
- April 9, 2009 — President Obama hosts a seder in the Old Family Dining Room, which he later called "the first-ever White House Seder"; eight followed over his two terms.
faq:
When is the first seder?
On the evening before the first day of Passover. A day in the Hebrew calendar begins at sundown, so 15 Nisan starts the night before the Gregorian date calendars print for it. For 2027, Hebcal puts the start at sundown on Wednesday, April 21, with the first full day, 15 Nisan 5787, on Thursday, April 22 — the date in the table on this page. A second seder follows the next night wherever eight days are kept.

Is Passover seven days or eight?
Seven in Israel and for most Reform Jews, eight in traditional Diaspora practice. The difference is a survival. Before the Hebrew calendar was computed mathematically, the new month was fixed by witnesses sighting the crescent moon in Jerusalem, and distant communities could not be sure which of two days it had begun on, so they kept each festival day twice. The calculation removed the original reason but the custom stayed. Reform Judaism traces its one-day standard to the 1846 Breslau rabbinical conference.

Is Passover a federal holiday in the United States?
No. Federal offices, banks and post offices operate normally, and there is no observed day off. The Postal Service's Jewish-holiday stamp series is Hanukkah, now in its ninth issue; no Passover stamp appears in its current or announced programs. The first seder hosted by a sitting president at the White House was in 2009.

How many American Jews hold a seder?
Six in ten, in Pew's survey fielded from November 2019 to June 2020 — the most widely practiced ritual that survey measured, ahead of fasting on Yom Kippur at 46 percent. Pew's earlier 2013 survey put it at 70 percent.

Why matzah?
Unleavened bread recalls a departure too hurried for dough to rise. Exodus 12 requires seven days of it and the removal of leaven from the house. In practice the two rules have different reach: the ban on leaven applies to the whole festival, while the obligation to eat matzah applies only at the seder.

Source conflict reported rather than averaged: seder attendance. Pew's 2013 survey found 70 percent and its 2020 survey six in ten. This is the same organization in two survey waves, not a contradiction, and the page uses the more recent figure with its survey window named, citing the 2013 number separately and labeled.

Second conflict: when Passover ends, on 21 or 22 Nisan. Britannica's video page says "the 21st or 22nd"; Hebcal gives 15 to 22 Nisan for the Diaspora and 15 to 21 Nisan for Israel. These agree once the Israel and Diaspora schedules are separated, and Hebcal, as a calendar computation that publishes both schedules explicitly, is treated as the more primary for date mechanics.

Third conflict: the first White House seder. The President's own 2016 statement in the Compilation of Presidential Documents says "the first-ever White House Seder in 2009." An institutional history records a 1993 seder held by Clinton staff in the Indian Treaty Room of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, across the street from the White House and without the President present. That refines rather than refutes the presidential statement, and this page uses the precise form: the first seder hosted by a sitting president at the White House. The 1993 staff event is not asserted, because it could not be confirmed from a source on the site's allow-list.

Omitted for want of an acceptable source: the claim that the Haggadah is the most-printed Jewish book, which no library or museum source consulted supports — the Library of Congress's "most widely read classic text in the Jewish tradition" is used instead; the convention that the youngest child asks the Four Questions; a definition of the cup of Elijah; the yellow cap on kosher-for-Passover Coca-Cola, and Manischewitz's founding year, founder or city; the Hebrew term shalosh regalim; publication of the Freedom Seder Haggadah in Ramparts; and any statement about historians' views on the historicity of the Exodus or divergence between archaeology and the biblical narrative, which would need a dedicated pass at books and journals rather than the sources reached here. The page therefore presents Exodus 12 as what the text prescribes, not as an account of events.

Less than fully confident, flagged deliberately: the afikoman. The practice of hiding the larger broken piece and eating it later is described in a first-person Smithsonian Folklife essay rather than in a reference definition, so the page states it in one clause and builds nothing on it. Also flagged: the statement that no Passover stamp exists is a negative finding from a search of the Postal Service's own newsroom and its announced 2026 program, and is worded as such rather than as a historical absolute.

On two sources used by considered judgment: reformjudaism.org, the Union for Reform Judaism, is cited only for claims about Reform practice and the movement's own history, where it is the administering organization; and sefaria.org is used as the digital locus for two published editions that are named every time they are cited, the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation of the Tanakh and the Koren William Davidson Edition of the Mishnah and Talmud.

Not used as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate, Wikipedia, and comparable aggregator and content-farm pages.

name: Patriot Day — National Day of Service & Remembrance
description: Patriot Day falls on September 11 and honors the 2,977 people killed in the terrorist attacks of 2001. Congress designated it by joint resolution in December of that year, which means the first Patriot Day was September 11, 2002. It is a day of remembrance and, since 2009, of service; it is not a holiday, and nothing closes.
body:
### History

The designation came quickly. House Joint Resolution 71 passed the House on October 25, 2001 and the Senate on November 30, and was approved on December 18 as Public Law 107-89. Its operative language, now at 36 U.S.C. 144, is four words: "September 11 is Patriot Day." The rest of the statute asks the president to issue a proclamation each year calling on governments and the public to observe the day, on federal agencies to fly the flag at half-staff, and on Americans to observe a moment of silence. The statute names no time for that silence.

An earlier proclamation is sometimes mistaken for the first Patriot Day. Proclamation 7462, signed September 13, 2001, designated Friday, September 14 as a National Day of Prayer and Remembrance, with "noontime memorial services, the ringing of bells at that hour, and evening candlelight remembrance vigils." That was a single day, not an annual observance.

The service half of the day arrived eight years later, and the law behind it is usually described wrongly. The Edward M. Kennedy Serve America Act, Public Law 111-13 of April 21, 2009, does not amend the Patriot Day statute and does not contain the word "Patriot" anywhere. What it did was add a provision to the national service laws authorizing the federal service agency, now AmeriCorps, to organize activities and make grants for "the September 11th National Day of Service and Remembrance" — an observance the 2009 proclamation credited to the victims' families. So "Patriot Day and National Day of Service and Remembrance" is the title of a presidential proclamation, not the day's name in statute — and administrations have used that longer title inconsistently.

The 8:46 a.m. Eastern moment of silence also comes from the proclamations rather than the law; it marks the time American Airlines Flight 11 struck the North Tower. The 2002 proclamation asked for silence "beginning at 8:46 a.m. eastern daylight time, or another appropriate commemorative time"; the 2009 one dropped the alternative, and recent proclamations have directed half-staff without naming a time at all.

### How to observe

The 9/11 Memorial maintains a searchable directory of every name inscribed on the bronze parapets, which locates a person by panel. Reading one entry, rather than a total, is the closest thing to the point of the day.

For the service half, AmeriCorps runs a volunteer search for projects tied to September 11, and the nonprofit 9/11 Day organizes meal-packing events that produced more than 6.5 million meals across eighteen cities in 2023. If you want primary material, the Library of Congress's September 11, 2001 Documentary Project holds oral histories recorded in the weeks after the attacks, with roughly 200 interviews online. The Flight 93 National Memorial near Shanksville and the Pentagon Memorial, with its 184 benches, are both open to visitors.
timeline:
- 2001 — Public Law 107-89, approved December 18, designates September 11 as Patriot Day; it is codified at 36 U.S.C. 144.
- 2002 — The first Patriot Day is observed on September 11 under Proclamation 7590.
- 2008 — The Pentagon Memorial, a bench for each of the 184 people killed there, is dedicated on September 11.
- 2009 — The Serve America Act authorizes federal support for a September 11 National Day of Service and Remembrance.
- 2011 — The 9/11 Memorial is dedicated on the tenth anniversary and opens to the public the next day.
faq:
Is Patriot Day a federal holiday?

No. The eleven legal public holidays are listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103, and Patriot Day is not among them. It sits in Title 36, the patriotic observances title, so no federal leave attaches.

How many people were killed?

The 9/11 Memorial counts 2,977 people killed at the three attack sites on September 11, 2001: 2,753 in New York, 184 at the Pentagon, and 40 aboard Flight 93. That figure counts victims and excludes the nineteen hijackers. The memorial bears 2,983 names, because it also honors the six people killed in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing. Among the 2,977 were 441 first responders from more than thirty agencies, including 343 New York City firefighters, 37 Port Authority police officers and 23 New York City police officers.

How many have died since of 9/11-related illness?

There is no official count. The federal World Trade Center Health Program states plainly that it does not track cause of death for its members, so its figures cannot answer the question. The Justice Department's Victim Compensation Fund reported 8,996 claims filed on behalf of people who had died as of December 31, 2025, but a claim is not a certified cause of death.

Is Patriot Day the same as Patriots' Day?

No. Patriots' Day is a state holiday in Massachusetts and Maine observed on the third Monday in April, commemorating the battles of Lexington and Concord in 1775.

What time is the moment of silence?

Proclamations have commonly set it at 8:46 a.m. Eastern, the moment of the first impact, though the statute itself names no time and recent proclamations have directed only that flags fly at half-staff.

name: Pi Day
description: Pi Day falls on March 14, because 3/14 matches the first three digits of pi, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. It began in 1988 as an in-house celebration at the Exploratorium, San Francisco's hands-on science museum, and spread from there into classrooms worldwide. It is one of the few modern holidays whose origin is fully documented, down to the man who thought of it and the pies on the table.
body:
### History

In 1988, three years after the death of Exploratorium founder Frank Oppenheimer, museum staff gathered at a retreat in Monterey, California, to regroup. There Larry Shaw connected March 14 with the digits of pi. The Exploratorium describes him as a former staff physicist, tinkerer, and media specialist; the San Francisco Chronicle called him the museum's technical curator of 33 years. On the first Pi Day, at 1:59 — the digits that follow 3.14 — Shaw and his wife, Catherine, set out a table of fruit pies and a tea urn on the museum floor.

The rituals accumulated afterward. Shaw built the Pi Shrine, a circular brass plaque set in a circular classroom made of circular cinderblocks, and led a parade through the museum with a boombox playing the digits of pi to "Pomp and Circumstance," ending by circling the shrine 3.14 times. A few years in, Shaw's daughter Sara noticed that March 14 is also Albert Einstein's birthday, and a chorus of "Happy Birthday" to Einstein joined the program. Shaw led the parade every year until his death in 2017, known around the museum as the Prince of Pi.

Washington arrived twenty-one years late and did less than it is credited with. Representative Bart Gordon of Tennessee introduced House Resolution 224 on March 9, 2009; the House agreed to it three days later, 391 to 10, on a motion to suspend the rules. The resolution supports "the designation of a 'Pi Day' and its celebration around the world," recognizes the National Science Foundation's math and science programs, and encourages schools to teach the day. It creates no holiday, it never went to the Senate, and it mentions neither the Exploratorium nor Einstein. Both the Exploratorium and NASA describe it more loosely than its own text supports — as Pi Day becoming "an official U.S. national holiday," or Congress "officially designating" the date.

### How to observe

Try the NASA Pi Day Challenge. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory has run one every March since 2014: illustrated problems that use pi on real mission data, pitched at grades four through twelve, with answers posted the next day.

Settle the argument about how many digits anyone needs. JPL's then-chief engineer for mission operations, Marc Rayman, answered it in public: for interplanetary navigation, the laboratory's most demanding work, they use 3.141592653589793 — fifteen decimal places. At that precision a circle 125 billion miles around comes out wrong by a little over half an inch, and thirty-seven places would size the known universe to within a hydrogen atom.

If you are near San Francisco, the Exploratorium still holds its Pi Procession at 1:59 p.m., circling the Pi Shrine 3.14 times, with a free slice of pie after.

And note what else the date carries: since 2020 March 14 has also been the International Day of Mathematics, which publishes a yearly theme and classroom activities at idm314.org.
timeline:
- 1988 — At a staff retreat in Monterey, Larry Shaw links March 14 with 3.14. He and Catherine Shaw mark the first Pi Day at 1:59 with fruit pies and a tea urn.
- 2009 — H. Res. 224 is introduced on March 9 and agreed to by the House on March 12, 391 to 10, supporting the designation of a Pi Day.
- 2014 — NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory runs the first NASA Pi Day Challenge.
- 2017 — Larry Shaw dies, having led the parade every year since the first.
- 2019 — UNESCO proclaims March 14 the International Day of Mathematics on November 26, at the 40th session of its General Conference.
- 2020 — The first International Day of Mathematics is held, on March 14.
faq:
Is Pi Day an official federal holiday?

No. The House of Representatives passed a resolution in 2009 supporting the designation of a Pi Day, but a House resolution is not law. It never went to the Senate, it created no holiday, and federal offices, banks, and schools operate normally on March 14.

Who started Pi Day?

Larry Shaw, at the Exploratorium in San Francisco, in 1988. He came up with the idea at a staff retreat in Monterey and marked the first one with his wife, Catherine, at a table of fruit pies set out at 1:59.

Why March 14?

Written American-style, the date is 3/14, the first three digits of pi. The International Mathematical Union notes the limit of that logic: in countries that write the day first, the date is 14/3 and the joke does not land.

How many digits of pi does NASA use?

For its highest-accuracy calculations, interplanetary navigation, JPL uses 3.141592653589793 — fifteen decimal places. Rounding there would misjudge a circle 125 billion miles in circumference by about half an inch.

Is Pi Day the same thing as the International Day of Mathematics?

They share the date but not the history. UNESCO proclaimed March 14 the International Day of Mathematics in November 2019, choosing the date precisely because it was already being celebrated as Pi Day; the first observance was in 2020.

name: Presidents' Day
description: The federal holiday on the third Monday in February is, in law, Washington's Birthday. Congress has never renamed it: "Presidents' Day" was proposed in 1951, got nowhere officially, and became the common name three decades later through holiday sales advertising. The holiday also cannot land on Washington's birthday — the third Monday in February falls between the 15th and the 21st, and he was born on the 22nd.
body:
### History

February 22 became a holiday for federal employees in the District of Columbia by an act of January 31, 1879. That law did not require that anyone be paid for the day off; an 1885 act fixed that, requiring pay for federal holidays and extending them to federal employees everywhere rather than only those near the capital.

The date moved in 1968. The Uniform Monday Holiday Act — Public Law 90-363, enacted June 28, 1968 and effective January 1, 1971 — reorganized the federal calendar around three-day weekends. It shifted Washington's Birthday from February 22 to the third Monday in February, moved Memorial Day from May 30 to the last Monday in May, moved Veterans Day from November 11 to the fourth Monday in October, and added Columbus Day on the second Monday in October. Veterans Day was returned to November 11 by a 1975 law. Washington's Birthday was not moved back, and has not fallen on February 22 since.

The name never changed, and the National Archives is blunt about it: neither Congress nor any president has ever stipulated that the holiday be called President's Day. The name was floated in 1951 and spread through retail advertising in the 1980s. The statute, 5 U.S.C. 6103, still reads "Washington's Birthday," and the Office of Personnel Management says the same when asked directly. The gap between the legal name and the one on the mattress circular is the most interesting thing about this holiday.

Washington was born on February 22, 1732 by the Gregorian calendar. Britain and its colonies did not adopt that calendar until 1752; under the Julian calendar in use when he was born, the date was February 11.

### How to observe

Read Washington's Farewell Address, or at least the passages on faction and foreign entanglement. The Senate still has one of its own members read all 7,641 words aloud in the chamber each year around the holiday, alternating between the parties, and has done so every year since 1896 — the tradition traces to a single reading on February 22, 1862, revived in 1888. The reader then signs a leather-bound notebook kept by the Secretary of the Senate and adds a few remarks, which makes the book a one-senator-a-year commentary on American politics going back to 1900.

Go to Mount Vernon. Washington's estate in Virginia admits visitors free on the holiday and treats it as an actual birthday: a wreath-laying at his tomb, cannon firings by the Presidential Salute Battery, fife and drum, a Revolutionary War encampment on the field, and an open house at the research library. Mansion tours are timed and first come, first served, with waits of two to three hours — check the year's schedule before driving out.
timeline:
- February 22, 1732 — George Washington is born, by the Gregorian calendar; under the Julian calendar then in use in the British colonies the date was February 11.
- January 31, 1879 — Congress adds February 22 to the holidays observed by federal employees in the District of Columbia. The act does not require that they be paid for it.
- 1885 — Congress requires pay for federal holidays and extends them to all federal employees, not only those near Washington.
- 1951 — The name "Presidents' Day" is proposed. The federal government never adopts it.
- June 28, 1968 — The Uniform Monday Holiday Act (Pub. L. 90-363) moves Washington's Birthday to the third Monday in February, along with Memorial Day and Veterans Day, and adds Columbus Day. It takes effect January 1, 1971.
- September 18, 1975 — Pub. L. 94-97 returns Veterans Day to November 11. Washington's Birthday stays on its Monday.
faq:
Is the holiday officially called Presidents' Day?
No. The federal holiday is "Washington's Birthday" in 5 U.S.C. 6103, and the Office of Personnel Management gives that as the official name. The National Archives notes that neither Congress nor any president has ever stipulated the name "President's Day." It became the common name through holiday sales advertising in the 1980s, after being proposed and rejected in 1951.

Can the holiday fall on Washington's actual birthday?
No. The third Monday in February can only fall between February 15 and February 21. February 22 is outside that range, so since the Monday rule took effect in 1971 the holiday has never landed on the date it was created to mark.

Why is it on a Monday?
The Uniform Monday Holiday Act of 1968, effective January 1, 1971, moved several federal holidays to Mondays to create three-day weekends. Washington's Birthday was one of four holidays it changed.

Does the federal holiday honor all the presidents?
Not in law. 5 U.S.C. 6103 names Washington's Birthday and nobody else. The broader meaning came from popular and commercial use rather than from Congress, and states are free to name and observe their own February holidays differently.

Is it a federal holiday?
Yes — one of the eleven legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103. Federal offices, banks and post offices close on the third Monday in February.

name: Rosh Hashanah
description: Rosh Hashanah is the Jewish New Year, observed on the first and second days of Tishri and beginning at sunset the evening before the date a civil calendar shows. It opens the ten days of repentance that close with Yom Kippur, and it falls in the seventh month of the Hebrew calendar rather than the first. The Torah commands the day but never calls it a new year; the name, and the idea, belong to the rabbis who compiled the Mishnah.
body:
### History

The textual basis is two short passages. Leviticus 23:23-25 instructs the Israelites that "in the seventh month, on the first day of the month, you shall observe complete rest, a sacred occasion commemorated with loud blasts." Numbers 29:1 repeats the instruction and adds, "You shall observe it as a day when the horn is sounded." Both renderings are from the Jewish Publication Society's gender-sensitive Tanakh. Neither passage uses the phrase Rosh Hashanah, and neither calls the day a new year.

Encyclopaedia Britannica dates the shift to the second century CE, when the scholars compiling the Mishnah designated the first of Tishri as the new year of years and tied it to the beginning of creation. The Mishnah is also where the oddity of a new year in the seventh month resolves itself, because it does not treat the Hebrew calendar as having a single new year at all. Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1 opens: "They are four days in the year that serve as the New Year, each for a different purpose." The first of Nisan is the new year for kings and for the order of the festivals. The first of Elul is the new year for animal tithes, with Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon dissenting in favor of the first of Tishri. The first of Tishri is the new year for counting years, for sabbatical and jubilee reckoning, for planting, and for tithing vegetables. The new year for trees is the first of Shevat according to Beit Shammai and the fifteenth according to Beit Hillel.

The Hebrew phrase itself does appear in scripture, once, and not as the name of a holiday. Ezekiel 40:1 dates a vision to "the twenty-fifth year of our exile, the fourteenth year after the city had fallen, at the beginning of the year" - and "at the beginning of the year" is how JPS renders b'rosh hashanah.

How long the holiday lasts is still not settled. Britannica describes a "major two-day Jewish holiday," kept for two days in Israel as well as the Diaspora. The Union for Reform Judaism's own answer, written by Rabbi Mark Washofsky, is blunter: "The answer is: one, mostly." Most North American Reform congregations keep one day, some keep two, and the Reform movement has observed single festival days since its nineteenth-century beginnings.

### How to observe

The central act is the shofar, a ram's horn. Chabad.org puts the count at 100 blasts across the Rosh Hashanah morning services - thirty after the Torah reading and as many as seventy more during and just after Musaf - and Britannica agrees on the hundred. The two differ on vocabulary: Chabad names three types of blast (tekiah, shevarim, teruah), Britannica four, adding tekiah gedolah, a longer tekiah. If the first day falls on Shabbat, the shofar is sounded only on the second.

On the first afternoon, many go to a body of water for tashlich and cast off the year's sins. Britannica notes that Jewish tradition argues internally about whether anything physical should go into the water at all, which is worth knowing before you turn up with bread.

The food is unusually legible. Apple slices dipped in honey; challah baked round instead of oval and dipped in honey rather than salt; pomegranates, which Britannica says are "said to have" 613 seeds for the 613 commandments; a fish head, from the wish in Deuteronomy 28:13 to be the head and not the tail. On the second night, a fruit you have not eaten since it was last in season, so the Shehechiyanu blessing has something new to attach to.

If you would rather have the holiday's own argument than its atmosphere, Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1 is two minutes of reading and free on Sefaria.
timeline:
- 2nd century CE - The scholars compiling the Mishnah designate the first of Tishri the new year of years and tie it to the beginning of creation. Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1 records four separate new years, with Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel still disagreeing about the one for trees.
- 11th or 12th century CE - Unetaneh Tokef - "On Rosh Hashanah it is inscribed, and on Yom Kippur it is sealed" - is attributed to Rabbi Amnon of Mainz, though Britannica notes it may be centuries older.
- 19th century - The Reform movement, from its beginnings, reinstates the observance of each festival day, Rosh Hashanah included, as a single day.
- September 23-24, 2025 - New York City's public schools close for both days of Rosh Hashanah; the system closed again for Yom Kippur on October 2.
- October 1, 2027 - Rosh Hashanah 5788 begins at sundown on Friday, October 1, and runs through nightfall on October 3.
faq:
When is Rosh Hashanah?
It falls on the first and second days of Tishri, which land in September or October, and it begins at sunset on the evening before the date a civil calendar shows. Rosh Hashanah 5788 begins at sundown on Friday, October 1, 2027.

Is Rosh Hashanah one day or two?
Both, depending on the congregation. Britannica describes a two-day holiday, and it is kept for two days in Israel as well as the Diaspora. But most Reform congregations in North America observe one day - the Union for Reform Judaism's own answer is "one, mostly" - because the movement reinstated single festival days in the nineteenth century.

Is Rosh Hashanah a federal holiday in the United States?
No. Federal law, 5 U.S.C. 6103, sets the list of federal holidays, and Rosh Hashanah is not on it, so federal offices run normally. Some school systems close anyway: New York City's public schools were closed on September 23 and 24, 2025.

Why is the Jewish New Year in the seventh month?
Because the Hebrew calendar has more than one new year. Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1 lists four, each for a different purpose: the first of Nisan for kings and the order of the festivals, the first of Elul for animal tithes, the first of Tishri for counting years and for sabbatical and jubilee reckoning, and Shevat for trees. Rosh Hashanah is the new year for counting years.

How many times is the shofar blown?
A hundred blasts over the course of the Rosh Hashanah morning services. Sources differ on the taxonomy - Chabad names three kinds of blast, Britannica four - and if the first day of the holiday is Shabbat, the shofar is sounded only on the second day.

name: Small Business Saturday
description: Small Business Saturday falls on the Saturday after Thanksgiving, wedged between Black Friday and Cyber Monday, and it was created by a credit card company. American Express launched it in 2010, during the recession, to push some of the holiday weekend's spending toward small and local businesses. Unlike the two days flanking it, it has been formally designated by the United States Senate, repeatedly and by name.
body:
### History

The day is a corporate initiative that acquired an official endorsement. American Express says it created Small Business Saturday "in the midst of the recession in 2010," placing it on the Saturday after Thanksgiving "to encourage people to Shop Small and bring more holiday shopping to small businesses." The company describes the Saturday as one part of a larger, year-round Shop Small movement, and says the first one, in 2010, was a success.

The following year it entered the congressional record. On November 10, 2011, Senator Mary Landrieu and thirty-two co-sponsors from both parties submitted S.Res. 320, which was considered and agreed to. It designated November 26, 2011 as "Small Business Saturday" and supported efforts "to encourage consumers to shop locally" and "to increase awareness of the value of locally owned small businesses and the impact of locally owned small businesses on the economy of the United States." American Express's account that the Senate passed a resolution in 2011 matches the record.

It then became a habit. The Senate designated the day again for November 24, 2012, in S.Res. 589, sponsored by Senator Olympia Snowe, and for November 29, 2014, in S.Res. 548, sponsored by Senator Maria Cantwell. Each was considered and agreed to. The resolutions make their case in findings rather than rhetoric: the 2014 text counts 28,200,000 small businesses in the United States, employing more than 48 percent of private-sector workers, paying more than 42 percent of private-sector payroll, and responsible for 63 percent of the net new jobs created between 1993 and 2013.

Two things are worth noting about the pairing. None of those resolutions mentions American Express. And the company's own pages, which state the founding year plainly, do not give the calendar date of that first Small Business Saturday in 2010.

### How to observe

The instruction in the Senate's own language is the simplest one available: shop locally. The practical version is to spend where the owner is on the premises — a hardware store, a bookshop, a repair counter, a restaurant that is not a franchise — and to do it on an errand you were going to run anyway, rather than as a gesture.

Two things are worth more to a small business than one Saturday's purchase. The first is a review: a few specific sentences on whichever platform your neighbors actually read. The second is a gift card or a deposit against future work, which moves cash into the business now, in the season when it needs it.

If you run a small business yourself, the Senate resolutions are public documents you can quote in your own promotion, and they cost nothing to use. American Express's Shop Small program is a sponsor's marketing platform, which you may or may not want to join. The day works either way.
timeline:
- 2010 — American Express creates Small Business Saturday, placing it on the Saturday after Thanksgiving, and the first one is held that November.
- November 10, 2011 — Senator Mary Landrieu and thirty-two co-sponsors submit S.Res. 320; it is considered and agreed to, designating November 26, 2011 as Small Business Saturday.
- September 22, 2012 — S.Res. 589, sponsored by Senator Olympia Snowe, is considered and agreed to, designating November 24, 2012.
- September 16, 2014 — S.Res. 548, sponsored by Senator Maria Cantwell, is considered and agreed to, designating November 29, 2014, with findings counting 28,200,000 small businesses in the United States.
- Since 2010 — American Express describes the Saturday as one part of its broader, year-round Shop Small movement.
faq:
Is Small Business Saturday a federal holiday?
No. The 11 legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) do not include it. The Senate has designated particular dates as Small Business Saturday by resolution in several years, which is a formal expression of support rather than the creation of a holiday.

Who started Small Business Saturday?
American Express, in 2010. The company says it created the day "in the midst of the recession in 2010" and set it on the Saturday after Thanksgiving. It remains a sponsored initiative, though the Senate resolutions endorsing the date do not mention the company.

When is Small Business Saturday?
The Saturday after Thanksgiving. Because federal law places Thanksgiving on the fourth Thursday in November, the Saturday falls between November 24 and November 30.

Has Congress officially recognized it?
The Senate has, several times, one year at a time. S.Res. 320 designated November 26, 2011; S.Res. 589 designated November 24, 2012; S.Res. 548 designated November 29, 2014. Each was considered and agreed to. These are Senate resolutions rather than statutes, and they oblige no one to do anything.

How much do people spend on Small Business Saturday?
This page does not give a figure. Spending and participation totals for the day circulate widely every year, but none could be traced to a primary record for this page, so none is published here rather than repeating a number that cannot be checked.

name: St. Patrick's Day
description: St. Patrick's Day falls on March 17, the traditional date of the death of Ireland's patron saint, and it is one of the few holidays Americans largely built for themselves. The parades, the green river in Chicago, the corned beef: almost all of it took shape in American cities, among Irish immigrants who were not especially welcome in them.
body:
### History

What is reliably known about Patrick comes mostly from Patrick. His Confessio, published with its manuscripts and translations by the Royal Irish Academy, is a first-person account and strikingly plain: he calls himself a sinner and a simple country person, the least of all believers, and says many look down on him. He names his father, Calpornius, a deacon, and his grandfather Potitus, a priest, and places his family home near somewhere he calls Bannavem Taburniae. He says he was about sixteen when he was taken prisoner there. The Library of Congress notes that legend holds he died on March 17, around 492 — the date the feast commemorates.

The stories most people can recite — the shamrock explaining the Trinity, the snakes driven into the sea — are later traditions. This page has no primary source for either, so it will not tell you when they began.

The American holiday is better documented, and it is an immigrant story before it is an Irish one. The Charitable Irish Society, founded in Boston in 1737 and still describing itself as the oldest Irish society in the Americas, has held a March 17 dinner since its founding; one of its two original purposes was relieving suffering among Irish arrivals in need. Parades came later: the Library of Congress dates New York's official parade to March 17, 1766, with an unofficial march in 1762, suggests Boston's may go back to 1775, and puts Savannah's at 1824.

Then came the famine. Irish immigration rose sharply in the 1840s after the potato famine of 1845–49, which killed more than a million people. Many arrivals met economic discrimination and open prejudice from an Anglo-Saxon Protestant majority hostile both to the Irish and to Catholicism, which is part of why a parade was never only a celebration. When New York's St. Patrick's Cathedral was completed in 1879, the route was extended up Fifth Avenue so the archbishop and clergy could review it from in front of the church.

### How to observe

Read Patrick in his own voice. The Royal Irish Academy's Confessio site carries the Latin alongside English translations and the manuscripts that preserve the text. It is short, and the distance between the man who wrote it and the figure on the parade float is the most interesting thing about the day.

Find out what your city's parade actually is; many are older than their green-beer reputation and are still run by Irish-American societies. In Chicago the river is dyed by the plumbers' union: NBC Chicago reports that plumbers in the 1960s used orange dye to trace a leak, saw it turn the water green, and the head of Local 130 then proposed doing it deliberately, with the agreement of his friend Mayor Richard J. Daley. The dyeing follows the parade weekend rather than March 17 — in 2026 it began at 10 a.m. on March 14.
timeline:
- 1737 — The Charitable Irish Society is founded in Boston and begins holding a St. Patrick's Day dinner on March 17.
- 1762 — An unofficial St. Patrick's Day march is held in New York City.
- 1766 — New York City's official St. Patrick's Day parade dates from March 17 of this year.
- 1845–49 — Ireland's potato famine kills more than a million people and drives a sharp rise in Irish immigration to the United States.
- 1879 — St. Patrick's Cathedral is completed in New York and the parade is extended up Fifth Avenue so the archbishop and clergy can review it.
- 1960s — Chicago plumbers find that orange leak-tracing dye turns the river green; the head of Plumbers' Local 130 proposes doing it on purpose for St. Patrick's Day.
faq:
Is St. Patrick's Day a federal holiday in the United States?
No. March 17 does not appear on the Office of Personnel Management's list of federal holidays, set by 5 U.S.C. 6103. Federal offices, banks, and the mail all run normally.

Is it a public holiday in Ireland?
Yes, one of the country's ten. If it falls on a day you would not normally work you still get public-holiday benefit, but there is no automatic legal right to take the next working day off.

Which American city had the first St. Patrick's Day parade?
It is genuinely contested, and the answer depends on what counts as a parade. The Library of Congress dates New York's official parade to March 17, 1766 and an unofficial march to 1762, and says Boston's may go back to 1775. The frequently cited Boston 1737 is the year the Charitable Irish Society was founded and began its March 17 dinner — a banquet, not a parade.

Did St. Patrick use a shamrock to explain the Trinity?
Not in anything he wrote. The Confessio, his own surviving account of his life, does not contain the story. It is a later tradition, and this page has no primary source for when it started.

Why is the Chicago River green?
Because the plumbers' union dyes it. NBC Chicago reports that plumbers in the 1960s used orange dye to find a leak, noticed it turned the water green, and the head of Local 130 proposed doing it on purpose, with Mayor Richard J. Daley's agreement.

- Charitable Irish Society, About Us — https://charitableirishsociety.org/About-Us → founding in Boston in 1737; the two original purposes, including relieving suffering and aiding members and other worthy recipients in need; the St. Patrick's Day dinner held on March 17 since its founding; and the society's description of itself as the oldest Irish society in the Americas. Cited as the organization's own account of its history.
- Citizens Information (Ireland), Public holidays — https://www.citizensinformation.ie/en/employment/employment-rights-and-conditions/leave-and-holidays/public-holidays/ → St Patrick's Day, 17 March, as one of Ireland's ten public holidays; entitlement to public-holiday benefit when the day is not a normal working day, with no automatic legal entitlement to the next working day off.
- U.S. Office of Personnel Management, Federal Holidays — https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/pay-leave/federal-holidays/ → the eleven federal holidays established by 5 U.S.C. 6103, and the absence of March 17 from that list.
- NBC Chicago, Why does Chicago dye its river green for St. Patrick's Day? Daley; and the 2026 dyeing beginning at 10 a.m. on March 14.

On the "first parade" question: the Library of Congress is followed throughout, and the frequently repeated Boston 1737 date is treated as the Charitable Irish Society's founding and dinner rather than a parade, per that society's own page. No aggregator claim is repeated. The shamrock and snake legends are left undated because no primary source for them was found.

name: Super Bowl Sunday
description: Super Bowl Sunday is the day the National Football League plays its championship game. Nobody declared it a holiday — the league simply schedules the game as part of each season, and the country rearranged its Sunday around it. Encyclopædia Britannica describes the day as having become an unofficial American holiday, which is the closest thing to a formal status it has.
body:
### History

The game exists because of a merger. The NFL and the rival American Football League agreed to combine in 1966, and the agreement called for an end-of-season championship game between the two leagues' champions. The merger itself was not finalized until 1970, so the first game was played while the leagues were still separate: January 15, 1967, at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, where the NFL's Green Bay Packers beat the AFL's Kansas City Chiefs 35–10. It was carried on two television networks and played before less than a sellout crowd — the only one of these games that has not sold out.

It was also not called the Super Bowl. That first game was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game. The name "Super Bowl" first appeared in 1969, and the Roman numerals arrived with it. Because each game is played in a calendar year after the season it decides, the numerals are what keep the game and its season from being confused.

What the name attached to is now a commercial event as much as a football game. Every Super Bowl after the first has sold out, and advertising time during the broadcast is the most expensive of the year: a 30-second spot cost roughly $4.8 million in 2016. Since the 1980s, public and press attention to the commercials has nearly matched attention to the game itself — which is an honest thing to say about a day whose observance, for a large share of the audience, consists of watching advertisements.

### How to observe

Look the date up rather than assuming it. The NFL fixes the game inside each season's postseason schedule, so it moves. Super Bowl LXI is set for Sunday, February 14, 2027, at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles, with ESPN carrying the broadcast. That date is Valentine's Day, which is worth noticing well before the second week of February if you owe someone dinner.

One detail that changes how the game looks on screen: for Super Bowl LXI the NFC champion is the designated home team and gets the choice of uniform color. The "home" team at a Super Bowl plays in a neutral stadium, so the designation is purely about jerseys and locker rooms.

If the football history interests you more than the broadcast, the Pro Football Hall of Fame in Canton, Ohio has been maintained by the NFL since 1963 and is where the primary record of the game's early years is kept — including the years when the championship had a duller name and could not fill a stadium.
timeline:
- 1966 — The NFL and the American Football League agree to merge; the agreement calls for an end-of-season championship game between the two leagues' champions.
- January 15, 1967 — The first game, the AFL-NFL World Championship Game, is played at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. Green Bay beats Kansas City 35–10, on two television networks and before less than a sellout crowd.
- 1969 — The name "Super Bowl" appears for the first time, along with the Roman numerals used to designate each game.
- 1970 — The NFL-AFL merger is finalized; from the 1970–71 season the game decides the NFL championship between the AFC and NFC champions.
- 2025–26 season — Super Bowl LX: the Seattle Seahawks beat the New England Patriots 29–13.
- February 14, 2027 — Super Bowl LXI is scheduled for SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles, televised by ESPN, with the NFC champion as the designated home team.
faq:
Is Super Bowl Sunday always on the same date?
No. The NFL schedules the game as part of each season's postseason, so the date moves; Britannica describes the game as played in January or February. Super Bowl LXI is set for Sunday, February 14, 2027.

Is Super Bowl Sunday a holiday?
Not an official one. It has no federal or state status and is not among the federal holidays, so nothing closes for it. Britannica calls it an unofficial American holiday, which describes the behavior rather than any designation.

Why was the first Super Bowl not called the Super Bowl?
Because the name did not exist yet. The January 15, 1967 game was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game, and "Super Bowl" first appeared in 1969.

Why do Super Bowls use Roman numerals?
Each game is played in a calendar year after the season it settles, so a plain year would be ambiguous. The numerals came in with the name in 1969 and identify the game itself.

Where is the 2027 Super Bowl being played?
SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles, on Sunday, February 14, 2027 — Valentine's Day. ESPN has the broadcast, and the NFC champion will be the designated home team.

Each is repeated everywhere, and none could be attributed to a primary or reputable secondary source in this run, so none appears above.

name: Thanksgiving Day
description: Thanksgiving falls on the fourth Thursday of November — November 26 in 2026 — and is a federal holiday. The story most people know, a 1621 feast at Plymouth, rests on a single eyewitness letter that never uses the word. The national holiday itself came later and more bureaucratically: presidential proclamations, a magazine editor's years-long campaign, a Civil War, and a 1941 argument over the Christmas shopping calendar.
body:
### History

The Plymouth gathering is real, and thinly documented. Edward Winslow, a colonist, described it in a letter of 1621: after the harvest the governor sent four men fowling, and Massasoit, the Wampanoag leader, arrived with about ninety men. The colonists "entertained and feasted" them for three days, and the visitors killed five deer. Pilgrim Hall Museum counts 53 surviving Mayflower colonists, so the Wampanoag guests outnumbered their hosts roughly two to one. Winslow lists no menu beyond fowl and deer, and he does not call the event a thanksgiving. That label arrived in 1841, when the editor Alexander Young annotated the letter: "This was the first Thanksgiving."

Public days of thanks were a separate, older habit. On September 28, 1789, the first Congress asked the president to recommend a national day of thanksgiving, and George Washington proclaimed Thursday, November 26. His successors issued proclamations too, with dates and even months that varied.

The fixed date traces to Sarah Josepha Hale, editor of Godey's Lady's Book, who campaigned for years for an annual national festival. In September 1863 she wrote to Abraham Lincoln hoping for "the permanency and unity of our Great American Festival of Thanksgiving." On October 3, 1863, a few months after Gettysburg, Lincoln asked Americans to "set apart and observe the last Thursday of November next as a day of thanksgiving and praise" — that year, also November 26. It was observed yearly on the last Thursday from then on.

In 1939 the last Thursday fell on November 30. Worried that a shorter Christmas shopping season would hurt the economic recovery, Franklin Roosevelt moved Thanksgiving to the second-to-last Thursday. Thirty-two states followed; sixteen kept the old date, and for two years the country observed two. Congress settled it in 1941: the House chose the last Thursday, the Senate changed it to the fourth so the holiday would land in the same week even in Novembers with five Thursdays, and Roosevelt signed on December 26.

The day also has a counter-observance. In 1970, Wamsutta Frank James, an Aquinnah Wampanoag man, was invited to speak at a state banquet marking the 350th anniversary of the Pilgrims' landing, then told he could not deliver his remarks. Native people and their supporters gathered in Plymouth instead and declared a National Day of Mourning, which the United American Indians of New England has held annually since.

### How to observe

Read Winslow's letter. The surviving eyewitness passage is a few sentences long, and Plimoth Patuxet Museums publishes it online. Set against the pageant version, it shows which parts of the story are documented.

Read the proclamations. The Library of Congress's Today in History entry for November 26 quotes both Lincoln's of 1863 and Washington's of 1789.

Hear the other account. The United American Indians of New England holds its National Day of Mourning observance at noon in Plymouth every Thanksgiving, with speeches and a march that ends near Plymouth Rock.

Watch the Lions. Detroit's Thanksgiving football game dates to 1934, when owner George A. Richards scheduled the reigning champion Bears to win newspaper space from the city's baseball team. The Bears won, 19–16.
timeline:
- 1621 — Colonists and about ninety Wampanoag men feast at Plymouth for three days; Winslow describes it in a letter.
- 1789 — Washington proclaims Thursday, November 26 a day of national thanksgiving, after a September 28 resolution of Congress.
- 1841 — Alexander Young annotates Winslow's letter "This was the first Thanksgiving," attaching the name to the 1621 feast.
- 1863 — Sarah Josepha Hale writes to Lincoln in September; on October 3 he proclaims the last Thursday of November a day of thanksgiving.
- 1939–1941 — Roosevelt moves the date a week earlier and the states split; Congress fixes the fourth Thursday, and he signs it on December 26, 1941.
- 1970 — Wamsutta Frank James is barred from delivering his speech at Plymouth; the National Day of Mourning begins.
faq:
When is Thanksgiving?
The fourth Thursday of November — November 26 in 2026. It is the fourth Thursday, not the last: in a November with five Thursdays, such as 2028, it falls on the 23rd rather than the 30th.

Is Thanksgiving a federal holiday?
Yes. Federal law (5 U.S.C. 6103) establishes it as a public holiday for federal employees.

Was the 1621 feast the first Thanksgiving?
It was a documented harvest gathering, but the only eyewitness account does not use the word. The name was added in 1841, and no complete menu survives.

Did Lincoln invent Thanksgiving?
No. Washington proclaimed a national day of thanks in 1789. Lincoln's 1863 proclamation set the last Thursday of November as the yearly date.

Where does the presidential turkey pardon come from?
The origin is contested. An 1865 dispatch describes Lincoln's son Tad pleading for a turkey bought for Christmas dinner. Turkeys were sent to presidents from the 1870s, Kennedy spared one in 1963, and the formal annual pardon dates to George H.W. Bush in 1989.

name: The Start of Daylight Saving Time
description: Daylight Saving Time begins on the second Sunday in March, when clocks across most of the United States jump from 2:00 a.m. standard time to 3:00 a.m. daylight time and the evenings gain an hour of light. The schedule is set by federal law, the Uniform Time Act of 1966 as amended, and it has started in March only since 2007. Hawaii and most of Arizona do not take part.
body:
### History

Clock-shifting in the United States began with the Standard Time Act, signed March 19, 1918, under the title "An Act to Save daylight and to provide standard time for the United States." It moved clocks forward on the last Sunday in March, at two o'clock in the morning. The idea was contentious, and Congress repealed the daylight saving provision in August 1919 over President Wilson's veto, keeping only the time zones the same act had created.

National daylight time came back for the Second World War, running without a break from February 1942 to September 1945, and then became a local matter for 21 years. The Uniform Time Act of 1966 fixed a single national schedule, starting on the last Sunday in April, and gave any state the right to opt out.

The start date has moved twice since, and both times the stated reason was energy. The Emergency Daylight Saving Time Energy Conservation Act of 1973 put the country on year-round daylight time in response to severe fuel shortages; daylight time began on January 6 in 1974 and on February 23 in 1975 before the April schedule returned. A 1986 law moved the start to the first Sunday in April from 1987 onward, and the Energy Policy Act of 2005 moved it to the second Sunday in March beginning in 2007. The statutes state energy conservation as the purpose; neither the Naval Observatory's account nor the Library of Congress's cites a study measuring the result.

### How to observe

The clocks that matter are the ones that will not change themselves: ovens, microwaves, cars, wall clocks, and anything running on its own battery. Phones and computers handle it without being asked.

The stranger thing to notice is the hour that does not exist. Clocks go from 2:00 a.m. standard time straight to 3:00 a.m. daylight time, so there is no 2:30 a.m. in most of the United States that morning. Anything scheduled inside that window has no time to run, and systems that store local time rather than universal time are where the problems surface.

It is also the morning to look at sunrise rather than sunset. The evening gets an hour of light, but sunrise moves an hour later overnight as well, which for anyone who walks, runs or waits for a bus before work is the half of the change that is actually felt. If you want to know what you are in for, look up your own sunrise times for the Saturday and the Monday either side of it.
timeline:
- 1918 — The Standard Time Act, signed March 19, creates U.S. time zones and the first national daylight saving time, beginning on the last Sunday in March.
- 1919 — Congress repeals the daylight saving provision on August 20, over President Wilson's veto.
- 1942 — National daylight time resumes for the war on February 9 and runs unbroken until September 30, 1945.
- 1966 — The Uniform Time Act sets a uniform national start on the last Sunday in April and lets any state exempt itself.
- 1974 — Under the Emergency Daylight Saving Time Energy Conservation Act of 1973, passed amid severe energy shortages, daylight time begins on January 6.
- 2007 — The Energy Policy Act of 2005 takes effect, moving the start to the second Sunday in March, where it remains.
faq:
When does Daylight Saving Time start in 2027?
Sunday, March 14, 2027. Clocks move forward one hour at 2:00 a.m. standard time, which becomes 3:00 a.m. daylight time.

Why is there no 2:30 a.m. that morning?
Because the clock jumps from 2:00 a.m. straight to 3:00 a.m. The hour in between is skipped, so no local time inside it occurs at all.

Did Daylight Saving Time always start in March?
No, and it is a recent arrangement. Under the Uniform Time Act of 1966 it began on the last Sunday in April. A 1986 law moved the start to the first Sunday in April from 1987, and the Energy Policy Act of 2005 moved it to the second Sunday in March beginning in 2007.

Which states do not change their clocks?
Hawaii and most of Arizona observe standard time all year. The Uniform Time Act of 1966 is what allows a state to exempt itself, and a state split across two time zones may exempt either the whole state or the part lying in one zone.

Will the clock changes ever stop?
Bills to make daylight saving time permanent have been introduced repeatedly and none has become law. The Sunshine Protection Act of 2021 passed the Senate by unanimous consent on March 15, 2022, then sat at the desk in the House with no vote. In the current Congress the House passed H.R. 139 by 308 to 117 on July 14, 2026 and the Senate referred it to the Commerce Committee the next day; its official record as of September 8, 2026 shows no Senate action since.

Rejected as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate, and content-farm or AI-generated listicles. Congress.gov refuses automated retrieval, so the bill histories here come from the Government Publishing Office's own Bill Status XML instead.

name: The Start of Hanukkah
description: Hanukkah is an eight-night festival that begins on 25 Kislev and marks the rededication of the Second Temple in Jerusalem after the Maccabean revolt. A day in the Hebrew calendar begins at sundown, so the first candle is lit on the evening the festival opens — the date listed here — while 25 Kislev itself is the Gregorian day that follows. It was for most of its history a minor holiday; its prominence in American life is a nineteenth- and twentieth-century development, and its nearness to December 25 has a good deal to do with that.
body:
### History

The name means dedication, and the event behind it is dated with unusual precision in its earliest source. 1 Maccabees puts the rededication of the altar on the twenty-fifth of Kislev "in the year one hundred and forty-eight" of the Seleucid era, and records that "for eight days they celebrated the dedication of the altar." Converting that Seleucid year is where sources part company: most scholarship gives 164 BCE, including Britannica and the Posen Library's guide to the period, while two Smithsonian object records give 165 BCE. This page follows 164 and reports the disagreement rather than splitting it.

Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Hellenistic Syrian king, invaded Judaea and desecrated the Second Temple by dedicating it to Zeus; the revolt against him was led by the priest Mattathias and his son Judas Maccabeus, whose family founded the Hasmonean dynasty. The Posen Library dates the raid on the Temple to 169 BCE and the cult of Zeus Olympios there to 167 BCE, while noting that "the differences among our sources make it difficult to determine exactly what happened."

Now the part most retellings leave out. The oil — one day's worth burning for eight — is not in 1 Maccabees, not in 2 Maccabees, and not in Josephus, who calls the festival the Festival of Lights and explains the name not by a miracle but by a liberty "beyond our wildest hopes." The cruse of oil first appears in the Babylonian Talmud at Shabbat 21b, compiled roughly six centuries later; Britannica calls it "a new twist" supplied by the rabbinic authorities, and the Jewish Theological Seminary separates the two strands explicitly. 2 Maccabees gives its own reason for the eight days: the people "celebrated joyfully for eight days as on the feast of Booths," having spent Sukkot that year hiding in caves.

Its American scale is recent. The Library of Congress notes that "it was only in the later 19th century that it became a widely observed Jewish holiday," and Britannica, calling it "originally a minor holiday," attributes its more lavish modern celebration to its proximity to December 25.

### How to observe

The lamp is the observance. A hanukkiah carries nine branches: eight for the nights, plus a holder set higher for the shammash, the "servant" candle, which exists because the Hanukkah lights themselves may not be used to kindle anything else. One candle the first night and one more each night after is Beit Hillel's position, which prevailed over Beit Shammai's, who began with eight and counted down. Shabbat 21b, which records both, also directs that the lamp be set at the entrance to the house on the outside, or at a window facing the street if you live upstairs — the window is what modern practice settled on.

Fried food follows the oil: latkes and sufganiyot. The potato latke is a latecomer. Smithsonian Folklife records cheese latkes in central and southern Europe and buckwheat or rye flour in eastern Europe, the potato not entering the eastern European Jewish diet until the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

The dreidel comes with a better story than the one most of us were told. Its four letters are traditionally read as an acronym for nes gadol haya sham, "a great miracle happened there." A Library of Congress folklorist traces the top itself to the European teetotum, borrowed probably in eighteenth-century German-speaking Europe, whose sides carried gambling abbreviations for all, half, nothing and put. On that account the Hebrew acronym is "just a later rationalization," and the familiar tale that dreidels disguised Torah study from the Greeks is "entirely ahistorical."

For something to attend, the National Menorah is lit each December on the Ellipse in Washington under a National Park Service permit held by American Friends of Lubavitch. For something to read, the Library of Congress's Chronicling America holds digitized American Jewish newspapers, and The Jewish Cookery Book of 1871, believed to be the earliest Jewish cookbook issued in America, is online in full.
timeline:
- 167 BCE — Antiochus IV Epiphanes introduces the cult of Zeus Olympios on the site of the Jerusalem Temple, two years after raiding it.
- 164 BCE — Judas Maccabeus and his followers rededicate the Temple on 25 Kislev; 1 Maccabees dates it to the year 148 of the Seleucid era and records an eight-day celebration. Some sources, including two Smithsonian records, give 165 BCE.
- c. 450–550 CE — The Babylonian Talmud is compiled. At Shabbat 21b it supplies the story of the single cruse of oil that burned for eight days, which appears in none of the earlier accounts.
- 1979 — The first National Menorah is lit in Lafayette Park in Washington, with President Carter taking part; it moves to the Ellipse, its present location, some years later.
- October 22, 1996 — The Postal Service issues the first United States Hanukkah stamp, a 32-cent joint issue with the Israeli Postal Authority and the first in its Holiday Celebrations series.
- December 10, 2001 — The first Hanukkah lamp is lit in the White House residence, a hundred-year-old menorah borrowed from the Jewish Museum in New York.
faq:
When does Hanukkah start?
On 25 Kislev, which moves against the Gregorian calendar and may fall any time from late November to late December. Because a day in the Hebrew calendar begins at sundown, the first candle is lit on the evening the festival opens, which is the date in the table on this page; 25 Kislev itself, the first full day, is the following Gregorian date. For 2026, Hebcal puts the start at sundown on Friday, December 4, with 25 Kislev 5787 falling on Saturday, December 5.

Why does Hanukkah last eight days?
Three answers, depending on the source. 1 Maccabees says the rededication was celebrated for eight days and the anniversary prescribed for eight. 2 Maccabees says the people kept eight days "as on the feast of Booths," having missed Sukkot while in hiding. The Talmud, centuries later, says one day's oil burned for eight. The first two are the earlier texts.

Is the miracle of the oil in the Book of Maccabees?
No. Neither 1 Maccabees 4 nor 2 Maccabees 10 mentions oil lasting eight days, and neither does Josephus, who describes the priests lighting the lamps and explains the festival's name by the unexpected recovery of liberty. The miracle first appears in the Babylonian Talmud at Shabbat 21b, roughly six centuries later.

Is Hanukkah a federal holiday in the United States?
No. Federal offices, banks and post offices operate normally. Federal involvement is ceremonial: the Postal Service has issued nine Hanukkah stamps since 1996, a Hanukkah lamp has been lit in the White House residence since 2001, and the National Park Service permits the National Menorah on the Ellipse each December.

Is Hanukkah the Jewish Christmas?
No, though the influence runs in that direction. The Library of Congress dates its emergence as a widely observed holiday to the later nineteenth century, and Britannica attributes its more lavish modern celebration to its nearness to December 25, naming gift-giving and home decoration as customs adopted from Christmas traditions.
