- Rowan University, American Jews Have Transformed Hanukkah, Rowan Author Says — https://today.rowan.edu/news/2013/11/american-jews-have-transformed-hanukkah-rowan-author-says.html → Dianne Ashton, Religion Studies professor at Rowan, author of Hanukkah in America: A History (NYU Press), and her thesis that the American transformation is an evolution two hundred years in the making.
- Library of Congress, Quick to the Party: Southern Jews and the Americanization of Hanukkah — https://www.loc.gov/item/2021687899/ → Dianne Ashton's 2007 lecture to the Southern Jewish Historical Society, hosted by the Library's Hebraic Section, part of a larger work on the history of Hanukkah observance in the United States.
- Pew Research Center, The Size of the U.S. Jewish Population, Jewish Americans in 2020 — https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2021/05/11/the-size-of-the-u-s-jewish-population/ → approximately 5.8 million Jewish adults, 2.4 percent of U.S. adults, and a total estimate of 7.5 million Jews of all ages.
- The Jewish Museum, New York, Accumulations: Hanukkah Lamps — https://thejewishmuseum.org/press/press-release/accumulations-hanukkah-lamps-release → the museum's Hanukkah lamp collection described as the largest in the world at nearly 1,050 pieces.

Source conflict reported rather than averaged: the year of the rededication. The primary datum is 1 Maccabees' Seleucid-era "year one hundred and forty-eight," not a BCE year at all. Of the derived dates, 164 BCE is given by Britannica in three separate articles, by Carol Bakhos's Posen Library guide published by Yale University Press, and by the New American Bible's footnote to John 10:22; 165 BCE is given by the Posen Library's own editorial gloss on the Josephus passage and by two Smithsonian object records. This page prints 164 BCE, names the disagreement, and does not assert a reason for it, because no source consulted explains the split.

Second conflict: the dreidel. Britannica and the Postal Service present the nes gadol haya sham acronym as the meaning of the four letters; the Library of Congress's folklife blog traces the letters to German gambling abbreviations and calls the acronym a later rationalization, with the Torah-study story "entirely ahistorical." The Library of Congress article is the more specific and more rigorous on origins and is preferred on that point; the acronym is still given as the traditional reading, because that is what it is.

Third conflict: where the first National Menorah was lit in 1979. The White House Historical Association and NPR say Lafayette Park; an Obama-era White House blog post says the Ellipse. Smithsonian Magazine's account of a later move to the Ellipse reconciles them in favor of Lafayette Park, and this page says Lafayette Park in 1979 rather than claiming the Ellipse since 1979.

Fourth conflict: the first White House menorah lighting. NPR calls President Clinton in 1993 the first to light a menorah in the people's house; the Bush White House archive says 2001 was the first year a menorah was lit in the White House residence. These are reconcilable, since the Oval Office is in the West Wing rather than the Executive Residence, and the page uses the residence formulation.

Omitted for want of an acceptable source: any figure for the share of American Jews who light Hanukkah candles. Pew has never asked the question — the word does not appear in the topline of either its 2013 or its 2020 survey of Jewish Americans — so any such statistic in circulation is unsourced, and none is printed here. Also omitted: the origin or history of Hanukkah gelt; any claim that work is permitted on Hanukkah, which no consulted source states; the ISBN and page count of Hanukkah in America, whose publisher page could not be read; the name of whoever lights the National Menorah in a given year; and any standalone congressional resolution recognizing Hanukkah itself, since only H.Res. 615 of 2005 could be verified and it addresses Hanukkah, Ramadan and Kwanzaa together on First Amendment grounds.

Less than fully confident, flagged deliberately: "the later nineteenth century" for Hanukkah's emergence as a widely observed holiday rests on a single Library of Congress blog sentence, and Britannica's "originally a minor holiday" is the only citable support for the minor-holiday framing. Both are reputable but neither is a dedicated scholarly treatment, and the page does not build anything further on them.

One source is used outside the site's usual allow-list and is named here deliberately: the White House Historical Association, for the sequence of White House menorahs and the 1993 Oval Office lighting. It is an author-attributed, footnoted institutional history, and every claim drawn from it that matters is corroborated by the George W. Bush White House archive or the Obama White House archive.

Not used as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate, Wikipedia, and comparable aggregator and content-farm pages.

name: The Start of Ramadan
description: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar and the month in which observant Muslims fast from dawn to sunset, one of the five Pillars of Islam. Its first day is not a fixed date but a determination, made fresh each year from a crescent moon that different authorities read in different ways — which is why mosques in the same American city sometimes begin on different days. Because the lunar year runs about eleven days shorter than the solar one, it moves backward through the seasons, returning to where it started roughly every thirty-three years.
body:
### History

The fast is prescribed in the Quran. Surah al-Baqarah 2:183 establishes fasting for believers as it was for communities before them; 2:184 provides that those who are ill or traveling make the days up later, while those who cannot fast may feed a needy person for each day missed; 2:185 names Ramadan as the month in which the Quran was revealed and says that God intends ease, not hardship. Tradition dates that first revelation to Laylat al-Qadr, around 610 CE, the night the last ten nights of the month commemorate. The daily boundary comes from 2:187: eat and drink until the first light of dawn can be told from the darkness, then complete the fast until night. Dawn, not sunrise — usually an hour or more earlier, a distinction some reference works get wrong.

The movement through the seasons is a function of the calendar. The Hijri year is twelve lunar months of 29 or 30 days, totaling 354 or 355, counted from the Hijrah of 622 CE. Because that year is roughly eleven days shorter than the solar one, the named months retrogress through the seasonal year about every 32.5 years.

The disagreement over when Ramadan begins is a question of religious law, not of science against superstition, and it is the thing most often described badly. Tradition starts the month on a naked-eye sighting of the crescent, the most conservative position requiring two credible witnesses. In 2006 the Fiqh Council of North America announced it would set dates by astronomical calculation instead, and the Islamic Society of North America adopted calculation the same year. Its criterion, taken from the European Council for Fatwa and Research, is that if anywhere on earth at sunset the moon's elongation is at least 8 degrees and its altitude at least 5 degrees, the new month begins the next day. Other mosques and the Central Hilal Committee of North America still prefer sighting, and the Fiqh Council accepts other opinions and encourages Muslims to follow their local masjid. As Imam Dawud Walid has put it, unity does not equal uniformity.

### How to observe

Two meals bracket the fasting day: suhur before dawn and iftar after sunset. Iftar follows the sunset prayer, is usually eaten with family or at a mosque, and traditionally begins with dates, after the Prophet's custom. Nights bring taraweeh, lengthy congregational prayers. Charity is a hallmark of the month — iftar for the needy, boxes of pantry staples, free communal meals — and zakat al-fitr is an obligatory payment at its end. Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, falls somewhere in the last ten nights, marked on the 27th by Sunnis and the 23rd by Shia. Eid al-Fitr ends the month.

If you work alongside someone who is fasting, the useful thing to know is the law: Title VII requires employers to reasonably accommodate a sincerely held religious practice absent undue hardship, and the EEOC states plainly that coworker objections rooted in hostility to religion, or customer prejudice, do not count as undue hardship.
timeline:
- 622 CE — The Hijrah, Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina, becomes the epoch of the Hijri calendar; year 1 begins on 1 Muharram, 16 July 622 in the Julian calendar. The caliph Umar I institutes the era in 639.
- 2006 — The Fiqh Council of North America announces it will set Islamic dates by astronomical calculation rather than moon sighting, and the Islamic Society of North America adopts calculation the same year.
- February 18, 2026 — 1 Ramadan 1447: the Fiqh Council's calculated date and Saudi Arabia's moon-sighting committee land on the same day.
- January 5 and December 26, 2030 — Ramadan begins twice in one Gregorian year, the clearest demonstration of the drift.
faq:
When does Ramadan begin?
Not something settled far ahead. The Fiqh Council of North America publishes a calculated date each year, while national committees and many individual mosques wait for a sighting. Any Ramadan date printed years out, including the one in the table on this page, is a projection rather than an announcement.

Why does the date move?
Twelve lunar months come to 354 or 355 days, about eleven short of the solar year, so Ramadan arrives ten to twelve days earlier each Gregorian year and works through every season in roughly 33 years. It falls twice in 2030.

Is it really no food or water all day?
Both, from dawn to sunset, along with marital relations during fasting hours. But Muslims eat every day of Ramadan, before dawn and after sunset; the common line that they go a month without eating is simply wrong.

Who is exempt from fasting?
Children, the ill, travelers, pregnant and nursing women, the elderly, and people with disabilities or mental health conditions. These are provisions of the religion rather than loopholes: the Quran allows the days to be made up later, or a poor person fed for each one missed.

(Verse numbers cited; the English wording is not quoted here because the page does not name its translator.)

- Encyclopaedia Britannica, iftar — https://www.britannica.com/topic/iftar → iftar eaten at sundown after the sunset prayer, often as a family or mosque gathering, and typically started with dates following the custom of the Prophet.
- Encyclopaedia Britannica, tarawih — https://www.britannica.com/topic/tarawih → taraweeh as lengthy prayers offered congregationally during Ramadan.
- Encyclopaedia Britannica, Laylat al-Qadr — https://www.britannica.com/topic/Laylat-al-Qadr → the Night of Power falling in the last ten nights, commonly marked on the 23rd by Shia and the 27th by Sunni Muslims; the first revelation through the angel Gabriel dated to around 610 CE.

- Fiqh Council of North America, Amount of Fidyah and Zakat al-Fitr — https://fiqhcouncil.org/fidyah-and-zakat-al-fitr/ → qada for a fast missed for a temporary reason such as illness or travel, against fidyah where the fast can never be made up; zakat al-fitr as an obligatory payment at the end of Ramadan; the fidyah grounded in Quran 2:184.
- Spokesman-Review, Setting the holiday (August 26, 2006) — https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2006/aug/26/setting-the-holiday/ → the Fiqh Council of North America announcing in 2006 that it would use astronomical calculation rather than moon sighting; the traditional requirement of two credible witnesses; scholars disagreeing over local sightings against Saudi sightings.
- Religion News Service, Reconciling the divide in Muslim life over when the moon appears (June 14, 2024) — https://religionnews.com/2024/06/14/reconciling-the-divide-in-muslim-life-over-when-the-moon-appears/ → the Islamic Society of North America deciding in 2006 to use astronomical calculations; moon sighting still preferred by other mosques and scholars; the Central Hilal Committee of North America's appeal for sighting; Imam Dawud Walid's "Unity does not equal uniformity."
- Associated Press (Mariam Fam), What is Ramadan and how do Muslims observe the Islamic holy month? (March 10, 2024), via PBS NewsHour — https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/what-is-ramadan-and-how-do-muslims-observe-the-islamic-holy-month → Islamic authorities declaring sightings differently or using different methods, so communities begin on different days; no sip of water during fasting hours; exemption for illness and travel with days made up later; charity as a hallmark of the month, including iftar for the needy and pantry boxes.
- Council on American-Islamic Relations, An Employer's Guide to Islamic Religious Practices — https://www.cair.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/An-Employer's-Guide-to-Islamic-Religious-Practices.pdf → Ramadan as the ninth lunar month; refraining from eating, drinking and smoking from break of dawn to sunset; travelers exempt; fasting employees eating after sundown or before dawn.
- Council on American-Islamic Relations, Ramadan Toolkit 2026 — https://www.cair.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/RamadanToolkit2026.pdf → the fast as abstaining from food, drink and marital relations from dawn (fajr) until sunset (maghrib), citing Quran 2:183.
- U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, Religious Accommodation Fact Sheet (October 31, 2024) — https://www.eeoc.gov/sites/default/files/2024-11/20241031_ReligiousAccommodationFactSheet_A.pdf → Title VII's requirement to reasonably accommodate sincerely held religious practice; coworker objections based on hostility to religion and customer prejudice not constituting undue hardship; schedule changes and workspace for prayer among the listed accommodations.
- Al Jazeera, Ramadan 2026: Fasting hours, suhoor and iftar times around the world (February 15, 2026) — https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/2/15/ramadan-2026-fasting-hours-suhoor-and-iftar-times-around-the-world → Ramadan starting 10 to 12 days earlier each Gregorian year with the lunar calendar about 11 days shorter; months of 29 or 30 days; Saudi Arabia's committee sighting the crescent on February 17 and announcing fasting from February 18, 2026; Ramadan beginning twice in 2030, on January 5 and December 26.

name: U.S. General Election Day
description: U.S. General Election Day falls on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November, which pins it somewhere between November 2 and November 8. It is the day Americans elect members of Congress and, every fourth year, the presidential electors who formally choose the president. Three separate federal statutes, passed seventy years apart, are what put all of that on the same Tuesday.
body:
### History

For the republic's first half-century there was no national election day. The Act of March 1, 1792 directed that presidential electors be appointed "within thirty-four days preceding the first Wednesday in December," so voting could sprawl across more than a month, and states ran their congressional elections on dates of their own choosing. By the early 1800s more than half the states had drifted toward voting in early November anyway.

The Act of January 23, 1845 fixed a single day. One sentence long, it provided that electors "shall be appointed in each State on the Tuesday next after the first Monday in the month of November of the year in which they are to be appointed." The motive stated on the House floor in 1844 was "to guard against frauds in the elections of President and Vice President": a thirty-four-day window let results from the early states travel to the late ones, and it prolonged the opportunity for mischief. Congress put House elections on the same Tuesday in 1872 — effective with the 1876 election, and tucked into an apportionment bill — and aligned the popular election of senators with it in 1914, after the Seventeenth Amendment took that choice away from state legislatures.

Why that particular Tuesday is less settled than it is usually told. The familiar reasons — that early November sat between the harvest and the winter, that Tuesday spared voters from traveling to distant polls on the Sabbath, and that the first Tuesday after a Monday can never fall on November 1, when merchants closed out their books — come from later scholarship rather than from the 1845 record. The often-repeated claim that Congress was avoiding All Saints' Day has no reputable source behind it at all.

### How to observe

Check your registration well before the day rather than on it. Deadlines vary by state, a handful of states allow registration at the polls, and vote.gov links through to each state's own system. Then look up a sample ballot. Down-ballot judicial retention questions and ballot measures are where most voters arrive unprepared, and the text is published in advance.

Consider working the election rather than only voting in it. States reported 772,433 poll workers for the 2024 general election, and more than half of them were 61 or older; the Election Assistance Commission's poll-worker page lists requirements, hours, pay, training and local sign-up. If you do only one thing, confirm your polling place and its hours — both change between elections more often than people expect.
timeline:
- 1788–1789 — The first federal elections run from November 24, 1788 to June 22, 1789; electors cast their ballots in February 1789 and Congress counts them in April.
- 1792 — Congress directs that presidential electors be appointed within the thirty-four days before the first Wednesday in December.
- 1845 — The Act of January 23 fixes the Tuesday after the first Monday in November as the day for appointing electors in every state.
- 1848 — November 7 is the first presidential election held on the same day nationwide.
- 1872 — House elections are moved to the same November Tuesday, effective with the 1876 election.
- 1914 — Congress aligns the popular election of senators with the biennial House elections.
faq:
When is Election Day?

It is the Tuesday after the first Monday in November, so it moves between November 2 and November 8. The next federal general election is November 3, 2026.

Is Election Day a federal holiday?

No. The eleven legal public holidays are listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103, and Election Day is not among them; federal offices keep normal hours. Federal employees may be granted excused absence to vote, but only in limited circumstances. A few states, including Virginia and Delaware, do make it a state legal holiday, and many more give employees statutory time off to vote — which is a different thing from a holiday.

Why is Election Day on a Tuesday in November?

Congress set the uniform date in 1845 to curb the fraud that staggered state voting made easy. The familiar harvest-and-Sabbath explanations are reconstructions by later historians rather than reasons Congress recorded at the time.

How many Americans actually vote?

For the 2024 general election, states reported 158,211,780 ballots cast and counted — 64.7 percent of the citizen voting-age population, by the Election Assistance Commission's tally of certified results. The Census Bureau's survey-based estimate for the same election is higher, at 65.3 percent, and the Bureau notes that surveys tend to report higher voting rates than official results do.

Can Election Day be moved?

Not administratively. The date is set by statute, so changing it would take a new act of Congress; no president or federal official has the power to move it.

name: Valentine's Day
description: Valentine's Day falls on February 14 and is, in the United States, a largely commercial occasion with a genuinely obscure past. The Library of Congress calls its origins "murky," and the honest version of the history is a series of plausible connections — a Roman fertility festival, one or more martyrs named Valentine, a Chaucer poem about birds choosing mates — rather than a line of descent anyone can trace end to end.
body:
### History

There were several early Christian martyrs named Valentine, and February 14 is the saint day associated with them; which one the day commemorates is not settled. The first known printed mention of Saint Valentine is believed to be in the Nuremberg Chronicle of 1493, and it says nothing about any role as a patron saint of lovers.

The Roman connection is the one repeated most often and established least firmly. Romans held the feast of Lupercalia, a mid-February spring festival with fertility rites, on February 15. Pope Gelasius I banned Lupercalia in the late fifth century and is sometimes credited with replacing it with St. Valentine's Day — but that is an attribution rather than a documented act, and Britannica presents it as uncertain.

Romance attaches to the date in the fourteenth century, and the earliest link anyone can point to is literary. Geoffrey Chaucer, who died in 1400, wrote in Parliament of Fowls of birds gathering in early spring on "seynt valentynes day" to choose their mates, which tracks a medieval belief that birds paired off on February 14. The oldest surviving valentine letter in English is later and more human: in February 1477 Margery Brews wrote to John Paston and signed herself "your Valentine, Margery Brews."

Handmade valentines appear in the sixteenth century, probably the first greeting cards of any kind, and mass production begins as early as 1800. The American industry has a name and an address. Esther Howland was born in Worcester, Massachusetts in 1828, graduated from Mount Holyoke Female Seminary in 1847, and received her first English valentine that same year. Working from a third-floor room of the family house on Summer Street, she had the business fully launched by the end of 1849. Her brother Allen took samples out expecting perhaps $200 in orders and came back with $5,000 worth. Her first advertisement ran in the Worcester Daily Spy in February 1850, with simple cards at five cents and elaborate ones reaching a dollar. Sales eventually grew to $100,000 a year. She incorporated as the New England Valentine Company in the early 1870s, moved into a Main Street factory in 1879, and sold the business in 1880 to care for her ailing father. A newspaper later called her the Mother of the American Valentine.

### How to observe

Read the Paston letter. Margery Brews's February 1477 note to John Paston survives in the British Library's Paston collection and is the earliest known valentine in English. It is also partly a negotiation about her dowry, which makes it a better document than a sentimental one.

Look at Esther Howland's actual cards. The American Antiquarian Society in Worcester holds her valentines alongside the Victorian cards around them, and the layered paper-lace construction explains at a glance why a hand-assembled card could cost a dollar in 1850.

Treat the spending figures as what they are. The National Retail Federation has surveyed Valentine's Day intentions annually since 2004 and put expected 2026 spending at a record $29.1 billion. That is a retail trade association's survey of what consumers say they plan to spend, not a government measurement of what they spent — worth citing, worth labeling.
timeline:
- 1493 — The Nuremberg Chronicle carries what is believed to be the first printed mention of Saint Valentine, with no reference to lovers.
- Late 5th century — Pope Gelasius I bans Lupercalia; the claim that he replaced it with St. Valentine's Day is a later and uncertain attribution.
- Before 1400 — Chaucer's Parliament of Fowls ties "seynt valentynes day" to birds choosing their mates.
- February 1477 — Margery Brews writes to John Paston signing "your Valentine" — the earliest surviving valentine letter in English.
- 1850 — Esther Howland's first advertisement runs in the Worcester Daily Spy; her cards sell from five cents to a dollar.
- 1880 — Howland sells the New England Valentine Company to care for her ailing father.
faq:
Who was St. Valentine?
Not one identifiable person. February 14 is the saint day associated with several early Christian martyrs named Valentine, and the record does not say which of them the day commemorates. The earliest known printed mention of him, in the 1493 Nuremberg Chronicle, says nothing about lovers.

Did Valentine's Day come from the Roman festival Lupercalia?
Possibly, but it is not documented. Lupercalia fell on February 15, and Pope Gelasius I banned it in the late fifth century; he is sometimes credited with replacing it with St. Valentine's Day. Britannica treats that as an attribution rather than a fact, and the Library of Congress calls the holiday's origins murky.

When did February 14 become about romance?
In the fourteenth century. The earliest surviving link is Chaucer's Parliament of Fowls, in which birds choose their mates on "seynt valentynes day" — reflecting a medieval belief that birds paired off on that date.

Who made the first American valentines?
Esther Howland of Worcester, Massachusetts built the first American valentine business, launched by the end of 1849 and advertising from February 1850. Handmade valentines in Europe date to the sixteenth century and mass production began as early as 1800, so she was not first in the world — she was first at scale in the United States.

Is Valentine's Day a federal holiday?
No. It has no official status and nothing closes for it. In 2027 it falls on a Sunday.

name: Veterans Day
description: Veterans Day falls on November 11 and honors everyone who served honorably in the United States armed forces, in wartime or peacetime, living or dead. The date is not symbolic: it is the hour the guns stopped in the First World War, 11 a.m. on November 11, 1918. For its first 36 years the holiday was called Armistice Day, and for seven years in the 1970s it was not observed on November 11 at all.
body:
### History

The armistice between the Allies and Germany took effect at the eleventh hour of November 11, 1918, signed at Compiegne in France. It was a ceasefire, not a peace — the Treaty of Versailles came the following year — but it is the moment the fighting ended, and it is why this holiday has an hour as well as a date.

President Wilson proclaimed the first Armistice Day in November 1919, speaking of "solemn pride in the heroism of those who died in the country's service." The original form of the observance was two minutes of suspended business beginning at 11 a.m., followed by parades and public meetings. On October 20, 1921, Congress declared November 11 of that year a legal federal holiday; that was the day the Unknown Soldier was buried at Arlington. In 1926 Congress directed the President to issue an Armistice Day proclamation every year, and on May 13, 1938, it made November 11 a permanent legal federal holiday.

All of that was about one war. The change came from a veteran of the next one. In 1947 Raymond Weeks, a World War II veteran, organized a National Veterans Day observance in Birmingham, Alabama, on November 11 — the date was still officially Armistice Day — and pressed for a holiday that covered everyone who had served. Representative Edward Rees of Kansas carried the bill, and President Eisenhower signed it on June 1, 1954. President Reagan presented Weeks with the Presidential Citizens Medal in November 1982.

Congress then moved the holiday and had to move it back. The Monday Holiday Law of 1968 set the federal observance on the fourth Monday in October, effective 1971. It did not hold: states returned to November 11 through the early 1970s, most of them by 1975, and legislation that year restored the federal date to November 11, effective 1978.

### How to observe

Keep the two minutes. The first Armistice Day was built around a two-minute pause at 11 a.m., and it remains the most exact way to mark a holiday that commemorates an hour rather than a day.

Record a veteran. The Library of Congress runs the Veterans History Project, which collects first-hand accounts from American war veterans and accepts interviews submitted by the public; it publishes a field kit with the forms, the release and interview guidance. An afternoon with a relative and a recorder puts their account into the national collection permanently.

Get the courtesies right. This day honors all who served; the day for those who died in service is Memorial Day, and the poppy — from John McCrae's 1915 poem "In Flanders Fields" — is traditionally worn then rather than now. There is also no apostrophe in Veterans Day: the Department of Veterans Affairs is explicit that the day does not belong to veterans, it honors them.
timeline:
- November 11, 1918 — An armistice between the Allies and Germany takes effect at the eleventh hour, signed at Compiegne, France, ending the fighting of the First World War.
- November 1919 — President Wilson proclaims the first Armistice Day, marked by a two-minute suspension of business beginning at 11 a.m.
- October 20, 1921 — Congress declares November 11, 1921 a legal federal holiday; the Unknown Soldier is buried at Arlington that day.
- May 13, 1938 — Congress makes November 11 a permanent legal federal holiday, Armistice Day.
- June 1, 1954 — President Eisenhower signs the bill carried by Rep. Edward Rees of Kansas, renaming the holiday Veterans Day.
- 1968–1978 — The Monday Holiday Law moves the federal observance to the fourth Monday in October from 1971; 1975 legislation returns it to November 11, effective 1978.
faq:
Is Veterans Day a federal holiday?
Yes. It is one of the eleven legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103, and it is observed on November 11 whatever the weekday. When November 11 falls on a Saturday, most federal employees observe it the preceding Friday; when it falls on a Sunday, the following Monday.

What is the difference between Veterans Day and Memorial Day?
Memorial Day honors military personnel who died in service, particularly those killed in battle or from wounds sustained in battle. Veterans Day honors everyone who served honorably, in wartime or peacetime, and is largely a day for thanking living veterans.

Is there an apostrophe in Veterans Day?
No. The Department of Veterans Affairs is explicit about it: the day does not belong to veterans, so the s is not possessive.

Why November 11, and why 11 a.m.?
The armistice that ended the fighting of the First World War took effect at the eleventh hour of November 11, 1918. The first observances in 1919 were built around a two-minute pause at that hour.

Was Veterans Day ever held in October?
Yes, from 1971 through 1977. The Monday Holiday Law of 1968 moved the federal observance to the fourth Monday in October. States went back to November 11 anyway, most by 1975, and 1975 legislation returned the federal date to November 11 effective 1978.

name: Yom Kippur
description: Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, falls on the tenth day of Tishri, nine days after Rosh Hashanah, and begins at sunset the evening before the date a civil calendar shows. It is the most widely kept fast in Judaism and the one day of the year on which the high priest of the Jerusalem Temple was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies. What the Torah actually commands is not a fast: it says to practice self-denial, and the specifics are the rabbis' work.
body:
### History

The day is established in Leviticus 16 and 23:26-32 and in Numbers 29:7-11. The instruction in Leviticus 23:27 is that "the tenth day of this seventh month is the Day of Atonement. It shall be a sacred occasion for you: you shall practice self-denial." The sunset-to-sunset reckoning is in the text too, at 23:32: "on the ninth day of the month at evening, from evening to evening, you shall observe this your sabbath." The Hebrew Bible also calls the day Shabbat Shabbaton, a sabbath of solemn rest. The phrase "practice self-denial" is the Jewish Publication Society's rendering; what self-denial consists of is nowhere specified.

Leviticus 16 describes what the day looked like when there was a Temple. Aaron took two goats and cast lots over them, "one marked for GOD and the other marked for Azazel." The first was offered; the second was "left standing alive" and then, after Aaron laid both hands on its head and confessed over it "all the iniquities and transgressions of the Israelites," sent into the wilderness "through a designated agent" to "carry on it all their iniquities to an inaccessible region." Britannica, which calls that second goat the scapegoat, adds that the high priest was clothed in white linen and entered the Holy of Holies - permitted only on this day - to offer incense and sprinkle sacrificial blood.

After the Temple was destroyed in 70 CE there was no sacrifice to make, and the day was rebuilt around what remained. Britannica records a Midrashic exchange in which Joshua ben Hananiah mourns that atonement has become impossible and his teacher Johanan ben Zakkai answers him from Hosea 6:6: "For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice." Sacrifice gave way to repentance, judgment and good deeds, and rabbinic literature gave the day a second name, Yom ha-Din, the Day of Judgment.

The prohibitions were set down in the Mishnah, and they arrived with an argument attached. Mishnah Yoma 8:1 forbids "eating and in drinking, and in bathing, and in smearing oil on one's body, and in wearing shoes, and in conjugal relations" - six activities, which the modern count compresses to five by treating food and drink as one. It then records Rabbi Eliezer permitting a king and a bride within thirty days of her marriage to wash their faces, and a woman after childbirth to wear shoes "because going barefoot causes her pain," followed by the flat sentence: "The Rabbis prohibit these activities."

One element of sacrifice survived in practice rather than in law. Britannica describes kaparot, in which a chicken is waved overhead three times and then slaughtered and given to charity, and notes that the ritual "appears neither in the Torah nor the Talmud but has been in practice since at least the 9th century CE," and that it has drawn objections from rabbis and animal rights activists alike.

### How to observe

The fast runs from sunset on the ninth of Tishri until the stars come out the next evening. Britannica puts it at 25 hours; Chabad's article says "nearly 26 hours" while Chabad's own summary of the same article says 25, so take the figure as approximate and the sunset-to-nightfall span as the real rule. Britannica notes that children below the age of bar and bat mitzvah - thirteen for boys, twelve for girls - are not required to fast. Chabad directs anyone who must eat to consult both a medical professional and a rabbi.

The day is unusual for holding five prayer services: Maariv on the eve, with Kol Nidrei; Shacharit, with a reading from Leviticus and the Yizkor memorial prayers; Musaf, which recounts the Temple service; Minchah, which includes the Book of Jonah; and Neilah, the closing of the gates, after which a single shofar blast ends the fast.

Two things worth knowing in advance. Kol Nidre annuls vows only "insofar as they concern oneself" - obligations to other people are expressly excluded, which is the opposite of how it is usually assumed to work. And the forgiveness owed to other people is asked for before the day starts, not during it: Britannica's phrasing is that obtaining forgiveness from one's fellows signifies God's forgiveness. White is worn as a symbol of purity, sometimes as a long robe called a kittel, and gold is avoided because it evokes the golden calf.

If you want one short primary text, read Mishnah Yoma 8:1 on Sefaria. It takes a minute, and the dissent it preserves about the king, the bride and the new mother is a better guide to how the day has been argued over than any summary of it.
timeline:
- 70 CE - The Temple in Jerusalem is destroyed. With sacrifice no longer possible, Yom Kippur is rebuilt around repentance, judgment and good deeds, and acquires the name Yom ha-Din.
- 2nd century CE - The Mishnah is compiled. Mishnah Yoma 8:1 sets down the prohibited activities and preserves Rabbi Eliezer's exemptions for a king, a new bride and a woman after childbirth, together with the majority's refusal of them.
- By the 9th century CE - Kaparot is in practice, though it appears in neither the Torah nor the Talmud.
- 11th or 12th century CE - Unetaneh Tokef - "On Rosh Hashanah it is inscribed, and on Yom Kippur it is sealed" - is attributed to Rabbi Amnon of Mainz, and may be older.
- October 6-26, 1973 - Egypt and Syria attack Israeli forces in the Sinai Peninsula and the Golan Heights on Yom Kippur. The fighting runs to October 26 and the war takes the holiday's name.
- October 2, 2025 - New York City's public schools close for Yom Kippur; the next closure on the published calendars is September 21, 2026.
faq:
When is Yom Kippur?
On the tenth day of Tishri, which falls in September or October, beginning at sunset the evening before the date a civil calendar shows. In 2027 it runs from just before sunset on Sunday, October 10, to after nightfall on Monday, October 11.

How long is the fast?
From sunset on the ninth of Tishri until the stars appear the following evening. Britannica gives 25 hours. Chabad's article says nearly 26 while its own summary of that article says 25, so the hour figure is approximate; the sunset-to-nightfall span is the rule that matters.

What exactly is forbidden?
Five things, as both Britannica and Chabad present them: food and drink, bathing or washing, applying oils or creams, leather shoes, and sexual relations. Mishnah Yoma 8:1 lists six, counting eating and drinking separately.

Who does not have to fast?
Britannica notes that children under the age of bar and bat mitzvah - thirteen for boys, twelve for girls - are not required to fast, though older children may fast partially in preparation. Chabad tells anyone who needs to eat to consult a medical professional and a rabbi rather than deciding alone.

Why is the 1973 war called the Yom Kippur War?
Because Egypt and Syria attacked on the day itself, October 6, 1973, striking Israeli forces in the Sinai Peninsula and the Golan Heights. Britannica notes the date also fell during Ramadan, which is why the same war is known elsewhere as the Ramadan War or simply the October War.

Is Yom Kippur a federal holiday in the United States?
No. Federal law, 5 U.S.C. 6103, sets the federal holidays and Yom Kippur is not among them. Some school systems close regardless: New York City's public schools were closed on October 2, 2025, and its 2026-27 calendar closes them on September 21, 2026.
